Scarcely had any forecourt been entered, and behold, here the pairs of contending ball-players were redoubled amid the wheeling turns of their feints; here, amid the rivalries of dice-players' voices, was heard the frequent rattle of the clattering dice-boxes and dice; here books in abundance ready to hand (you would have thought you saw either the bookshelves of grammarians, or the wedge-rows of an Athenaeum, or the built-up cabinets of booksellers). So it was, however, that the volumes which were among the chairs of the ladies were found to be of a religious style, while those that were among the benches of the heads of households were ennobled with the buskin of Latin eloquence; though certain volumes of certain authors preserved, in unlike subjects, an equality of style: for men of like learning—here Augustine, there Varro, here Horace, there Prudentius—were read.

2.9.5. Among whom Adamantius Origen, interpreted by Turranius Rufinus, was diligently examined by readers of our faith; and, as each had it at heart, we discoursed, judging various things—why he was disapproved by some of the chief mystics as a perverse and dangerous expositor, although he had been so translated to the word and the sense that neither did Apuleius transcribe the Phaedo of Plato so, nor Tullius the Ctesiphon of Demosthenes so, to the use and rule of Roman speech.

2.9.6. While each of us was busied with these studies, as it had pleased, behold, one came from the head cook to warn that the time pressed for refreshing our bodies; whom indeed, a messenger keeping the increments of the hours by the spaces of the water-clock, the departing fifth hour proved to have entered fittingly. We lunched, briefly yet abundantly, after the senatorial manner, whereby it is inbred and established that many viands be set on in few dishes—though the banquet was varied by foods now roasted, now in sauce. Amid the drinking, little tales, by the knowing of which we were made merry and instructed; for, woven in a twofold strand, gaiety and skill accompanied them. What more? Holily, beautifully, abundantly we were received.

2.9.7. Then rising, if we were at Vorocingus (this was the name of one estate), we carried our foot back to our baggage and lodging; if at Prusianum (so the other farm was called), we cast Tonantius and his brothers, the choicest princes of our noble coevals, out of their own couches, since not easily could the furniture of our beds be carried about so often. The midday torpor being shaken off, we rode a little while, that we might the more easily whet our palates, sluggish with food, to a dinner-time hunger.

2.9.8. Each host had baths in process of building, neither in use; but when the throng of my followers and servants, drinking-companions—over whose brains the hospitable bowls, too deeply plunged, lorded it—had ceased to drink even a little, a pit was quickly dug near a spring or river, into which, when a heap of heated stones chanced to be let down, the trench, kindling, was covered over with a vault woven into the form of a hemisphere from flexible hazel-rods, yet so that, with Cilician hangings thrown over, the open intervals of the rods were darkened, the light shut out, to drive back the rising vapour which is struck off the flaming flints by the sprinkling of the boiling water.

2.9.9. Here the hours were drawn out for us not without salt and jesting talk; among which, the place being filled and wrapped with the breath of the hissing mist, a most healthful sweat was drawn out; when which, poured forth as it pleased, we were thrust into the heated waters, and, dissolved by their warmth wiping away our crudity, we were afterward braced either by the cold of spring and well, or by the abundance of the river: since between the houses runs the river Vardo, which—except when, fed by melted snow, it grows pale—is red over its yellow gravel, and clear through its channel, quiet and pebbly, yet none the less productive of delicate fish.

2.9.10. I would tell of the dinners too, and those most richly dressed, had not the page set a limit to our loquacity which modesty does not apply; the recounting of which also would be pleasant in the telling, did we not blush to soil the back of the letter with wet pens. But since we ourselves are on the point of setting out, and it pleases us, by Christ's help, to visit you straightway, the dinners of friends will be more readily recounted to you at my dinner and yours—provided only that the completed spaces of the past week restore us as soon as possible to a longed-for hunger, since nothing is wont better to repair a stomach burst by gluttony than abstinence. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Hesperius, greetings.

2.10.1. I love in you that you love letters, and I strive everywhere, with most heaped-up praises, to honour the nobility of so great a diligence, by which you commend to us not only your own beginnings but our own studies. For when we see the talents of the young growing up into a discipline of this kind—for which we too withdrew our hand from the cane—we reap the most abundant fruit of our labour. Add this, that the multitude of the slothful has so increased that, unless even a very few of you vindicate the pure propriety of the Latin tongue from the rust of common barbarisms, we may soon lament it abolished and slain: so all the purple robes of noble speech will be discoloured through the carelessness of the crowd.

2.10.2. But of this elsewhere. Meanwhile receive what you ask. You ask that, if any little verses have flowed from me since we parted from each other, I should count them out to you as a kind of payment for the delays. I obey the word; for you are endowed, though young, with such maturity of mind that we are eager to humour you even before your elders. A church has lately been built at Lugdunum, which by the zeal of Bishop Patiens has reached the summit of the work begun—a man holy, energetic, severe, merciful, and one who, by abundant munificence toward the poor and by kindness, raises summits of good conscience no less lofty. At the request of the aforesaid prelate, then, I inscribed for the outer parts of this building a hasty poem in trochaic triplets, very familiar by now to me and to you.

2.10.3. For from the hexameters of the eminent poets Constantius and Secundinus the neighbouring sides of the basilica grow bright next to the altar; whom my modesty most of all forbids to be admitted to this page—a modesty which, as I tremulously publish my idle pieces, the comparison of better songs oppresses.

2.10.4. For just as nothing less becomes a new bride than a matron of honour fairer than herself; just as, if a man be clothed in white, every dark man is made darker; so my stalk of straw, however small it is, surrounded by mightier trumpets, grows cheap—which to be pronounced middling in place, lowest in merit and more contemptible, not only ignorance but arrogance brings about. Wherefore more justly do their epigrams gleam than these of mine, which I fashion only in imagination and, in a manner, in shadow. But to what end this? Rather let the beggarly stalk of the demanded song murmur on:

"Whoever you are who here praise the labour of Patiens,
our bishop and father,
may you, with your wish fulfilled, experience by supplication
the thing granted that you shall ask.

The lofty church shines, and is drawn neither to the left
nor to the right, but with the height of its front
looks upon the equinoctial east.
Within, the light gleams, and the sun
is so drawn to the gilded panelled ceiling
that it strays, one-coloured, over the tawny metal.
The marble, marked with varied brightness,
runs through the vault, the floor, the windows;
and beneath the varied figures
the springing green crust bends sapphire-blue stones
through the leek-green glass.

To this a threefold portico is joined,
proud with Aquitanian columns;
after whose model the more distant
courts enclose a second portico,
and the stony grove, far set among the columns,
clothes the middle field.

Here the highway sounds, here the Saône re-echoes,
here the foot-traveller and the horseman turn back,
and the driver of the screeching carts;
here the choir of bent bargemen
lifts to Christ, with the banks answering "Alleluia,"
the river boat-song.

2.10.5. Behold, I have obeyed your commands like a younger man: only do you take care to remember that I am to be repaid with multiplied interest; and that you may do this the more easily and pleasurably, you must read without dissembling, and crave to read without end; nor must you suffer your wife, soon to be happily led home, to turn you from this purpose; and you must be exceedingly mindful that once Marcia held the candles and candelabra for Hortensius, Terentia for Tullius, Calpurnia for Pliny, Pudentilla for Apuleius, Rusticiana for Symmachus, as they read and meditated.

2.10.6. Surely, if you complain that, besides oratory, in the fellowship of women your poetic talent and the file of your tongue, polished on the whetstones of frequent studies, is blunted—remember that often Corinna completed a verse with her Naso, Lesbia with Catullus, Caesennia with Gaetulicus, Argentaria with Lucan, Cynthia with Propertius, Delia with Tibullus. So it would clearly grant that, through marriage, occasion of learning is given to the studious, an excuse to the slothful. Therefore apply yourself, nor let the crowd of the unskilled cheapen literary pursuits with you; for it is so ordered by nature that in all arts the display of knowledge is the more precious, the rarer it is. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Rusticus, greetings.

2.11.1. If we were neighbours, according to the situation and spaces of our regions, and our mutual presence were not sundered from each other by the length of a vast journey, I would allow nothing to the rareness of my letters in the offices of our begun friendship, nor would I cease to build up, with diverse kinds of honours, the foundations once laid of an emulous friendship. But our settled habitation, separated for each of us by farther-stretching bounds, opposes itself to the conjunction of our minds—though indeed it will harm little hearts once bound together.

2.11.2. But nevertheless from the very separation of our common towns it comes that, although we are most friendly, the rareness of converse, coming from the long interposition of lands, we wish to transfer into a common fault, though, by reason of the difficulty of natural things, neither blame nor pardon ought to remain with us. Illustrious lord, the bearers of this letter, formed by the training of your discipline and bearing the modesty of their master's manners, I have admitted in good time, heard patiently, and dispatched suitably. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Agricola, greetings.

2.12.1. You did indeed send a skiff, swift and solid, large enough for a couch and now stocked with fish; and besides a steersman far skilled, oarsmen too sturdy and ready, who fly past the back of the adverse river with the same swiftness as they do downstream. But you will pardon me that I decline to come as your companion to the fishing when you invite me; for nets of grief, far stronger, hold me, because of those of mine who are lying ill—nets to be grieved over by friends and even by strangers. Hence I think that you too, if you are moved rightly by brotherly affection, at whatever point of time you take up this page, will think rather of returning.

2.12.2. Severiana, our common care, disturbed first by the assault of a slow cough, is now wearied by fevers also, and these growing worse through the nights; on which account she longs to go out into the suburb. Finally, when we were taking up your letter, we were already preparing to go out to the little villa. Wherefore whether you come or delay, aid our prayers with your orations, that, as she desires the air of the country, the very restoration may wholesomely follow. Certainly I, or your sister, suspended between hope and fear, believed that her weariness would be increased if we opposed the will of one lying ill.

2.12.3. So, by the leading of Christ, we are taking out from the heat and torpor of the city both ourselves and the whole household alike, and at the same time we shun the counsels of the physicians who sit by and disagree, who, too little learned and quite too zealous, most officiously kill many sick men. Indeed, by the right of friendship, Justus will be added to our company, whom, if it were lawful to jest in sad matters, I could easily convince to be trained rather in the art of Chiron than in that of Machaon. The more diligently, therefore, must Christ be asked and besought that the supernal power may heal a health whose cure our care does not find. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Serranus, greetings.

2.13.1. Marcellinus, an advocate, presented to us your letter—a man skilled, and one of friends—which, the salutation tasted in its first words, in the rest of its course, which indeed is large, contained the praises of your patron Petronius Maximus, the emperor; whom, however, you call most fortunate, more persistently or affectionately than rightly and truly, namely on this account, that he was carried up through the most ample titles of office even to the empire. But to such a sentence I never assent, that I should think those fortunate who stand upon the headlong and slippery summits of the commonwealth.

2.13.2. For it cannot be told how much, hour by hour, the life of those fortunate ones in this life bears of miseries—if indeed those are so to be pronounced who, like Sulla, presume this name for themselves: those, namely, who, having overstepped common right and law, esteem the highest power the highest blessedness, by this very thing the more wretched, that they too little understand themselves to be subject to a most restless servitude. For as kings lord it over men, so the desires of domineering lord it over kings.

2.13.3. Here, if we pass over the misfortunes of preceding princes or of those who followed, this peculiar Maximus of yours alone could be the greatest proof to us of these things; who, although he had ascended fearlessly to the prefectorian, patrician, and consular citadel, and, unsatisfied, had repeated the magistracies he had held as if in recurring orbits, yet, when he came with all his might to the precipice of the principal eminence, suffered a kind of vertigo of immense power under the crown, nor could he endure to be a lord, who had not endured to be under a lord.

2.13.4. In short, seek out in the aforesaid the grace, power, and long duration of his former life, and on the other side the origin, the whirlwind, the end of a principate a little more than two months long: assuredly you will find that the man was happier before he was named most happy. So he, whose feasts, manners, moneys, pomp, letters, offices, patrimonies, patronages flourished before, whose very spaces of life, in short, were so guarded that they were unfolded by the water-clocks set out hour by hour—he, named Augustus, and under this appearance shut within the Palatine thresholds, groaned before twilight that he had come to his wishes; and since, by the mass of cares, he was prevented from keeping the measure of his former quiet, he at once renounced the laws of his old rule and perceived alike that the business of a prince and the leisure of a senator cannot go together.

2.13.5. Nor did the future deceive him as he mourned; for whereas he had run through the other court honours most tranquilly, he ruled the court itself most turbulently, amid the tumults of soldiers, of the people, of the federates; which his end too betrayed—new, swift, bitter—stained with blood by the treacherous end of a Fortune long flattering, who struck the man, like a scorpion, with her last part. A man learned, and through the merits of his talent of quaestorian rank—certainly a great part of the good party—Fulgentius was wont to say that he had often heard from his mouth, when, hating the weight of empire, he longed for his old security: "Happy you, Damocles, who endured the necessity of a kingdom no longer than one luncheon."

2.13.6. For this Damocles, as we read, was by province a Sicilian, by city a Syracusan, and a familiar of the tyrant Dionysius. When he was extolling the goods of his patron, like everything else of course untried by him, with too great praises: "Will you," said Dionysius, "today at least at this table enjoy my goods alike with my evils?" "Gladly," he said. Then he at once enriches the joyful client—though astonished—his plebeian covering being snatched away, with a robe dyed in the shellfish of Tyrian or Tarentine purple, and sets him, gleaming with gems and pearls, on a golden couch and a silken tapestry.

2.13.7. And when, as he was about to dine, bread made from the Leontine harvest was given him after the manner of Sardanapalus, and besides choice viands were set on in choicer dishes, and the capacious gems foamed with Falernian, and the unguents grew warm in the icy crystals, and the dining-room, perfumed with cinnamon and frankincense, scattered foreign odours to the nostrils, and the garlands of flowers poured round dried his hair wet with nard—there began, above the back of him as he thus reclined, suddenly to be brandished a drawn sword-point from the panelled ceiling, which seemed about to fall, at any instant, into the throat of the purple-clad man; for, bound by a thread of horse-hair and so threatening by its weight, it bridled with its point the throat of the frightened man after the example of Tantalus, lest the food entering should go out through the mouth, through the wound.

2.13.8. Whence, after prayers mingled with weeping and manifold sighs, scarcely released and leaping out at a bound, he fled those riches and royal delights with that swiftness with which they are wont to be sought, brought back to the desires of the middling by fear of the highest, and taking sufficient care lest he should hereafter call or count happy one who, hedged about with arms and guards, and on that account brooding over plundered wealth, pressed by the steel, pressed the gold. Wherefore, toward a state of this kind, my lord brother, I know not whether it is agreed that the happy strive; it is at least plain that the wretched arrive. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Maurusius, greetings.

2.14.1. I hear that the vintage answers to your industry and our common wishes with a richer yield than the barren year threatened. Whence I suspect that you will tarry rather long in the district of Vialoscum, which in nearer times was called Martialis on account of the winter quarters of the Julian legions; in which place you have both a fruitful vineyard, and besides it an estate worthy of no small master, which detains you and your household with a manifold dowry of crops and of lodgings.

2.14.2. So if, with barns and store-rooms or larder filled, you intend to pass there, until the coming of the swallow or the stork, the snowy months of Janus and Numa in sooty leisure or in tunicked quiet, the causes of our delays in the town—of little profit—will likewise be at once cut off, so that, while you enjoy the country, we may enjoy you; to whom, as you recognize, a field with ample revenues is no more at heart or a pleasure than a neighbour, my equal, with good morals. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Avitus, greetings.

3.1.1. By many bonds of affection, from earliest boyhood right up to the time we came into youth, the care of mutual goodwill had knit us together: first because between our mothers there was the highest tie of joined blood; then because we ourselves, born at the same times, used the same masters, were trained in the same arts, took our leisure in the same sports, were advanced by the same princes, and served out the same terms of military pay. And—what for enlarging friendships is more powerful and effective than these—in each and every person, whether equally to be sought or to be guarded against, we strove with a like parity of judgement.

3.1.2. On account of all which (I pass over our shared conscience, which inwardly is far more excellent and eminent for you) the multitude of public actions run through together had greatly coupled our wills. But—what must be confessed—when the engines of love had long been raised on either side, you yourself placed the precious summit, enriching with a most opportune gift the church of the little township of Auvergne, over which, though undeservedly, I seem to be set; to whose possession you contributed very greatly by the suburban estate of Cuticiacum, deigning to enrich the brotherhood of our profession no less by the nearness of the place than by its revenue.

3.1.3. And although you two seem to be the joint heirs of a sister's inheritance, yet, by the example of your faith, your surviving sister was stirred to the imitation of a good work. So to you, by heaven's justice, is repaid the merit of your own deed, the incitement of another's; whence it comes that you are found most worthy to be one whom the Divinity exalts by an unusual kind of succession—which, however, has neither long deferred to enrich your religious devotion with hundredfold gifts, and which, as we trust, will no less readily bestow heavenly things, when it now pays the earthly. For the Nicetian inheritance, if you do not know, was the heavenly price of Cuticiacum.

3.1.4. For what remains, we beg that, as of our church, so also of our city, the care may be alike common to you—a city which, both formerly and now especially from this time, ought to belong to your patronage, or for the sake of your patrimony, of what merit that may be able to be, namely if your presence frequently visits it. Or believe the Goths, who often even disdain or give back their own Septimania, provided they may possess, even in its desolate ownership, the property of this enviable corner.

3.1.5. But it is right, by God presiding, for you, set in the midst between them and the commonwealth, to conceive quieter things in your mind; for, even if they, the bounds of the old frontiers being broken, with all their force or with the whole mass of a turbulent possession push forward their boundaries to the Rhône and the Loire, yet your authority, by the dignity of its judgement, will so moderate each party that ours may learn what it ought to deny when it is asked, and the adversary may cease to demand when it is refused. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Constantius, greetings.

3.2.1. The people of Auvergne salute you, whose small huts you, a great guest, filled—not ambitious in your retinue but to be courted for your affection. Good God, what joy it was to the afflicted when you set your holy foot within the half-ruined walls! How thronged you were, beset by every order, sex, and age! What a balance of salt in your speech toward each! How gracious the boys, how courteous the young men, how grave the old men measured you! What tears, like a father of all, you shed over the houses thrown down by fire and the half-burnt dwellings! How you grieved over the fields buried with unburied bones! What was then your exhortation, what the spirit of one urging restoration!

3.2.2. To this is added that, when you had found the city emptied no less by civic feud than by barbarian incursion, by persuading peace to all you restored to them affection, and them to their fatherland. And as, at your warning, they returned no less to one counsel than to one town, the walls owe you the people brought back, the people brought back owe you their concord. Wherefore they reckon you altogether their own, themselves altogether yours; and—what is your greatest glory—they are by no means deceived.

3.2.3. For it is set before the minds of each, day by day, that you, a person grave with age, frail with infirmity, sublime in nobility, venerable in religion, by the plea of love alone burst through so many bars, so many opposed difficulties of coming—namely, the length of the journeys, the shortness of the days, the abundance of snows, the scarcity of fodder, the breadth of the wastes, the narrowness of the lodgings, the gulfs of the roads, either rotten with the wet of rains or rough with the dryness of the frosts; and besides, either embankments rough with stones, or rivers slippery with ice, or hills rugged in the ascent, or valleys scraped bare by the constant fall of landslides. Through all which discomforts, since you were not seeking private comfort, you carried back the public love.

3.2.4. For what remains, we pray God that, the goals of your life being advanced according to your wishes, you may unweariedly seek, gain, and bring back the friendships of good men, and that the affection which you leave behind may follow you; and that the favours begun through you, wherever they be, may long be repaid to you—both the foundations and the summits. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Ecdicius, greetings.

3.3.1. If ever, now most of all you are longed for by my Arvernians, over whom love of you holds monstrous dominion—and that multiplied for many reasons: first because the land that bore him rightly usurps to itself the chief part in a man's affection; then because in your age you are almost the only mortal who made his fatherland feel no less longing before his birth than joy at his birth. The witnesses of these assertions are the times of your mother's travail of old, which, as the conception advanced, were numbered with the concordant prayers of the citizens.

3.3.2. I pass over those things common indeed, but no slight incitements of affection—the clods of this turf crept over by you; I pass over that here you first broke these grasses in your walking, these rivers in your swimming, these woods in your hunting. I pass over that here you first had ball, dice-tower, hawk, dog, horse, and bow for your sport. I omit that here, for the favour of your boyhood, the studies of letters flowed together from all nations, and that what was once owed to your person—that the nobility, about to lay aside the scale of Celtic speech—was imbued now with the orator's pen, now even with the measures of the Muses.

3.3.3. This kindled the affection of all toward you chiefly: that those whom you had once compelled to become Latins, you henceforth forbade to be barbarians. For it can never slip from the breasts of the citizens, what manner of man, and how great, all ages, orders, sexes lately beheld you from the half-ruined embankments of the walls, when, the intervening plains being traversed in the opposite direction, and accompanied by a fellowship of scarcely eighteen horsemen, you crossed through some thousands of Goths in mid-day no less than in mid-field—a thing posterity will hardly believe.

3.3.4. At the rumour of your name and the sight of your person, amazement overwhelmed a most practised army, so that, for wonder, the leaders of the enemy party did not know how many accompanied themselves and how few you. The whole battle-line was at once drawn up onto the brow of a steep hill, which, though it had first been applied to a siege, when you were seen was not deployed for the encounter. Meanwhile you, with all the best of them slain—those whom not cowardice but audacity had made last in the column—none of your own being missed in so great a contest, alone possessed the plain, however open it was, when the battle did not give you so many comrades as the table is wont to give guests.

3.3.5. From here, now brought back at leisure into the city, what offices, applauses, weepings, joys went forth to meet you, prayers rather attempt to conjecture than words to unlock; since one might see, in the crowded courts of a most capacious house, that very most happy ovation of your thronged return, while some snatch your dust with kisses, some take the bridle fat with blood and foam, some lay back the supports of the riding-saddles wet with sweat, some unbuckle the bands of the bending plates for your helmet about to come off your head, some are entangled in unfastening the knots of your greaves, some count up the toothed sides of the swords blunted with slaughter, some with livid fingers measure the rings of the breastplates pierced by cut and thrust.

3.3.6. Here, though many, dancing for joy, clung to the embraces of their own, yet upon you the greatest rush of popular gladness was heaped; and at last you had come into a crowd unarmed indeed, but from which not even armed could you extricate yourself; and you bore, with elegance no doubt, the absurdities of those who congratulated you; and while you were torn apart by the tumultuous embrace of those rushing in, you had come to such a condition, most loving interpreter of public love, that it was necessary for you to return a richer gratitude to him who had done you the freer injury.

3.3.7. I pass over next that you gathered, by private forces, the appearance of a public army, aided from outside by the small resources of greater men, and that you checked the unbridled forays of the enemy by chastising their ravages. I pass over that, with some surprise attacks, you slaughtered squadrons in their bands, scarcely two or three of your own being missed after the battle, and brought so much calamity, by unexpected contests, on the unconquered adverse party that they planned, by a more shameful counsel, to hide the great number of their slain. Since those whom the hurried night had forbidden to bury, they left with their corpses beheaded, as though it were a smaller token to be recognized by their hair than to have sent away the long-haired man truncated.

3.3.8. And after, the light returned, they understood that the theft of their own ruin had been laid bare by a cruel cheapness, then at last they were openly occupied with funeral offices, hiding the disaster no more by fraud than the fraud by haste; yet so that they neither entombed the bones with a mass of hurried turf, to which, neither washed, did they grant garments, nor, clothed, sepulchres—paying such just rites justly to the dead. The bodies lay everywhere, carried together in dripping wagons, which, since you pressed unceasingly upon the stricken, were hastily shut up in kindled dwellings and buried with the funeral fragments of the gliding roofs.

3.3.9. But why do I prattle of these things a little more than is just—I who have presumed not to weave a complete history of your labours, but to make a memorial in part, that you might the more believe the prayers of your own people, to whose ailing expectation no remedies will heal more wholesomely and swiftly than your arrival? Therefore, if you yield anything to the entreaties of our countrymen, make haste straightway to sound the retreat into your fatherland, and quickly take away your constant attendance from the dangerous familiarity of kings, whose intimacy each most experienced man rightly compares to the nature of flames, which, as removed a little from themselves they give light, so brought too near themselves they burn. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Felix, greetings.

3.4.1. Gozolas, a Jew by birth, a dependant of your eminence—whose person would be at heart to me also, were not his sect a thing of contempt—delivers my letter, which I wrote out grandly anxious; for the arms of the nations poured around us terrify our town as a kind of barrier of their frontier. So, set in the midst, a lamentable prey of peoples that rival one another, suspected by the Burgundians, neighbours to the Goths, we lack neither the wrath of attackers nor the envy of defenders.

3.4.2. But of this elsewhere. Meanwhile, if at least with you things are right, it is well. For we are not of such a breast that, although we ourselves are punished with open penalties on account of the hidden things of our crimes, we should not wish things to go prosperously even anywhere; for it is certain that he is no less a captive of vices than of enemies who has not, even amid evil times, kept good wishes. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Hypatius, greetings.

3.5.1. If the distinguished Donidius, an admirer and reverer of your character, had had regard only to the reckoning of his own domestic advantage, your good faith would suffice abundantly and to spare for his interests, even if no intercessor were added. But he was led by his love for me to make me request what he had himself by his own means obtained; and so now this addition accrues to your honour, that we are made two debtors, although yet one of us obtains the benefit.

3.5.2. He desires that the desolate half of the Eborolacan estate—even before the barbarians desolate, and which now looks to the rights of a patrician house—be joined, by your support, to his own right. Nor is he led to this bargain by the spur of cupidity, but by regard for ancestral remembrance. Since the whole of that farm looked, as the dominion of his own family, to the death of his stepfather, who lately departed this life; but now the man, not coveting another's, sparing of his own, is distressed by the loss of an old possession alienated from himself not so much by the damage as by the shame; and that he should attempt to redeem it, he is compelled not by the vice of avarice but by the necessity of modesty.

3.5.3. Deign to grant to his wishes, my prayers, and your own character, that, by your patronage, he may attain to the entirety of that estate—of which, since his parents' property is known to himself and even crept over among the rudiments of his joyful infancy, as to have recovered it would be little profitable, so not to have earned it would seem too slothful. But I shall be so bound by your indulgence as if it profited my own property peculiarly—whatever my brother in age, my son in profession, my fellow-citizen in standing, my friend in good faith shall have received. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Eutropius, greetings.

3.6.1. If of our old fellowship in service, if of the favour renewed since then day by day, your good faith rightly remembers at present, assuredly you understand that, as you ascend to the summits of dignities, so we to those of our desires. For we all so congratulate you on your high office that we reckon raised through it no more your house than our friendship. Witness is that deliberation in which the incitements of my exhortation availed not a little.

3.6.2. By which you could scarcely be induced to join the prefecture to philosophy, when the wrestling-school of the Platonists, your fellows clinging to the doctrines of Plotinus, had snatched you into the profound leisure of an untimely quiet—of which discipline I then asserted that the free profession would be when you owed nothing to your family. For, moreover, that contempt of public service was thought nearer to sloth, to which men of the good party boast that they cannot, rather than will not, ascend.

3.6.3. Therefore—what it is right should be done in the first place—we give abundant thanks to Christ, who, as he hitherto adorned the state of your loftiness with the nobility of your parents, so now crowns it with a parity of titles; and at the same time, the hopes of our minds being raised, it is right henceforth to hope better things. Certainly there is a frequent saying of the provincials, that a good year is to be reckoned not so much from great fruits as from great powers. On which account it is yours, my honoured lord, to reward our expectation with suitable arrangements. For, mindful of your origin, the whole community of the nobles has persuaded itself that, so long as the family of the Sabini rules us, the family of the Sabiniani is not to be feared. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Felix, greetings.

3.7.1. It is long since you abstained from letters. So each of us keeps his own custom: I prattle, you keep silence. Whence, too, a man distinguished in the other offices of good faith as you are, I reckon it a kind of virtue that you cannot be wearied by so much leisure. Will you indeed never be moved by regard for our old intimacy, so that at last you may draw back your foot from the purpose of continued silence? Or do you not know that not to answer a chatterer is an affront? You keep silence, whether amid libraries or amid law-gowns, and expect from me the office of beggarly speech, who, if you well perceive, have for writing rather facility than means.

3.7.2. At least let even our fear make matter for your pen, and remember to load the hands of travellers with papers, that the care of friends may be relieved; and hasten to tell whether, by God going before, the quaestor Licinianus has opened to our mutual alarm any door of security. He is indeed a person, as they report, greater in his coming than in great expectation, more sublime in inspection than in report, and remarkable for all the gifts of fortune and of nature.

3.7.3. His censorship is supreme, his courtesy equal, and his prudence and good faith befitting both the man sent and the man sending; nothing affected or feigned, and to the weight of his words a true severity rather than an imitation of severity; and not, as very many, who, when they allege things entrusted to them distrustfully, wish to seem to have acted more cautiously; nor yet of that number, as they say, who, peddling the secrets of the princes who direct them, court the barbarians, that things may go well rather with the envoy than with the embassy.

3.7.4. This tenor of the man's character favourable rumour has brought us. Send word swiftly, if indeed the deeds square with the sayings, that for so long they may take breath from their sleepless station whom from the walls' watches neither a snowy day nor a moonless and stormy night persuades to sound the retreat; because, even if the barbarian withdraws into winter quarters, they rather put off than abandon the dread once rooted in their hearts. Soothe us with prosperous things, since our cause is not so far from you as our country. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Eucherius, greetings.

3.8.1. I revere the ancients, yet not so as to set after them the virtues or merits of my coevals. Nor, if the Roman commonwealth has flowed down to these extremities of misery, so that it never rewards those zealous for it, do my ages on that account fail to bring forth Bruti and Torquati. To what end these things? you ask. Of you, to you, is my speech, most effective sir, to whom the commonwealth owes what history praises as paid by the aforesaid men.

3.8.2. Wherefore let those ignorant of affairs suspend their rash judgements, nor persist either to look up too much to the men of the past or to look down on those of the present; since it easily becomes clear that the commonwealth delays its benefits, that you deserve them—although it ought not greatly to be wondered at, when a nation of federates not only uncivilly administers the Roman forces but even fundamentally uproots them, if of noble and military men, and warlike beyond either our party's hope or the adverse party's opinion, not so much the deeds as the rewards have been lacking. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Riothamus, greetings.

3.9.1. The custom of our speech is kept; for I mix complaint with greeting—not at all studying this, that my pen should be courteous in the salutations and harsh in the pages, but because there always befall things about which it is agreed that a man of my place or order is set at odds: if he speaks, he sins; if he is silent, he suffers. But I myself look upon the burden of your modesty, whose shame has always been this, that you should blush for the faults of others.

3.9.2. The bearer of this letter, humble, obscure, and despicable even to the loss of an innocent helplessness, deplores that his own slaves have been led away by the Britons who secretly solicited them. It is uncertain to me whether the charge is sure; but if, between persons set face to face, you untie the objections with even mind, I think this toil-worn man can prove what he objects—if, that is, amid sharp, armed, tumultuous men, defiant in valour, number, and fellowship, a man alone, unarmed, abject, a rustic, a stranger, a pauper, can be heard in equity and good. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Tetradius, greetings.

3.10.1. Our young men add very much of praise to their own character as often as, doubting about the merits of their affairs, they have recourse to the counsels of the skilled, as now the most distinguished Theodorus, noble at home indeed, but more highborn by the repute of a most modest manner of life, who, by my letter, sets out to your letter—that is, to the purest fount of knowledge—with laudable eagerness, not only to find there himself what he may learn, but perhaps also to bring back thence what he may teach.

3.10.2. To whom, against the powerful and the factious, if your skill did not abundantly aid him, the prudence of counsel would suffice. Answer, we beseech—unless, however, the joint prayers of both of us shall be reckoned by you a burden or a weariness—by your own judgement, on my testimony; and prop up the substance and the wavering cause of the suppliant with the wholesomeness of a healing reply. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Simplicius, greetings.

3.11.1. Even if so great an adversity attends our desire that even now you are grudged to our gaze, you are not on that account such a man, best of men, of whose character the things lofty in the telling should lie hidden from us; so do all our countrymen, and likewise our chief men, attend you with concordant praise as the most excellent head of a household of the best and most exact party.

3.11.2. There supports this verdict about you of good men either a son-in-law so chosen or a daughter so brought up; in whose union your prayers have brought you so happy a controversy that you may doubt whether you have prevailed by judgement or by training. But yet hence chiefly, both venerable parents, be secure: you surpass the rest for this reason, that your children have passed you by. Therefore grant pardon for the first letters, which, as not yet to have sent was sloth, so I fear lest to have sent be loquacity. Indeed our office will lack the blemish of talkativeness if, by the example of an answering address, you absolve the impudence of the present page. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Secundus, greetings.

3.12.1. The tomb of my grandfather, your great-grandfather, yesterday—alas the grief!—a profane hand had almost violated; but God was at hand, that so great a wrong should not be perpetrated. The field itself, long since filled both with the ashes of pyres and with corpses, had for a long time now received no trench; but yet the earth, which is drawn over the buried, had returned to its former level, stretched out, the heaps settling under the weight of snow or the long flux of rains: which was the cause that the corpse-bearers dared, with their funeral mattocks, to defile the place as though vacant of bodies.

3.12.2. What more? Already the turf was black instead of green, already fresh clods above the ancient sepulchre, when, chancing to be going to the city of Auvergne, I caught sight of the public crime from the brow of a neighbouring hill, and, hurling myself with loosened rein as much over level as over broken ground, and even thus impatient of the slightest delay, before I arrived, I checked the bold deed with a clamour going before me. While those caught in the crime hesitate whether to slip away or to stand, I came upon them too (I confess the error): I could not defer the punishments of the captives, but above the very covering of our old man I racked the robbers, so far as could suffice for the care of the survivors, for the security of the dead.

3.12.3. Moreover, in that I reserved nothing for our bishop, foreknowing my own case and his person, I took counsel for the common good, lest either this should be avenged more mildly than was just, or that should avenge more severely than was just; to whom, however, when I had communicated the whole order of the matter, as one making satisfaction from the road, the holy and just man gave glory to my anger, when I asked nothing more than pardon, pronouncing, after the manner of the elders, that men guilty of so great a rashness were seen rightly slain.

3.12.4. But lest anything in future should be permitted to chances, which we ought to shun by example, I ask that straightway, even in my absence, by your care but at my cost, the scattered heap may rise again into a mass, which a smoothed slab may cover. I have left with the venerable Gaudentius the price of the stone and the wage of the work. This song, indeed, which follows, I made the last night—not, I believe, an unsuitable one, since I was not a little intent on my journey.

3.12.5. Which I beg may be quickly set on the tablet, of whatever quality it is; but see that the stone-cutter make no fault in the marble; which fault, whether from industry or through carelessness, a malicious reader will ascribe to me rather than to the mason. But if, with pious zeal, you take care of what is asked, I shall give thanks as if nothing of praise or glory accrued to you also—you to whom, your uncle removed, the entire care of the present office would have remained, in the degree of kinship.

A late song, after uncles and a father,
I, a grandson not unworthy of his grandsire, have dedicated,
lest perchance in after time, O traveller,
not knowing the reverence due to the buried,
you should tread the earth that has not been raised.

Here lies the prefect Apollinaris,
who, after rightly governing the Gauls,
was received into the bosom of a mourning fatherland,
most wise and most useful,
a cultivator of country, of warfare, and of the forum,
and, by an example perilous to others,
free under tyrant lords.

But this is proved his greatest dignity,
that, cleansing his brow with the cross, his limbs with the font,
he first of the number of his fathers
renounced the sacrilegious rites.

This is the first glory, this the proud virtue,
to go before in hope those whom you join in honour,
and to surpass yonder, in merits,
those parents who here are equal to you in titles.

3.12.6. I know indeed that the quality of the epitaph does not answer to the learning of its author; but a skilled soul does not refuse musical funeral-rites. To you also it ought not to seem slow, that I, a third and fourth heir, pay it, since, the cycle of so many years being rolled round, we have learned that the great Alexander made offering to the shade of Achilles, and Julius Caesar paid the rites to Hector as his own. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Apollinaris, greetings.

3.13.1. I singularly approve, rejoice, and marvel that, from love of chastity, you flee the company of the unchaste, especially those with whom there is nothing weighed, nothing holy, in the seeking and prattling of foul things, and who, because by shameless words they defile the reverence of public ears, think themselves grandly witty. Understand that the chief standard-bearer of this vileness in our country is Gnatho.

3.13.2. For this whirlpool of a man is of the cobblers of fables, of the concocters of crimes, of the doublers of sinister opinions—talkative himself yet not witty, ridiculous yet not gay, arrogant yet not steadfast, curious yet not perspicacious, and, with his unbecoming, affected charm, the more boorish; courting present times, carping at the past, disdaining the future; of a benefit, if he is about to ask one, importunate in the asking, a disparager of what is denied, a cunning contriver of recasting what is received, querulous when dunned, garrulous when it is restored; but if he is to be asked, a feigner of readiness, a dissembler of the request, a vaunter of what he has lent, a publisher of what was hidden, a slanderer of the man who delayed, a denier of what was paid.

3.13.3. A hater of fasts, a follower of feasts; bringing forth a praiseworthy sentence not about one who lives well but about one who feeds well; among which things yet himself most avaricious, whom no good bread feeds so much as another man's bread, eating this alone at home, if he has sent ahead anything from the dainties snatched amid the storms of slaps. But surely the man's frugality is not in all to be passed over in silence, praiseworthy as it is: he fasts as often as he is not invited; but even so, with parasite's levity, excusing himself if he is invited, spying out if he is shunned, reproaching if he is shut out, exulting if he is admitted, biding his time if he is beaten.

3.13.4. When he has reclined at table, he is straightway carried, if he eats slowly, into rapine; if he is quickly filled, into tears; if he thirsts, into complaints; if he is made drunk, into vomiting; if he wearies others, into insults; if he is wearied, into furies—altogether like the filth of a sewer, which the more it is stirred, the more foul it is. So living, a pleasure to few, a love to none, a laughingstock to all; a burster of bladders and a breaker of canes; greedy of drinking, greedier of detracting; with rabid mouth alike breathing mire, foaming wine, speaking poison, he makes it doubtful whether the more rotten, the more drunken, or the more wicked he is to be esteemed.

3.13.5. But you say: the quality of his body colours the disgraces of his mind, and the appearance of his person deprecates the ineptitude of his mind—an elegant man, no doubt, and most graceful, whose person is to be admired by those who behold it. But in truth that person of his is more sordid and more deformed than a funeral corpse which, the torches applied, half-burnt, and presently, the pile of brands settling, rolled off, even the by-now disdainful undertaker shudders to give back to the pyre. Besides this, he carries eyes that lack the light, which, in place of a Stygian marsh, roll tears through the darkness.

3.13.6. He carries ears too, elephantine in their monstrousness, whose two-fold opening an ulcerous skin surrounds, with stony knots and tufaceous warts jutting out from their wet along the curved margin. He bears a nose too, which, since it is ample in its openings and tight along its ridge, so opens to horror that it is narrowed to smelling. He thrusts forth a mouth too, leaden in its lips, beast-like in its gape, festering in its gums, boxwood-coloured in its teeth, which a mephitic odour, breathed frequently from the hollow of the rotting molars, befouls, and which a belching from the dishes of yesterday is heaped up by the eructation of food and by the bilge of overflowing dinners.

3.13.7. He produces a forehead too, which by a most foul gesture folds the skin and stretches the brows. He nourishes a beard too, which, now growing grey with age, yet is made black by Sulla's disease. In short, the whole face of the wretch is so pallid as though, hour by hour, saddened by ghostly shades. I pass over the rest of his bulk, bound by gout, dissolved by fatness; I pass over his brain, furrowed with frequent weals, which it is agreed is covered little more by hair than by scars; I pass over that, for the shortness of his neck, the joinings of his shoulder-blades cling to his back-turned occiput.

3.13.8. I pass over that honour has fallen from his shoulders, grace from his arms, strength from his upper arms; I pass over his gout-ridden hands wrapped in the greasy rags of poultices as if in boxing-gloves. I pass over that, fenced about at his captive sides by the goatish and sour caves of his armpits, he makes deadly, with the fanned plague of a twofold Ampsanctus, the nostrils of those who sit about. I pass over that his breasts, broken by the weight of their fat, hang down—breasts which it would be foul on a man's chest even to jut out, but these to have fallen like a mother's udders. I pass over that the hanging nets of his curved belly afford, to his genitals—since they are feeble, twice shameful—a covering more shameful by their foul wrinkles.

3.13.9. Now why should I here recall his back and spine? Although, bursting out from the joints of its vertebrae, the curvature of the ribs weaves the chest's coffer, none the less this whole branching frame of bones lies hidden under one, as it were, sea of an overflowing abdomen. I pass over the corpulence of his loins and buttocks, compared to whose thickness the belly is reckoned slender. I pass over his dry and bandy thigh, his huge knees, his delicate hams, his horny legs, his glassy ankles, his small toes, his large feet; and although he bristles with such distorted lineaments, and through a manifold pestilence is bloodless and half-alive, and neither, carried, sits, nor, supported, walks—yet he is more execrable in his words than in his limbs.

3.13.10. For although he labours under an itch of dishonourable speech, yet he is chiefly to be guarded against in the secrets of patrons, of whom he is a praiser in prosperity, a betrayer in doubtful times; and if the reckoning of the moment solicits to publish the hidden things of one's intimates, presently through this Spartacus whatever things are shut are broken open, and whatever are barred are unbarred; so that those houses which he cannot assail with the engines of open enmity he attacks with the mines of clandestine treachery. By this contrivance our Daedalus builds up the summit of friendships, who, as he is joined to his comrades like a Theseus amid prosperity, so afterward, like a Proteus, slips away from them amid adversity.

3.13.11. Therefore you will do according to my wish if you join yourself to the fellowship of such men not even in a first meeting—especially of those to whose prostituted and theatrical speech modesty sends ahead no reins, no bars; for those in whom, boasting without the brightness of honour, the unbridled tongue is polluted with the dregs of talkative petulance, have a conscience too most befouled. In short, it more easily happens that someone speaking serious things lives obscenely, than that one can be shown who is alike wicked in words and upright in character. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Placidus, greetings.

3.14.1. Although your own Gratianopolis holds you, yet I have learned, by the faithful report of old guests, that you deign to deem my trifles—whether finished in prose work or made tuneful by the poet's pen—worthy more than the reading of stored volumes. I rejoice in this very thing, that I have recognized your leisure to be occupied with my little papers; but I well understand that, with your character, it is not the effect of the work that strikes out this pleasure, but the author's affection; and therefore I owe the more, since you give to friendship the point of glory which you would deny to the composition.

3.14.2. But of the other disparagers of our study, what I should fully pronounce I have not yet deliberated. For he who seems to himself most learned re-reads sound and unsound composition with almost equal appetite, no more desiring the lofty that he may praise it than the despised that he may laugh at it. And in this way the knowledge, the display, the propriety of the Latin tongue is held in the greatest contempt by the verdicts of the idle, whose scurrility carelessness accompanies—wishing to read only that which it may carp at; so it does not use letters, in that it abuses them. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Probus, greetings.

4.1.1. The sister who is mine is the wife who is yours: hence between us there is the highest and chiefest tie of kinship—and that indeed a cousin's, not a brother's, brotherhood, which most often loves itself the more purely, strongly, and unmixedly. For, the strife over property between brothers having first been laid to rest, those who are now born of brothers contend with one another over nothing; and hence often the affection among cousins is greater, because the feud ceases with the division, while the affection does not cease from the common seed. A second bond of minds was added to us from the parity of our studies, since we feel, blame, and praise the same things in letters, and any composition pleases or displeases us alike.

4.1.2. Although I claim too much for myself in weighing my own judgement against yours. For who of the young or the old does not know that you were my own particular master, when you seemed to be a master shared by us in common—and that, whatever the heroic poet made lofty, the comic playful, the lyric tuneful, the orator declamatory, the historian truthful, the satirist figurative, the grammarian regular, the panegyrist applaudable, the sophist serious, the epigrammatist wanton, the commentator lucid, the jurist obscure, in their manifold ways, that you handed on to each in every way—unless someone lacked talent and himself? Good God! How our fathers gloried in this, when they saw that by Christ's help you could teach, I could learn; and that not only did you do what you could, but you also willed what you did, and were therefore pronounced good no less than skilled!

4.1.3. And truly, within the household of Eusebius, a certain mint of such disciplines had received you, formed on whose philosophic anvil you now unfolded to us the various reckonings of things and of words, with even the very man who had taught you approving; now, as Plato the disciple, now well-nigh superior, under Socrates, so you, under our Eusebius, a craftsman dialectician, atticized amid the Aristotelian categories, while he still seasoned our age—mobile, tender, raw—now boiling it down with chastening severity, now flavouring it with the wholesomeness of his precepts.

4.1.4. But of what kind, good God, and how precious, were these things—which, if anyone, to play the philosopher, were to carry off either to the marsh-dwelling Sygambri, or to the Caucasus-born Alani, or to the mare-milking Geloni, the horny hearts and icy fibres of those bestial and rigid nations would beyond doubt be softened and thawed, nor would we laugh at, despise, and dread their ferocity and stupidity, which, after the manner of beasts, plays the fool, grows brutish, and is inflamed.

4.1.5. Therefore, since both affinity and studies have joined us, I pray, in whatever place you are, that you keep the rights of friendship unshaken, and that long, even if we are absent in dwelling, we may be present in affection: whose unviolated part, so far as concerns you, shall by us be made everlasting for an age, if any of life remains. Farewell.
Claudianus to Sidonius the Bishop, greetings.

4.2.1. If it were possible to be done that I should meet you, my lord, even sometimes and a little, I should not inquire from anywhere the wishes or needs of any persons that could be of use to me in the matter of my due; since the power of revisiting is, in many ways and by wretched causes alike, cut off. Indeed the means of writing either rarely is fittingly at hand, or is not at hand at all. Whether these very things are pardonable or not, you yourself will have judged.

4.2.2. Moreover indeed, that very often your writings are imparted to others, who neither seek that very thing as much as I myself perhaps do, nor deserve it more, I do not think is committed with impunity against the laws of friendship. This, too, I shall make a grievously silent reproach: that those little books which you do not refuse to be ennobled with my name you have never imparted by any rescript. But perhaps you have no empty time, which you, a little, might spend upon a very great friendship.

4.2.3. With what business do you ever swell, anywhere, in which you are entangled, but that it turns back to the advantages of others? When by entreaty you appease God, you reconcile the same not only to friends but to strangers also. When you search out the mysteries of the heavenly scriptures, the more studiously you imbue yourself, the more abundantly you pour out learning into others. When you lavish your wealth on the uses of the needy, you indeed take counsel chiefly for yourself, but for others also. Accordingly, nothing—plainly, assuredly nothing—is so unfruitful of all your actions that it bears rich fruit to you alone and not to many others with you.

4.2.4. No occasion, therefore, of anyone's impediment can be alleged even falsely, why I myself, your special and intimate friend, should bear no fruit from my special one, from whom strangers too, very many, take much; but, as I suppose, after the form of the evangelical giver, what you do not give to a hungry friend you will give to a shameless knocker. Moreover, if you still grow hard as usual, I shall do something you will regret, since, if you sin further by keeping silent, I shall straightway avenge myself by writing; for it is without doubt that you are as much to be punished by my writing as I myself am punished by your silence. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Claudianus, greetings.

4.3.1. You pronounce, my honoured lord, that an offence is committed against the rights of intimacy, in that, as regards the greeting owed you, I long abstain from pen and tablets, and that henceforth no palms of travellers has my paper burdened, which should impart to you the homage of an earnest salutation. You conjecture these things beyond what is fair, if you reckon that any mortal—who yet has it at heart to converse in Latin—is not afraid when, written, he is brought into the examination of your ears; of your ears, I say, to whose skill—if the prerogative of the ages run down to this time does not overwhelm me—I would not match the thunderbolt of Frontonian gravity or of Apuleian weight, beside which the Varros, whether of Atax or of Reate, the Plinies, whether the uncle or Secundus, set at present would play the rustic.

4.3.2. This judgement of mine is supported by that volume which you, most rich in the knowledge of things and of words, published on the state of the soul. In which, while you make a preface to my name, I received this gift above all: that the fame of my person, which it was not worth the labour to make famous by the titles of its own books, was perpetuated by the benefit of yours. But what, great God, and how great a work that is—shut up by its subject, conspicuous by its declamation, blocked by its proposition, unlocked by its disputation; and, although thorny by reason of the hooked points of its syllogisms, yet softened by the flower of a vernal eloquence!

4.3.3. There the words are new, because old, and compared with which even the style of the old literature might rightly be made to seem antiquated; and—what is more precious—that whole composition is so terse, cut into clauses, that it flows on; which, ample in matter and strict in sentences, you would feel teaches more than it speaks. In short, this was once, and not unjustly, reckoned the chief eloquence, whose care—comprising many things in few—was rather to fill the cause than the page.

4.3.4. But truly in your books, what manner of thing is this too, that a continuous maturity admits tenderness, and inserts a seasonable sweetness amid its censure, so that it suddenly fosters the reader's attention, wearied through the threshed-out members of the disciplines of philosophy, with pleasurable digressions, as with certain harbours of its own sea? O book powerful in many ways, O eloquence not of a thin but of a subtle wit, which neither swells with hyperbolic gushings nor is thinned by depressed tapinosis!

4.3.5. Besides this, a unique and singular learning, remarkable in the assertion of diverse matters, whose custom it is to philosophize about each art with the masters of each, and which, if chance demands, does not refuse to hold with Orpheus the plectrum, with Aesculapius the staff, with Archimedes the rod, with Euphrates the horoscope, with Perdix the compasses, with Vitruvius the plumb-line; and which has never ceased to investigate with Thales the seasons, with Atlas the stars, with Zetus weights, with Chrysippus numbers, with Euclid measures.

4.3.6. In short, no one in my age was able so to affirm what he wished; since, while he exerts himself against the man he speaks against, he rightly claims for himself the token of the character and studies of both tongues: he perceives like Pythagoras, divides like Socrates, unfolds like Plato, involves like Aristotle; like Aeschines he flatters, like Demosthenes he is angry; he blooms like Hortensius, he burns like Cethegus; he urges like Curio, he delays like Fabius; he feigns like Crassus, he dissembles like Caesar; he advises like Cato, he dissuades like Appius, he persuades like Tullius.

4.3.7. Now if one comes for comparison to the most holy fathers: he instructs like Jerome, he destroys like Lactantius, he builds up like Augustine; he is exalted like Hilary, he is humbled like John; like Basil he rebukes, like Gregory he consoles; like Orosius he flows, like Rufinus he is restrained; like Eusebius he narrates, like Eucherius he stirs; like Paulinus he provokes, like Ambrose he perseveres.

4.3.8. Now indeed, if you ask what I think of your hymn: it is concise, copious, sweet, exalted, and it surpasses any lyric dithyrambs whatever in poetic charm and historical truth; and this is your own peculiar excellence in it, that, the feet of the metres being kept, the syllables of the feet, and the natures of the syllables, a poor verse shuts up, within the limit of its own space, rich words; nor does the brevity of the cramped song banish the length of the bedizened speech. So it is easy for you, with little trochees and littler pyrrhics, to surpass not only the molossic and anapaestic groupings of three, but even the four-fold junctures of epitrites and paeons.

4.3.9. The amplitude of the discourse outgrows the regular straits, and, like a great gem in a little gold, is scarcely contained and flashes forth like the spirit of a powerful horse, which, neighing—if it be held, by the law of the bridle, among wastes or rough ground—you understand to lack not so much the course as the field. What more? With me for judge, in both kinds of speaking neither will Athens be judged so Attic nor the Muses so musical—if only a too-long sloth has not taken from me the means even of judging. For while, under the cover of an imposed profession, I gradually seek a new manner of writing and unlearn the old by leaps, of a good orator I have nothing more left than that I have begun the more to be a bad poet.

4.3.10. Therefore, I pray, grant me the favour of this offence, that, mindful of myself for a little while, I more rarely mingle my dry little vein with your river. Your trumpet the whole world, so far as it extends, will rightly venerate, which it is agreed sang with a twofold felicity, since it found neither rival nor equal, when long ago it ranged through the ears and mouths of peoples, with me too carrying it about. But for us it is great audacity if we so much as prattle even among municipal and chair-bound orators or forensic ranters, who, even when they make their perorations—saving the peace of their betters—are, a most numerous crowd, occupied with most unlettered letters. For you, to whom, whether it please you to alternate free or bound speech, it is at hand to thunder both ways, are among the few whom kindly favour has loved—the few who shall be changed. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friends Simplicius and Apollinaris, greetings.

4.4.1. Here at last is my promise, your expectation—Faustinus, a father of a household noble at home, and now to be numbered among the greatest ornaments of a country shared by me and by him. He is my brother by the parity of birth, my friend by the likeness of minds. Often have I mixed serious matters with him, often jests too; and when, long ago, we were young men, in ball, in dice, in leaping, running, hunting, swimming, there was always to us both a holy contention, because affection remained. He is indeed somewhat older than I, yet only so much that it was not so much necessary to honour him as a delight to imitate him; and at the same time he himself was the more taken with this, that I understood myself to be loved by him rather than, as it were, courted. But by the advance of age and by his clerical service, when he was lovable before, he has now begun to be venerable.

4.4.2. Through him I send greeting, desiring, by Christ's help, to see you as soon as ever possible, if the public state permits. Wherefore, unless my desire seems burdensome, when the aforesaid returns, I shall be made acquainted with the state of your places and times. It is my fixed resolve to struggle through the opposing difficulties of private occupations, and to assign to the embracing of your hearts a duty however long—if, however (what even now we fear), no greater force confounds my arrangements.

4.4.3. Which it is not unfitting that you too, with brother Faustinus, as the times warn, deliberate, the matter being shared in conference. Whom, because I love, I have sent as one who loves me: if he answers to my judgement, I give thanks; moreover, since a good man is so judged by all, no man is the worse if he is not the best. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Felix, greetings.

4.5.1. A repeated greeting repeats its bearer: your Gozolas—may God grant that he be ours—is made for the second time the carrier of my letters. Therefore take away from both of us the shame we share; for if you still intend to keep silence, all will judge unworthy both me, to whom, and him, through whom, you ought to write.

4.5.2. Of the state of the times I now ask nothing, as before, lest it be a burden to your character, if you should signify adverse things, when prosperous ones do not follow. For since it does not befit you to send false reports, and likewise things to be wished for are wanting to relate, I flee to learn, by the tidings of good men, whatever that evil is. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Apollinaris, greetings.

4.6.1. Through Bishop Faustinus—bound to me no less by the fellowship of our old companionship than by the communion of his new profession—I had charged him by word with certain things to be guarded against: that you obeyed the word I rejoice. Since to the prudent it is inwardly inborn to avoid chance accidents, as likewise it is absurd, if the outcome opposes bold undertakings, to rise up into complaints and to turn the blameworthy issues of ill-advised arrangements into the defaming of the uncertain things of chance.

4.6.2. To what end these things? you say. I confess that I came too much in fear, lest, in a time of public fear, you should not fear, and the unshaken security, to this age, of a solid house should, for an untimely devotion, tremble at the tempestuous incursions of enemies, and the longed-for solemnity should begin to grow cheap among the tenderness of matronly minds—although in their breasts a native holiness has so measured out for itself a peculiar dwelling that, if anything had befallen them as they travelled, they would have rejoiced that they had endured a kind of martyrdom for a martyr. But I, to whom a lesser innocence makes greater diffidence, in this doubtful matter more gladly cling to the more cautious counsel, and am not with difficulty attached even to those who fear safe things.

4.6.3. Accordingly it was well done that you wholesomely deferred the doubtful journey, and that the state of so great a household was not within the cast of so great a die. And although the journey, once begun, might have prospered, yet I will by no means cast a white pebble for a counsel of this kind, whose rashness cannot be absolved except by the benefit of good fortune. The Divinity will indeed grant such vows to be advanced by worthy successes, and it will be permitted yet to remember these terrors amid the pleasantness of peace; but present things make those cautious whom future things shall see secure.

4.6.4. Meanwhile, for the present, the bearer of my letter sighs over certain damages inflicted on him through your Genesius. If you perceive that his complaint does not differ from the truth, grant, I pray, reformation to the man who convicts, swiftness to the stranger; but if punishable envy fans a calumny, in that vengeance has already gone before the man assailed, since the impudent suitor, worn out by cost and journey, sweats out the inconveniences of a suit rashly proposed—and this in the greatest harshness of winter and the highest heaps of snows and crusts of ice; which time, so far as concerns the followers of lawsuits, is indeed often short for a hearing, but always long for an injury. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Simplicius, greetings.

4.7.1. He is wont to say "You warn one already running" who is asked to do what he was going to do even unasked. You may inquire, perhaps, to what these prefatory words tend. The bearer of this letter earnestly entreats that he may carry to you a letter from me; his journey to you having been learned by us, he was in any case to be entreated for this very thing, even if he had kept silent; for it is your love rather than regard for the bearer that has drawn out this office. Moreover, this very man reckons that he, who granted, has earned a benefit, although again and again he received what he asked—but as one by no means recognizing the rights of our friendships.

4.7.2. Whence, although absent, I easily conjecture with what sudden amazement he will be struck when, deigned admittance for our sake, he understands that he has begged for my page more idly than for the delivery of it. I seem to see how all things will be new to a man not facetious to the point of envy, when, a stranger, he will be invited to a dwelling; alarmed, to conversation; a rustic, to gaiety; a pauper, to a table; and when, whereas among men coarse and gorged with the surfeits of onions this man plays the common sort, there he will be entertained with such courtesy as if among Apician feasters and Byzantine carvers he had hitherto belched.

4.7.3. Yet such and so great as he himself is, he has most abundantly made me partaker of a wished-for office. But although persons of this kind are often well-nigh despicable, yet in the cultivating of comrades by letters affection sustains much loss if it is recalled, by the meanness of the bearers, from the practice of more frequent address. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Evodius, greetings.

4.8.1. When the courier delivered to me your letter, which confessed to certain friends that you would soon set out for Toulouse at the king's command, we too were seeking the country far removed from the town. Me indeed, at first light, the occasion of your page scarcely shook out of the clinging crowd of escorters who delayed me, that I might be able to satisfy your charge at least as a traveller, at least as a horseman.

4.8.2. For the rest, at daybreak my household had gone before, to pitch the tent at eighteen miles, in which place many conveniences attend the loosening of one's little baggage: a cold spring on a wooded hill, a field below abounding in grass, a river before the eyes filled with many birds and fish; besides these, having a house joined to its bank—a new house, an old friend, to whose immense kindness you can set no measure, whether you yield or whether you refuse.

4.8.3. So, our people having gone ahead to this place, when we had halted for your sake, that a boy might be sent back more quickly even from the head of the village, already two hours after noon had easily passed, already the grown sun, with its increasing ray, had drunk up the moisture of the dewy night: the heat and the thirst grew strong, and in the profound serenity there was, against the heat, only such cloud as the dust made for cover. Then the length of the way, displayed to those who looked over the green plain of the open country—since for this very reason we were to lunch late—was groaned over; for though it did not yet wear the travellers down with labour, yet it already terrified them with expectation.

4.8.4. All which prefatory things, my lord brother, tend to this: that I may prove to you that I was not at leisure much, either in mind, or in body, or in time, when I obeyed your demands. So, to return now to the tenor of your letter: after the words which first brought a greeting, you asked this, that I should send an epigram ended in twelve verses, which could be fitted to a capacious shell, which through each side of its handles, to the outermost of its circuit, is hollowed from the wheel of its base with six flutings.

4.8.5. Of which I think you intend to inscribe either the curved bellies with single verses, or, by a better counsel—if that should be more becoming—the curved heads; and, polished with this adornment, you arrange to offer it to Queen Ragnahild, about to prepare an invincible patronage for your vows and likewise your acts. I serve your injunctions as best I can, not as I wished; but first pardon your own fault, you who gave more space to the silversmith than to the poet, since beyond doubt it did not escape you that, within the workshop of men of letters, if the metrical anvil has produced any song, it is polished by a file no less strong and rasping. But to what end these things, or the like? Behold, now sing:

The shell which on the fish-bearing Triton bears Cytherea—
let it not doubt, compared with this, to yield.
We beg you, incline a little while your mistress' height,
and, great patroness, receive a small gift,
and do not gladly spurn Evodius your client,
whom, making him great, you yourself will be the greater.
So may the son too, for you—whose father, father-in-law, and husband
is a king—be a king with his father and after his father.
Happy the waters, which, enclosed in the light of the metal,
yet foster the brighter face of their mistress!
For when the queen deigns to dip her countenance herein,
brightness is sent into the silver from her face.

If you are so far held by love of me that you do not blush to write these trifles, conceal the author, more rightly secure of your own part; for in such a forum, or Athenaeum, your dish will be more praised than my writing. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Industrius, greetings.

4.9.1. I lately visited Vettius, an illustrious man, and inspected his daily doings most thoroughly, and as it were at leisure. Which, since I found them worthy to be known, I have judged not unworthy to be reported. In the first place—what we shall rightly set before his other praises—the household keeps unimpaired a chastity equal to its master's; the slaves useful: the country ones obedient, the town ones friendly, compliant, and content with their patron; a table feeding the guest no less than the client; great kindness, and greater sobriety.

4.9.2. Those are the lighter things: that the man himself of whom we speak is second to none in training, watching, and parading horses, dogs, and hawks; the highest neatness in his garments, elegance in his belts, splendour in his trappings; a stately gait, a serious mind (the latter asserts his public good faith, the former his private dignity); a relaxation that does not corrupt, a rebuke that does not draw blood, and his severity of such a temper as is not loathsome but austere.

4.9.3. Amid these things, a frequent reading of the sacred volumes, by which, while eating, he more often takes the food of the soul; he frequently reads the psalms, more frequently sings them; and by a new kind of life he fulfils the monk, not under the little cloak but under the war-cloak; he abstains from the flesh of wild beasts, he gives himself to coursing; and so, secretly and delicately religious, he uses the hunt and yet does not use the venison.

4.9.4.
