His only little daughter, left as the solace of his widowhood after his wife's death, he rears with a grandsire's tenderness, a mother's diligence, a father's kindness; toward his household neither menacing in uttering speech, nor scornful in admitting counsel, nor too eager in investigating a fault; the state and condition of his subjects he rules not by lordship but by judgement; you would think that he does not possess his own house but rather administers it.

4.9.5. Which industry and temperance of the man, observed, I judged to pertain also to the instruction of the rest, if such a life were even superficially published to others—to whose following all men of our profession would, most usefully, be incited, besides the habit by which meanwhile one is set above the present age; for—be it said with the peace of my order—if there shall be only single good things in single men, I more admire a man of priestly quality than a priest. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Industrius, greetings.

4.10.1. I burst forth into a greeting, though late, my lord—I myself now for many years ungreeted—not daring to keep up the frequency of the old office, after the adversities of exile broke me, banished from the bounds of my native soil. Wherefore it is fitting that you too pardon those who blush, since it is fitting that the humbled follow humble ways, nor hold an equal constancy of intimacy with those to whom it might perhaps be shameless to spend more of love than of reverence. On this account, in short, I have now long been silent, and I bore it more patiently than gladly that you too were silent, when my son Heliodorus came hither.

4.10.2. But you used to say, though in mockery, that you stood, as it were, in awe of my eloquence. That excuse, even if it had been true, had passed away; since, after the little book I finished—which is too little polished—I weave the rest of my letters again in everyday speech, although, careful, I am not made better; for it is not worth so much to polish formulas that will lack publication. For the rest, if you restore the manner of your affection to the old course of our conversations, we too shall run back into the ruts of our old loquacity; and besides this, eagerly, by Christ going before, wherever you may be—provided only that my patron, now returned, indulge it—we shall fly to you, that friendship may be invigorated by deeds, which, unused in words, had grown torpid. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Petreius, greetings.

4.11.1. The loss of my age distresses me exceedingly, your uncle Claudianus being lately snatched from our eyes—I doubt whether they will hereafter behold any equal. For he was a man provident, prudent, learned, eloquent, keen, and the most ingenious of the men of his age, his place, his people, and one who unceasingly played the philosopher, his religion being kept safe; and although he did not nourish hair and beard, now derided, now even execrated the cloak and the club, yet from the college of his fellow-Platonists he was separated by habit and faith alone.

4.11.2. Good God, what a thing it was, as often as we came together to him for the sake of consultation alone! How he opened the whole to all at once, not doubting, not disdaining, reckoning it most pleasurable if perchance, by the labyrinthine insolubility of some questions that had arisen, the treasures of his knowledge were aired. Now if we had sat down in numbers, assigning to all the office of hearing, to the one alone whom we had perhaps chosen the right of speaking, man by man and in turn, not tumultuously, nor without the artful gesture of some figure, he would dispense the riches of his learning.

4.11.3. Then whatever he had said, we straightway met with the contrarieties of resisting syllogisms; but he repelled the rash oppositions of us all: and so nothing was received that was not weighed and proved. Hence also there was to him among us the greatest reverence, that he did not too ill bear with a sluggish docility in any. With him this was a pardonable fault; whence it came that his patience was praiseworthy to us without being imitable. For who would unwillingly consult a man about hidden things, from the fellowship of whose disputation not even the inquiry of laymen and the unskilled was rejected?

4.11.4. These few things of his studies; but for the rest, who could extol the rest with fitting praise—that, mindful in all things of the human condition, he consoled the clergy by deed and word, the people by exhortation, the bereaved by solace, the captives by ransom, the fasting by food, the naked by covering? And at the same time I resolve that to unfold more concerning these things is superfluous. For his own merits, by which he enriched a rich conscience, though impoverished in goods, he the more studied to conceal, in the hope of a future recompense.

4.11.5. . . . observing his elder brother, the bishop, most affectionately, whom he loved as a son, while he venerated him as a father. But that one too looked up to him greatly, having in him a counsellor in judgements, a deputy in churches, a procurator in business, a steward on the estates, a registrar in the tributes, a companion in readings, an interpreter in expositions, a tent-mate on journeys. So to each, by the other, the mutual offices of brotherhood were rendered, by a good faith even to the point of being an enviable example.

4.11.6. But why, intending to moderate our grief, do we rather supply fuel to the causes of grief? Therefore, as we had begun to say, for him now—as is that Maronian phrase—"to the thankless ash" (that is, to one who will return no gratitude) we have composed a dirge, sad and well-nigh sorrowful, with labour, because disuse of composition made difficulty—save that grief, heavy with weeping, kindled a mind by nature most slothful. This is his song:

Glory and grief of his brother Mamertus,
the singular pomp of admiring bishops,
to this turf Claudianus gives his limbs,
under whom as master a threefold library—
Roman, Attic, Christian—shone;
all of which, a monk in his green years,
he drank in by a hidden discipline;
orator, dialectician, poet,
expositor, geometer, and musician,
skilled to loose the bonds of questions
and with the sword of the word to cut the sects,
if any assail the catholic faith.
Here the modulator of psalms and the choir-trainer,
before the altars, his brother rejoicing,
taught the instructed companies to sound.
Here for the yearly solemnities he prepared
what readings should suit each season.
He was a bishop in the second rank,
relieving his brother of the episcopal burden;
for of the supreme pontiff's office
the one took the insignia, the other the labour.
But you, whoever you are who grieve, friendly reader,
as though of so great a man almost nothing remained,
spare to water the marble with wet cheeks:
the mind and the glory cannot be buried.

4.11.7. Behold what song, when I first arrived, I wrote over the bones of my soulmate brother; for then I was absent, when they were performing his funeral; nor on that account, however, did I altogether lose the most longed-for occasion of weeping. For while I chanced to be meditating it, my soul, bringing forth, loosed the reins to my tears, and I did at the epitaph what others did at the sepulchre. These things, then, I have written to you, lest perhaps you should think that we cultivate only the fellowship of the living, and that we should be at fault in your judgement, did we not always remember our friends who lack life equally as the safe. For even from this, that the imaginary good faith is scarcely preserved even to survivors, you will not think beyond what is fair, if you conjecture that they are very few who love the dead. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friends Simplicius and Apollinaris, greetings.

4.12.1. Good God, how conformable to a shipwrecking sea is the motion of our minds, since by the adverse whirlwinds of tidings it is confounded as by its own storm! Lately I and our common son were ruminating the wit of the Terentian Hecyra; I was sitting beside him as he studied, mindful of nature and forgetful even of my profession, that he might the more freely follow, with quickened docility, the comic rhythms; I myself too had in hand a play of like argument, that is, the Epitrepontes of Menander.

4.12.2. We were reading together, praising, and jesting; and—what are the common wishes—the reading took him, he took me; when suddenly a household boy stood by, with a long face. To whom we: "Why so?" And he: "I saw," he said, "a reader, Constans by name, before the doors, returning from the masters Simplicius and Apollinaris; he gave indeed the letters which he had received, but he lost those he had been given to bring back."

4.12.3. On learning which, the serenity of my gladness was straightway befouled by the cloud of overspread grief, and the contrariety of this news stirred up in me so much bile that for very many days I, inexorable, kept that most stolid blockhead himself from coming before my eyes, about to bear it ill if he did not deliver to me letters either any whatever or from anyone whatever—I say nothing of yours, which, while a mind sound and master of itself endures, will be judged by me, even if least frequent, most desirable. But after, by the interval of time, my anger gradually died down, I asked, the man being admitted, whether he had brought any word besides. He answered himself—though he was trembling and grovelling, and for guilt stammered with his mouth, was blind in his gaze—that all by which I could be instructed, by which I could be delighted, had been entrusted to the pages which had been lost. Wherefore have recourse to your tablets, unfold your parchments, and re-write what was written. For so long I admit with even mind that an unlucky chance should stand in the way of my desire, until it come to you by my speech that yours did not come to us. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Vectius, greetings.

4.13.1. Lately, at the request of the distinguished Germanicus, I inspected the church of Cantilla. He himself is easily first of those settled there, who, though he is now passing his twelfth lustrum, yet daily, with conspicuous habit and grooming, not only grows young but in a manner grows boyish again. For indeed his garment is close-fitting, his buskin taut, his hair cut to the likeness of a wheel, his beard, with the shears sunk to the skin within the hiding-places of his wrinkles, trimmed.

4.13.2. To this, too, by the supernal gift, a solid joining of limbs, unimpaired sight, an ample stride in his swift gait, gums of an uncorrupted, milky structure of teeth; his stomach does not turn, his vein is not inflamed, his heart is not struck, his lung does not gasp, his loin is not stiff, his liver does not swell, his hand does not soften, his spine is not bent; but, endowed with youthful health, he claims for himself, out of old age, reverence alone.

4.13.3. On account of which peculiar benefits of God, since between you great rights of friendship flourish—for you are neighbours—I beseech and warn that, by your counsel, to whose following he gives, through a great conscience, the greatest authority, he should not trust much to doubtful things, nor believe too much in too great a soundness, but at last, the profession of religion being seized, should rather grow strong by the forces of a rising innocence, and make himself, old in years, new in merits.

4.13.4. And since there is well-nigh no one who lacks punishable hidden things, let him be loosed, by openly making satisfaction, concerning those things which he remembers to have committed in secret. For the father of a priest and the son of a bishop, unless he is holy, is made like the bramble, which, sprung from roses and bringing forth roses, and amid begotten and begetting flowers, the harshness of the thorns, comparable to sins, fences about with its pricking. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Polemius, greetings.

4.14.1. Gaius Tacitus, one of your ancestors, a consular of the times of the Ulpii, reported in his history under the words of a certain German leader, saying: "Between me and Vespasian there was an old friendship; and, while he was a private man, we were called friends." To what does it look, you say, to preface these things? Namely, that you may remember that, at the time when you bear a public character, you ought always to be mindful of private favour. Nearly two years are now drawing to a close in which we rejoice that you are prefect of the praetorium of the Gauls—not by your new dignity but by our affection, still old—and we, if the adversity of Roman affairs allowed it, would scarcely endure it, were not single persons—I will not say provinces—amplified by various benefits through you.

4.14.2. And now, since what your means do not have modesty does not ask for, I should like you to say how kind you would have been in deeds, who hold out avaricious in words; for, compared with the skill of your kindred, you can surpass not only the Cornelian orators but the Ausonian poets too, if a new glory for your jurisdiction has suddenly taken you, who have hitherto played the philosopher: we too have borne some name and honour.

4.14.3. But if the humility of our profession is to be held in contempt, because to Christ, who is to heal human affairs and lives, we of our own accord lay open the squalid ulcer of rotting consciences—which, in the men of our order, even if something still reeks of negligence, yet now swells with nothing of pride—I would have you know that it is not, as it is before the president of the forum, so before the judge of the world; for as he who has not kept silent his own crimes before you is condemned, so with us he who shall have confessed the same to God is absolved. Whence it plainly appears that it is incongruous for him to be pronounced by your party too much a culprit, whose cause looks rather to another's tribunal.

4.14.4. Wherefore you will by no means be able further to pour out the threatening complaint of our grief, since, prosperous things succeeding, whether you forget or neglect the old favour, it is alike bitter. Accordingly, if you weigh future things as great, write to a clergyman; if present things, write to a colleague; and cultivate this virtue in yourself—if it is natural; if not, add it as something grafted—by which you may never disdain old comrades for the novelty of those who follow. For otherwise you will seem to use friends as flowers, welcome only so long as they are fresh. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Elaphius, greetings.

4.15.1. Prepare a manifold feast and most capacious banqueting-couches: by very many roads, by many throngs (so it has settled, in the fellowship of good men), one comes to you, since the time of the future dedication has become known to all. For the baptistery which you were once building, you write can now be consecrated. To which festival your vow, our ministry, the office of many, the cause of all the faithful solicits; since it is a thing of great example that, at this time, new summits of churches should be built by you, when scarcely another would dare to repair the old.

4.15.2. For what remains, we wish that, as you render your vows to our God through abundant years, so you may vow to render them—and that not only by a hidden religion, but by a manifest conversion; and, the state of the times being mitigated, may Christ indulge both my desire and that of the Ruteni, that you may be able to offer sacrifices also for those for whom you now offer altars.

4.15.3. For the rest, although the latest autumn now shortens the day, and surrounds the anxious ears of travellers with the crackling crash of leaves falling throughout the whole grove, and into the fortress to which you invite—girt as it is with Alpine crags—it is harder to ascend in the wintry season, yet we, with God going before, coming along the rugged sides of your mountains, shall fear neither the rocks below nor the snows above, although the deep declivity of the ridges must often be retraced by an embankment broken in a spiral; for, even if there were no solemnity, you yourself are sufficiently worthy—as is that Tullian phrase—"for whose sake Thespiae is visited." Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Ruricius, greetings.

4.16.1. I received through Paterninus your page, which it is uncertain whether it has more honey or more salt. For the rest, it shows this abundance of eloquence, smells of these flowers, so that it well appears that you profit not only by open but by stealthy reading too—although even this theft, which, deprecating, you confess about a copied little book, glory rather than pardon ought to regard; for what would you do without virtue, who do not commit even your very sins without praise?

4.16.2. But I gladly hear of whatever fraud has been imposed on me, absent as I was, and embrace it as a princely gift, that in some way I have endured an unharmed harm. For neither has what accrued to your use departed from our property, nor have you come to the increase of your knowledge through the loss of another's; nay rather, you yourself by right will not henceforth lack rich praise, who have, by a fiery wit, becomingly imitated the nature of fire—from which, if you wish to take anything away, it remains whole, and is wholly transferred. Wherefore now cease to be alarmed, and to believe a little wrongly about the character of a friend; for in this deed the wound of fault would the more pollute us, if the blow of envy should strike. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Arbogast, greetings.

4.17.1. Your friend Eminentius, my honoured lord, presented to me the lettered letters which you yourself dictated, filled with the cultivation of a grace shining threefold. Of which virtues the love is surely the first, which compelled you to deign to notice things humble in us—who are strangers, or who now desire to lie hidden; then your modesty, by whose impulse, while you tremble undeservedly, you praise deservedly; the third, your urbanity, by which you most wittily allege that you play the fool, and, filled from the fount of Quirinal eloquence, a drinker of the Moselle you belch the Tiber—so familiar with the barbarians, yet ignorant of barbarisms, equal to the ancient leaders in tongue and hand—but those whose right hand was wont to handle the pen no less than the sword.

4.17.2. Wherefore the pomp of Roman speech, if any anywhere still survives, once abolished in the Belgic or Rhenish lands, has settled in you; by whom, whether safe or making your peroration, even if at the very frontier the Latin rights have fallen, the words do not stumble. Wherefore, returning your greeting in turn, I greatly rejoice that at least in your illustrious breast the traces of fading letters have remained; which, if you continue by frequent reading, you will experience day by day that, by as much as men excel beasts, by so much the trained are to be preferred to rustics.

4.17.3. As for what you wish—that I, a wicked interpreter, should prattle something on spiritual pages—these things are more justly asked of priests near in place, advanced in age, famous in faith, well known in their work, ready in speech, retentive in memory, and, in short, more powerful by every gift of sublime merits. For, to leave aside the bishop of your city—a most consummate man, and by the conscience and fame of all virtues alike blessed—it is much more opportunely that, about any questions whatsoever, the renowned fathers and chief mystics of the Gauls are consulted by you—Lupus, set not too far off, and Auspicius, not a little near; to the airing of whose abundant learning not even your consultation suffices. Accordingly, that I have not obeyed in this part of your requests, pardon me—kindly indeed, but just too; for, if it is right for you to flee unskilfulness, it also befits me to shun boastfulness. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Lucontius, greetings.

4.18.1. You forget what you ask, and, on the contrary, if you enjoin anything, you remember it to the full. It is too long to recall what you and yours promised to me and mine about a quick return, of all which not even the least things have been fulfilled. Nay rather, when you were contriving your flight from us—whereby we thought you would return at holy Easter—no heavy baggage was led from the town to the estate, no wagons, no carriages were brought up to carry the loads.

4.18.2. And, that I may complain nothing of the fraud of the matronal party, which you carried off with your light impedimenta, both you and our common brother Volusianus were attended by a retinue scarcely of single clients and boys apiece; whereby you presently cheated the solicitude of those who followed you with the vain hope of returning soon. Certainly brother Volusianus, chancing to be going to the estates of Bayeux and about to range through the whole province of Lugdunensis Secunda, eluded our expectation under the appearance of a shorter journey.

4.18.3. And now you yourself, thus idling against your faith for many days, say that, if I have sportively made any trifles in metre afterward, they ought to be sent to you. I grant your injunctions, since you are worthy to read such things; for the very song which now slips from my hands is so rustic and so unpolished that you would think I send it, not to a country-house, but rather from a country-house.

4.18.4. The basilica of the holy bishop and confessor Martin, Bishop Perpetuus—a most worthy successor to so great a predecessor—has rebuilt much more capacious than the former which it was hitherto. It is, as they say, a great work, and to be named, which, made in honour of such a man, such a man ought to have made. The aforesaid priest compels me to inscribe on its walls this epigram, which you will review—being, as he is in these things, in whatever he demands, most imperious by the privilege of affection.

4.18.5. And would that the offering of this homage of mine in no way disfigure the pomp or the votive gifts of that mass—which I greatly fear will be otherwise, unless perhaps among all things beautiful the foulness of this epigram so pleases as a black mole on a white body, which indeed is wont so to cause laughter as to receive approval. But what more of this? Lay aside your shepherds' pipes yourself, and stretch out a hand to my elegy, since it limps on its foot.

Martin's body, venerable in all lands,
in which, after the times of life, honour lives,
a building first covered here with plebeian adornment,
which was not equal to its confessor.
Nor did it cease to burden the citizens with shame—
the great glory of the man, the scant grace of the place;
but the bishop who is reckoned sixth from himself,
Perpetuus, took away the long reproach,
removing the inner shrine of the modest chapel
and raising ample roofs with an outer house;
and there grew together, the strong patron granting it,
the building in space, the founder in merits—
a building able to contend with Solomon's temple,
which was the seventh wonder of the world.
For if that shone with gems, gold, and silver,
this surpasses all metals in faith.
Begone, biting envy, and let the former men be absolved,
let chattering posterity make nothing new or add nothing;
and, while Christ comes, who shall raise up all peoples,
let the summits of Perpetuus endure perpetually.

4.18.6. We have offered, as you see, what of a recent song was at hand; but no less than this, if you weave delays, will we shake the stars, about to use even satiric verses, if the matter demands—which you will falsely think are to be equalled to this song in mildness; for the nature of mortals blames some things more effectually, quickly, and ardently than it praises. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Florentinus, greetings.
4.19.1. You accuse both our delays and our silence; each is excusable; for both we come and we write. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Domnicius, greetings.

4.20.1. You, to whom it is frequently a pleasure to look upon arms and armed men, what delight, do we think, you would have conceived in your mind, if you had seen Sigismer, the royal youth, adorned in the fashion and dress of his people, as a bridegroom or suitor, seeking the praetorium of his father-in-law! Him a horse indeed, decked with trappings—nay, horses laden with radiant gems—preceded, or even followed; while yet this was seen there more becoming, that he himself, on foot, walked in the midst of his runners and footmen, flame-coloured with scarlet, ruddy with gold, milk-white with silk; then, to so great an adornment, his hair, of one colour with his ruddiness and his skin.

4.20.2. But the form of the chieftains and allies accompanying him was terrible even in peace; whose feet were bound, first, up to the ankle with hairy buskins; the knees, legs, and calves without covering; besides this, a high, close, many-coloured garment scarcely reaching to the bare knees; sleeves veiling only the beginnings of the arms; green cloaks bordered with crimson hems; their swords, hanging from the shoulder by overlapping baldrics, had girt their sides shut with studded skins. By the very adornment with which they were decked, they were defended.

4.20.3. Their right hands were filled with barbed lances and throwing-axes, their left part shadowed by shields, whose snowy light on the rims, and tawny on the bosses, so betrayed both their wealth and their zeal—everything altogether of this kind, that in the action of the nuptials the pomp of Mars seemed not less than that of Venus. But why these things at greater length? To such a spectacle your presence alone was lacking; for when I saw that you did not see the things which are beautiful to you, at that time I longed for the very impatience of your longing. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Aper, greetings.

4.21.1. There is indeed a chief prerogative of the father's side in showing one's lineage; but yet much is what we owe to our mothers too; for it is not right that anything in us be honoured the more meanly because we are the burdens of the one rather than the seeds of the others. But let the matter or reason of defining our origin be with the natural philosophers: let us pursue the point from which we set out.

4.21.2. Your father is an Aeduan, your mother an Arvernian. You are owed to the Aedui first—therefore not to them alone—even on account of that example of our Maro, by whose witness Pallas, thus reckoned an Arcadian because at once a Samnite too, could have moved against Mezentius, as a stranger, the arms of the Etruscans, had he not, mingled with a Sabellian mother, drawn thence also a part of his fatherland. Behold, you have a great proof, with the greatest author, that the region of one's mother too is to be reckoned a part of one's fatherland—unless you will judge that the poets lie even when they do not depart from history.

4.21.3. Therefore if the Arvernians in turn rightly claim for themselves at least a portion of you, patiently admit the complaint of those who long for you, who, through the office of one mouth, have poured out the secret of not one breast—whom imagine to be saying, openly and to your face: "What so great evil have we committed against you, ungrateful man, that for so many years you flee, as though enemy soil, the ground that once nursed you? Here we cherished your cradle; here we shaped the boastful limbs of your wailing infancy; here you were carried as the burden of citizens' arms."

4.21.4. Hence your grandfather Fronto, gracious to you, severe to himself, who could have been an example to those whom we have as an example; hence your grandmother Auspicia, who, after the death of your mother left you orphaned, paid alone the care of two; but your aunt too was from here, and from here was Frontina, holier than holy virgins, whom her mother feared, her father venerated—a girl of the highest abstinence, of the highest rigour, and with such great faith so fearing God that she was feared by men. Here, that you might be imbued with the liberal disciplines, the flourishing studies of the grammarian and the rhetor fostered you by a rivalling warning; whence you came forth not so meanly trained that it is permitted you not to love the Arvernians even on account of letters.

4.21.5. I pass over the peculiar pleasantness of the territory; I pass over that plain of the fields, in which without danger the gainful waves of the standing crops billow, which each industrious man, the more he frequents, the less he suffers shipwreck; soft to travellers, fruitful to ploughmen, delightful to hunters; which the backs of mountains gird with pastures, their sides with vineyards, the level land with villas, the rocky with fortresses, the shady with lairs, the open with cultivation, the hollow with springs, the precipitous with rivers; which, in short, is of such a kind that, once seen, it often persuades many strangers to forget their fatherland.

4.21.6. I pass over the city itself, always so most loving toward you that you ought to prefer to it nothing of the fellowship of the nobles, into which you, a hand laid upon you, were happily snatched and inserted; and so the pleasure of your presence is to all such that yet no satiety has taken any. Now what shall I say here of your private property, whose state is this, that it would endure your expenditure by that very offence by which it is more frequent? For a master, a husbandman, if he cherishes his hearth here, so makes his expense as to increase his revenue too. These things I, one of all the citizens—certainly of the good ones—prattle by their wish, their petition, in their stead; who, since with so great honour they demand you, with so great love long for you, it is given to understand that you yourself will obtain more of joy, while you grant what you are asked. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Leo, greetings.

4.22.1. The magnificent Hesperius, a gem of friends and of letters, when he lately returned to the city from the country of the Toulousans, said that you charge me that, the books of letters now being finished, I should turn my pen to the style of history. With the highest reverence, and with the highest affection, I embrace so great a counsel; for you pronounce him fit for greater works whom you think ought to leave middling ones. But—what must be confessed—I dare to look up to a judgement of this kind rather than to undertake the counsel.

4.22.2. The thing is indeed worthy that you should bid it, but no less worthy that you should do it; for of old too, when Gaius Cornelius had urged the like on Gaius Secundus, he himself afterward seized upon what he enjoined; and this, by the example, you will now better attempt, since both I rise as a disciple to Pliny, and you, by your ancient kind of narrating, rightly outstrip Cornelius—who, if he came back to life in our age and beheld of what quality and how great you are held to be in letters, would now be more truly a Tacitus.

4.22.3. And so you rightly take up the mass of the theme proposed, you who, besides singular eloquence, have a great opportunity of vast knowledge; for daily, through the councils of a most powerful king, you, anxious for the whole world alike, learn its affairs and rights, treaties and wars, places, distances, merits; whence who would more justly gird himself to these things than he who, it is agreed, has learned the movements of nations, the varieties of embassies, the deeds of leaders, the pacts of rulers—in short, all the secrets of public affairs—and who, set on an excellent summit, has no need either to suppress the truth or to concoct a lie?

4.22.4. But our condition is far unequal, to whom this new exile is a grief and the old reading no use; then religion is for profession, humility for ambition, mediocrity for obscurity; nor in present things is so much of substance placed as in future things of hope; finally, languor is an impediment, and now, even late, on account of this very thing, sloth is at heart; and certainly there is now no praise of care, even contemporary, over my studies—nay, not even posthumous.

4.22.5. Chiefly it is fixed that I should seek small glory from history, since through men of clerical office our own things are rashly, others' things boastfully, past things unfruitfully, present things half-fully, false things basely, true things dangerously told. For the theme is of such a kind that, in it, if you make mention of good men, scant favour is prepared; if of the notable, the greatest offence; so straightway a satiric colour and odour mingles itself with that composition. So it is: historical writing seems much to abhor from our order, whose beginning is envy, whose continuation is labour, whose end is hatred.

4.22.6. But these things come about, if anything is composed with clergymen for authors; who, fixed by the snaky molars of revilers, if we publish anything simply, are called madmen; if anything exactly, presumptuous. But if you yourself, to whom it is given to be able by leaps to trample, or to overrun, the necks of disparagers, should willingly draw by lot the province of this matter, no one would write more loftily than you, no one more in the ancient manner—even if it should please you to speak of recent things; since, filled before with abundance of words, now of matter, you have left no reason for being cut by a venomed bite. And therefore for the future it will be a profit to consult you, a pleasure to hear you, an authority to read you. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Proculus, greetings.

4.23.1. Your son—nay, our common son—has run to me, who, having left you, grieves that he has erred, overwhelmed by the shame of penitence for his desertion. So, the tenor of his fault being heard, I rebuked the man as he hid himself—loving in words, with a menacing face—and with my own voice but in your stead, crying out that he was worthy of disowning, of the cross, of the sack, and of the other parricidal punishments. At this he, confounded, blushed, deprecating his error by no shameless excuse; but when I refuted him, convicted on all points, he joined to his modesty the companions of tears, so flowing and abundantly streaming that they gave faith to a correction to follow.

4.23.2. I ask, then, that you be merciful to one severe upon himself, and, following God, not hold guilty, with you for judge, one who professes himself worthy of condemnation; whom, if, inexorable, you should bid receive unheard-of kinds of punishments, he cannot be tortured more by grief through you than by shame through himself. Free your own despair from fear, free my confidence; and, if I rightly interpret the necessity of fatherly love, absolve yourself too, who are consumed by a hidden grief, by which your son is consumed in a public one. To whom it is agreed I have done very much injury, if you nevertheless do even a little—which certainly, as I hope, you will not do, unless you are harder than the rocks, or persist more rigid than the unbreakable adamant.

4.23.3. Therefore, if of your character and of your friendships I justly presume better things, propitiously indulge the excused, whom, reconciling, I steadfastly pledge will be faithful for the future; and, he being quickly loosed from his fault, I am bound by the benefit, greatly demanding not only that you pardon, but that you do so straightway, and that you admit him, returning, not only to your house but to your heart. Great God, how joyful will the day rise for you, the message for me, the spirit for him, when, cast at his father's feet, from that wounded mouth, that terrible mouth, while he expects a reproach, he shall have received a kiss! Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Turnus, greetings.

4.24.1. Well does that Mantuan phrase agree with your name and your business:
"Turnus, what none of the gods would have dared to promise to one who wished it,
behold, the rolling day has brought of its own accord."
Your father Turpio, a man of tribune's rank, asked of old, if you remember, for money on loan from Maximus the Palatine, and obtained it, setting aside or pledging nothing—neither of silver, nor binding any of his estates—by way of surety and pledge; but, as is shown by the bond made, the interest is secured to the lender, which, drawn out over a ten-year period, brought the amount of the principal up to double.

4.24.2. But when your father, the disease pressing on him, was sinking down to a near death, and on this very account public authority was the more violently constraining the failing head of the household to make good the debt, nor could the wickedness of the executors be sustained, he, now despaired of, commanded me by letter, as I was setting out for Toulouse, that, at my request, your creditor should grant at least a modest respite. To the prayers of the petitioner I quickly assented, since with Maximus I had old rights not only of acquaintance but of hospitality. So I gladly proceeded to my friend out of my way, although the villa was distant not a few miles from the public highway.

4.24.3. When I came, he himself met me, whom I had known before erect in body, free in step, free in voice, liberal in face—much unlike his old self in his gait, in his garb a man, in his pace modesty, in his colour and speech religious; then short hair, a long beard, three-legged chairs, Cilician hangings hung at the doors, a bed having nothing of feather, a table nothing of purple, kindness itself so benign as to be frugal, abounding not so much in flesh as in pulse; certainly, if there was anything richer in the food, indulging not himself but his guests.

4.24.4. When we rose, I secretly inquired of the bystanders which kind of life, out of the three orders, he had seized—whether he played the monk, or the clergyman, or the penitent. They said he was lately fulfilling a priesthood thrust upon him, to which civic love had bound him, refusing, by faction. The light returned, while the boys and clients were occupied in catching the animals, I sought the means of a secret conversation; he granted it. I embraced him, suspecting nothing; and I first confirm that I congratulate him for the height of his rank, then I mingle the prayers that followed.

4.24.5. I set forth the request of our Turpio, I allege his necessities, I deplore his extremities, which seemed the harder to his grieving friends for this, that, bound by usury, he was being loosed by his body: he should remember, then, his new profession, his old fellowship, and should moderate, by granting a respite for a while, the barbarous instance of the exactors barking around him; and, if the sick man should die, he should grant to the heirs a year of mourning free; if—as I would wish—Turpio should have recovered his former health, he should indulge the exhausted man, by leisure, the means of growing strong again.

4.24.6. I was still asking, when suddenly the man of charity began to weep greatly—not over the delay of the debt but over the danger of the debtor; and, his sob bridled: "Far be it from me," he said, "that I, a clergyman, should demand back from a sick man these things, which I should scarcely have asked, as a soldier, from a man in health. But I love his children too in such a way that, even if anything turn out adverse to my friend, I am about to ask of them nothing more than the reckoning of my office permits. Wherefore write to the anxious (and, that they may believe your letter more, join mine), that, whatever the issue of his sickness shall be—which, however, we wish prosperous for our brother—I will both prolong the space of a year for payment, and remit the additional half which has accrued under the name of interest, content with the restitution of the simple principal alone."

4.24.7. I gave at this the greatest thanks to God, great thanks to my host, who so loved both his fame and his conscience, confirming that the friend sends ahead of himself what he remits to you, and from this buys the supernal kingdom, in that he does not sell earthly benefits. Therefore, for what remains, strive that, on your initiative, at least the loaned sum be paid straightway, in such a way that you nonetheless give immense thanks even in the name of those who, joined to you by brotherhood, cannot perhaps, by reason of their age, understand what gift they obtain.

4.24.8. There is no reason why you should begin to say: "I have joint-heirs, the division has not yet been celebrated; it is agreed I have been treated more avariciously than my co-heirs; my brother and sister still act under their years of tutelage; for my sister no husband, for my brother no guardian, for the guardian no surety has yet been found." Which indeed is altogether said well to creditors, but to bad ones; but when such a person has a contract, who would relax the half when he could exact the whole, if he suffers delay, whatever he had conceded mercifully out of pity, he justly demands back on account of the injury. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Domnulus, greetings.

4.25.1. I cannot put off imparting to you in haste, a partaker of a great joy, what our father in Christ and likewise bishop, Patiens, having set out for Chalon after the manner of religion, after the manner of his own steadfastness, did—when he had come into the aforesaid town, the college of provincial priests partly going before, partly accompanying, namely that some supreme bishop might be ordained for the township, whose church-discipline was tottering after the younger bishop Paulus had departed and died. The pontifical council was met by the various wishes of the townsmen, and also by those private interests which always overturn the public good;

4.25.2. which a kind of triumvirate of competitors had kindled, of whom this one belched out the ancient prerogative of his birth, destitute of the remaining gift of character; this one, by parasitic uproars procured by the suffrage of his kitchens, was thrust forward with Apician applause; this one had promised, by a tacit compact, that, if he obtained the wished-for eminence, the church's estates would be a prey to his applauders.

4.25.3. When holy Patiens and holy Euphronius saw this—who held the rigour and firmness of the sounder judgement, free from hatred and favour—the counsel being first secretly shared with their fellow-bishops before it was openly disclosed, and the clamour of the raging crowd being despised, suddenly, with joined hands, they seized holy John, a man distinguished for honesty, kindness, and gentleness—who then wished and suspected nothing less than what was being done.

4.25.4. (He was here first a reader, then a minister of the altar, and that from infancy; afterward, by the advance of labours and times, archdeacon; in which degree or ministry, much held back on account of his industry, he could long not be augmented in dignity, lest he could be released from the office.) Yet him, now a priest of the second order, amid the discordant voices of the parties—which deferred to praise one not ambitious, but did not dare to blame one praiseworthy—the factious being astonished, the bad blushing, the good acclaiming, none crying out against it, they consecrated as their colleague.

4.25.5. Now therefore, if the Jura monasteries now send you back—into which you were gladly wont to ascend, now playing a prelude to the heavenly and supernal dwellings—it is fitting that you rejoice over the concord of our common fathers or patrons, whether so feeling in agreement or so agreeing in feeling; and exult also in the name of him whom Euphronius created by his testimony, Patiens by his hand, both by their judgement; in which Euphronius did what would befit not only his own old age but also the longevity of his dignity; and Patiens too did—a man equal, however, to even great praises—what well befitted a person to do who is the head of our city through his priesthood, and of the province through the city. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Petronius, greetings.

5.1.1. I hear that you spend a pleasurable patience in reading through my letters. This is a great thing, and most befitting a man of letters, that, though you yourself excel in the greatest studies, you should embrace these things, even the least, in others; but from this very thing the most consummate glory is repaid to you, for he stands out sufficiently by the merits of his own talent who has been the patron of another's.

5.1.2. I commend Vindicius, my kinsman, a religious man, and most suited to the levitical dignity which he has lately attained. To copy out for him from my tablets what you had bidden was a task that did not suit a province at leisure; here I have delivered to you some trifles by way of a little gift—although, such is your holiness, you always reckon our letters great rewards.

5.1.3. Meanwhile I make known the need of the aforesaid bearer, whom a twofold condition of business that has arisen has drawn hither; since he set out on this determination, either to enter a suit or to enter upon an inheritance. For, a paternal cousin having died unmarried and intestate, he prepares to succeed by the prerogative of agnation, unless, however, factious force opposes his undertakings. Against all which difficulties, you alone, after the help of Christ, suffice for your suppliant; of whom I am confident that, if the person earns favour, the cause will obtain victory. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Nymphidius, greetings.

5.2.1. The book on the state of the soul, illustrious in its three volumes, Mamertus Claudianus—the most skilled of Christian philosophers and the first of all learned men—took care to adorn and embellish with all the members, arts, and parts of the philosophy he pursued, revealing the nine, which they call Muses, to be disciplines, not women. For in his pages the watchful reader will find the truer names of the Camenae, which beget for themselves their own proper appellation about themselves. For there grammar divides, and oratory declaims, and arithmetic numbers, and geometry measures, and music weighs, and dialectic disputes, and astronomy foreknows, and architecture builds, and metric modulates.

5.2.2. Gladdened by the novelty of this reading and excited by its maturity, you asked that it be hastily reviewed and copied, as you had seen; as you had asked, you obtained it, under the promise of a swift return. It is fitting neither that I be deceived nor that you deceive me. It is time that what was lent be restored, since the book itself, if it pleased, ought to have given satiety; if it displeased, ought to have stirred distaste. But you, whatever the case is, discharge your faith quickly, lest, if you prepare to return the requested little book too late, you should seem to love the parchment rather than the letters. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Apollinaris, greetings.

5.3.1. It were fitting indeed that our garrulity should be bridled by the retaliation of your silence. But since perfect love ought not so much to reckon up what offices it pays as to remember what it owes, even now, the reins of modesty being loosed, we repeat the homage of an impudent address. Whose shamelessness is from this most of all discerned, that you keep silent. Did I, then, not deserve to know what you were doing in the time of hostility, brother? Did you conceal from a friend alarmed on your behalf either your security or your fear?

5.3.2. What else is it, if to one who inquires you suppress your doings, than to suspect that he who is anxious for you would either not rejoice on learning of prosperous things, or would not be sad if adverse ones turned out? Let this opinion of impiety depart from good morals, and let true affection banish, from its own brightness, the blemish of so wretched a suspicion. For, as your Crispus affirms, "to wish the same and to refuse the same—that, in the end, is firm friendship."

5.3.3. Meanwhile, if at least you are well, it is well. But I, weighed down by the mass of an unhappy conscience, lately, by the force of fevers, came near to the extremity of my safety—as one upon whom, most unworthy, the weight of so great a profession has been thrust, who, wretched, compelled to teach before to learn, and presuming to preach the good before to do it, like a barren tree, since I have not works for fruits, scatter words for leaves.

5.3.4. For what remains, pray that it be worth the labour that we have returned almost from the infernal seat, lest, if we remain in our past crimes, what we live should begin to pertain rather to the death of the soul. Behold, what I do I declare; behold, I still inquire what you do. From our part is done what is pious; do you henceforth do what seems good. But that, indeed, believe to be cut in bronze, like the Attic laws: that we, by Christ's help, will never admit an end of the love whose beginning we have striven to found. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Simplicius, greetings.

5.4.1. That I have not received writings, who had sent them, I impute to friendship, but I rather assign to modesty; for, unless I reckon beyond what is fair, that the greeting owed me was withheld, that was not contumacy but bashfulness. But if you further close your door to my prattling page, and set up the bolt, I yield, not unwillingly, to your quiet indeed; but I declare that I shall find my culprits not far from you.

5.4.2. For it is not unjust to turn all the odium of your silence to the pride of your sons, who, feeling themselves loved, suffer a kind of distaste at our earnestness; whom you ought to admonish, by your fatherly authority, that they cease not to sweeten, with polished addresses, the bitterness of the offence contracted with us. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Syagrius, greetings.

5.5.1. Since you are the great-grandson of a consul, and that by the male succession (although that matters little to the case I am about to set forth), since therefore you are of the seed of a poet, to whom letters would beyond doubt have given statues, if the consular robes had not given them (as even now the words of that author, polished in verses, attest), from whom the studies of his posterity have not degenerated even a little—at least in this respect—it is monstrous to tell how greatly I am astonished that you have seized the knowledge of the Germanic tongue with such ease.

5.5.2. And yet I remember that your boyhood was fittingly imbued with the liberal schools, and I have it sufficiently ascertained that you often declaimed keenly and eloquently before the orator. And since these things are so, I should like you to say whence your breast suddenly drank in the euphony of an alien race, so that now, after the canes of the Maronian reading, and after the toiled-over copiousness and loquacity of the varicose man of Arpinum, you burst forth to me like a new falcon from an old eyrie.

5.5.3. It can by no means be reckoned how much of a laugh it is to me and to others, as often as I hear that, in your presence, the barbarian fears to make a barbarism in his own tongue. The bent old age of the Germans is amazed at you when you interpret their letters, and takes you, in their mutual affairs, as arbiter and umpire. A new Solon of the Burgundians in expounding laws, a new Amphion in tuning lyres—but three-stringed ones—you are loved, you are sought out, you delight, you are chosen, you are called in, you decree, you are heard. And although they are alike stiff and unhewable in body and in mind, they embrace in you, and at once learn, the tongue of their fathers, the heart of a Latin.

5.5.4. This one thing remains, most witty man: that, no less diligently, even when you have leisure, you spend something on the reading of literature, and keep, as you are most elegant, this measure—that this tongue be held by you, lest you be laughed at; that the other be exercised, that you may laugh. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Apollinaris, greetings.

5.6.1. As soon as summer gave way to autumn, and the fear of the Arvernians could for a little while be tempered by the reckoning of the season, I came to Vienne, where I found Thaumastus, your brother—whom, by the right of blood and of age, I embrace with a reverend intimacy—most sorrowful; who, although he was greatly afflicted by his recent widowhood, was yet little less anxious on your behalf: for he feared and dreaded lest the barbarian whirlwind or military wickedness should concoct some calumny against you.

5.6.2. For he affirms that it was secretly whispered to the master of soldiers Chilperic, a most victorious man, by the venomous report of certain wicked men, that, chiefly by your machination, the town of Vaison was being attached to the party of the new prince. If from this any suspicion is struck into you and yours, swiftly inform me by the return of a familiar page, lest the opportunity of my solicitude or my presence be lost to you. It will be peculiarly my care—if, however, you shall judge anything must be guarded against—to make you either secure by favour obtained, or more cautious by anger explored. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Thaumastus, greetings.

5.7.1. We have at last tracked down who, before our tetrarch, slandered the friendships of your brother and, on the other side, those of the party of the new prince—if, that is, the clandestine footprints of the informers have not cheated the faithful sagacity of our comrades. These men, surely, are—as you yourself, set face to face, heard—those whom Gaul has long groaned to endure even among the more clement barbarians. These are they whom even those who are feared, fear. These are they whom this province peculiarly awaits: to bring in calumnies, to denounce persons, to bring on threats, to carry off property.

5.7.2. These are they whose occupations in leisure, whose plunderings in peace, whose flights amid arms, whose victories amid wine, you hear praised. These are they who delay causes when called in, hinder things omitted, disdain things charged, forget things admonished, once enriched. These are they who buy lawsuits, sell interventions, appoint arbiters, dictate what is to be judged, tear up what is dictated, drag in those about to litigate, drag out those to be heard, draw the condemned, draw back those settling. These are they whom, if you ask, even with no one opposing, a benefit, it irks them to promise, shames them to refuse, repents them to have granted.

5.7.3. These are they to whose comparison Narcissus, Asiaticus, Massa, Marcellus, Carus, Parthenius, Licinus, and Pallas would raise the finger in surrender. These are they who envy the tunicked their leisure, the war-cloaked their pay, the couriers their travel-money, the merchants their markets, the envoys their little gifts, the informers their customs-dues, the provincials their estates, the townsmen their priesthoods, the keepers of records their weights and measures, the enrolled their salaries, the praetorian accountants their arrangements, the cities their gratuities, the publicans their respites, the clergy their tributes, the nobles their reverence and their lineage, the elders their seat of honour, their equals their meeting, the girt their rights, the ungirt their privileges, those to be instructed their schools, the teachers their fees, the instructed their letters.

5.7.4. These are they who, drunk with new wealth, that you may know even the least things, by the intemperance of using betray their unskilfulness of possessing; for they gladly come armed to feasts, white-robed to funerals, fur-clad to churches, in mourning to weddings, in beaver-skins to litanies. No kind of men, of orders, of seasons is at heart to them. In the forum Scythians, in the bedchamber vipers, at the banquet buffoons, in exactions Harpies, in disputes statues, in inquiries beasts, in negotiations snails, in contracts money-changers; for understanding stony, for judging wooden, for being kindled flaming, for forgiving iron; for friendships leopards, for pleasantries bears, for deceiving foxes, for pride bulls, for consuming minotaurs.

5.7.5. They hold firm hopes in the upheavals of affairs, they love doubtful times the more surely; and, trembling alike from cowardice and from conscience, since they are lions in the praetoria, hares in the camps, they fear treaties, lest these be discussed; wars, lest they fight. Of whom, if the breeze of a rusty money-bag has anywhere breathed upon their nostrils, you will straightway see there applied both the eyes of Argus, and the hands of Briareus, and the claws of the Sphinxes, and the perjuries of Laomedon, and the cunning of Ulysses, and the deceits of Sinon, and the good faith of Polymestor, and the piety of Pygmalion.

5.7.6. By these morals they overwhelm a man excelling no less in goodness than in power. But what can one man do, fenced about on all sides by a venomous interpreter? What, I say, can he do, whose nature is with the good, whose life is with the bad? By whose counsels Phalaris would be made more bloody, Midas more covetous, Ancus more boastful, Tarquin more proud, Tiberius more cunning, Gaius more dangerous, Claudius more dull, Nero more impure, Galba more avaricious, Otho more audacious, Vitellius more extravagant, Domitian more truculent.

5.7.7. Surely—what chiefly heals the afflicted—his own Tanaquil tempers our Lucumo, and clears away the ears of her husband, filled with the poisonous dregs of whisperers, by the opportune use of salted speech. By whose zeal it is fitting that you know that meanwhile nothing of the poisons of the younger Cibyratans has harmed the quiet of our common brothers in the mind of our common patron, nor will anything harm, God being propitious—if only, so long as the present power rules Lugdunensian Germany, our and his own Germanicus is governed by the present Agrippina. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Secundinus, greetings.

5.8.1. It is long indeed since, astonished and proclaiming you, we used to read you serving more familiarly the hexameter. For the matter was pleasant, whether the nuptial torches of the bridal chamber were described by you, or wild beasts pierced by royal blows. But in the triple trochees lately compacted into the hendecasyllabic metre you have made nothing like, not even by your own judgement.

5.8.2. Good God, what of gall, of charm, of peppered eloquence I, by no means silent, beheld therein! save that the thunderbolt of your fervent wit and the salted freedom of your eloquence were hampered perhaps by the persons rather than by the causes; so that to me neither does Ablabius the consul seem to have more figuratively pricked the house and life of Constantine in a twin verse, nor to have bitten it with such a distich, secretly hung at the Palatine doors:
"Who would ask back the golden ages of Saturn? These are of gems—but Neronian."
since, namely, the aforesaid Augustus had, at well-nigh the same times, destroyed his wife Fausta by the heat of a bath, and his son Crispus by the cold of poison.

5.8.3. You, nevertheless, no less diligently, undaunted, spend your labour at least on the witty colours of satires; for your writings will be enriched by the increasing vices of our tyrant-townsmen. For those whom our judgements, by the fault of the age, think fortunate, swell with no such mediocrity that posterity will one day have to labour to recall their very names; for the disgraces of the wicked, equally as the praises of the good, remain immortal. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Aquilinus, greetings.

5.9.1. I reckon it to my own credit, most capacious of all virtues, if you too think it worthy, that we should have as many friendships ourselves as we have causes of friendship. It is an ancestral thing that I demand back; my witnesses in this matter at present shall be called our grandfathers, Apollinaris and Rusticus, whom a likeness of letters, dignities, dangers, and consciences had joined in a praiseworthy intimacy, when they execrated together, in Constantine inconstancy, in Jovinus pliancy, in Gerontius perfidy—single faults in single men, all crimes at once in Dardanus.

5.9.2. In the age that was the middle, our fathers, under one fellowship, scarcely yet borne from boyhood into full youth, served the prince Honorius as tribunes and notaries, sojourning together with such affection that among them the least cause of concord was that they were recalled to be the sons of friends. In the principate of the emperor Valentinian, the one presided over a part of the Gauls, the other over the whole; but the titles of both were so in a manner balanced by a brotherly compensation, that he was first in the time of his office who was second in dignity.

5.9.3. It has come to us—that is, it has come to the grandsons, whom it would befit to guard against nothing more than lest, through us perhaps, the affection of our parents and our forefathers should seem antiquated. To this, into a like intimacy, besides the hereditary prerogative, we are compelled by a manifold opportunity: the age of each of us no less joined than our fatherland; one sport exercised us, one master trained us; one gladness relaxed us, severity restrained us, discipline formed us.

5.9.4. For the rest, if God grants, in the years now knocking at the thresholds of old age, let us be, unless you reject it, two souls, one mind; and let us imbue our children, loving one another, to wish and to refuse the same things, to flee and to follow the same. But this would be of our fathers now above their prayers: if, through Rusticus and Apollinaris, the hearts of our praiseworthy great-grandfathers are reformed as well as their names. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Sapaudus, greetings.

5.10.1. If the illustrious Pragmatius does anything at all well among the other virtues of his mind, this he does best: that, from love of studies, he loves you singularly, in whom alone, or most of all, he marks that the traces of old skill and diligence have settled. And indeed not unjustly is he your patron; for a most copious honour is owed by him to letters.

5.10.2. Him once, declaiming and breaking the rhetorical benches with applaudable oratory, his eloquent father-in-law of his own accord admitted into a patrician family—although age, comeliness, and modesty pleaded for him to this end, to say nothing of his birth or wealth. But, as I have learned, even then the serious man blushed to have pleased by the gift of his form, since by the merit of his talent it would have sufficed him to be loved. And truly each best man pleases more excellently by his character than by his beauty; moreover, the passing adornments of the body waver with the advance and decline of running time. Him too, his judgement remaining, Priscus Valerianus, afterward prefect of the Gauls, joined to his counsels and tribunals, most perseveringly holding the old judgement, that to whom he had joined his offspring under the plea of knowledge, he should join also dignity.

5.10.3. But your composition is so bright, so distinguished, that, compared with it, the division of Palaemon, the gravity of Gallio, the abundance of Delphidius, the discipline of Agroecius, the strength of Alcimus, the tenderness of Adelphius, the rigour of Magnus, the sweetness of Victorius would write not only nothing superior but scarcely things equal. Indeed, lest I should seem to you, under this as it were hyperbolic catalogue of rhetoricians, to have flattered and gratified you in anything, I do not doubt—nay rather, I acquiesce—that to you alone the keenness of Quintilian and the pomp of Palladius are to be compared.

5.10.4. Wherefore, if anyone after you favours Latin erudition, he gives thanks to this friendship, and, if he has anything of a man, wishes to be added as a third to your fellowship; although—what is the more grievous—that ambition of his will not be enough to stir distaste in you, since few now honour studies, and at the same time it is fixed and rooted in human breasts, by a natural vice, that those who do not understand arts do not admire artists. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Potentinus, greetings.

5.11.1. We love you much; and indeed the affection of this love is not erroneous or fortuitous. For, that I might be made a comrade the more bound to you, I made a judgement—for it is my custom to choose first, to love after. "What, then," you say, "in me pleased you, to be approved?"

5.11.2. I will say gladly and briefly—of which one thing favour, the other the paper, compels me to make. I revere in your doings that you do many things imitable by every good man: you cultivate as one most skilful; you build as one most orderly; you hunt as one most effective; you feed your household as one most exact; you jest as one most witty; you judge as one most fair; you advise as one most sincere; you are moved to anger as one most slow; you are appeased as one most swift; you love in return as one most faithful.

5.11.3. All these examples of living, if my Apollinaris from these years of his youth follows, I rejoice; certainly I admonish him to follow them; in the teaching and training of whom—provided only that, by Christ's help, what is arranged succeeds—I most greatly rejoice that I shall borrow the greatest pattern of life from your character. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Calminius, greetings.

5.12.1. That a page travels to you from us more rarely, it is not our pride but another's tyranny that brings about; nor should you seek anything plainer concerning these things, since an equal fear with you interprets the necessity of this silence. This alone, however, I freely groan: that, made separate by the whirlwind of dissenting parties, we by no means enjoy a mutual sight of each other, nor are you ever offered to the anxious gaze of your fatherland—except perhaps when, at the will of another's terror, the breastplate covers you, the battlements us; where you yourself, brought captive to this alone, are compelled to empty your quivers of arrows, to fill your eyes with tears—we too not refusing it, since your wishes contrive something far other than your javelins.

5.12.2. But since meanwhile, even if not through the truth of treaties, at least through the semblance of truces, a certain window of the hope of our liberty shines out, I earnestly beg that you impart to us, when most you can, the address of a frequent page, knowing that there remains for you, in the minds of your besieged fellow-citizens, that gratitude which forgets the besieger's enmity. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Pannychius, greetings.

5.13.1. Do you know that Seronatus is returning from Toulouse? If not yet—and I believe that not yet—learn it at least by this: already Euanthius is going to Clausetia, and already gathering the assembled labour-gangs to clear, if perchance the embankment has been fouled by any fall of dropping leaves. Certainly if there is anything full of holes, he himself, alarmed, levels it, earth being carried in, the pits filled—as one who, like a leader, is about to go before his own monster from the valley of the Tarn—like the little mussels that pilot the bulk of whales amid rocks or shallows.

5.13.2. But that man—so swift in anger, so slow in bulk—like a serpent scarcely unrolled from its cave, is now borne in from close at hand upon the Gabalitani, expiring with fear; whom, single, scattered, townless, he now drains by unheard-of kinds of taxes, now nets about with the winding fraud of calumnies, not permitting the toil-worn to return home even then, when they have paid the yearly tribute.

5.13.3. And this too is a sure sign of his impending arrival: that in droves, wherever he turns, the bound are dragged, dragging their chains; in whose pain he rejoices, on whose hunger he feeds, reckoning it especially fine to disfigure those to be condemned before punishing them. He nourishes the hair of men, cuts that of women; of whom, however, if a rare pardon has regarded some, these venality looses, those vanity, none mercy. But to unfold such a beast neither the prince of orators, Marcus of Arpinum, nor of poets, Publius of Mantua, can suffice.

5.13.4. Accordingly, since this very plague is said to be drawing near—against whose treacheries may God interpose—forestall the disease by the wholesomeness of foresight, and against the suits of the quarrelsome, if any are stirred, take counsel by agreements; against tributes, by receipts; lest the evil man find, in the affairs of good men, either what to harm or what to bestow. In sum, do you wish to receive what I think about Seronatus? The rest fear to be afflicted, by his agency, with loss; to me even a robber's benefits are suspect. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Aper, greetings.

5.14.1. Does warm Baiae now delight you, and the sulphur-water belched, cavern-wise, from the rough pumice, and the pool medicinal for the liver-sick and the consumptive feeble? Or perhaps a mountain seat among the fortresses, and, in choosing a seat of refuge, do you suffer a certain difficulty from the multitude of strongholds? Whatever it is, whether you are at leisure or at business, you will yet, unless I am mistaken, be recalled to the city by the consideration of the Rogations.

5.14.2. Of which solemnity Mamertus, father and bishop, first found, instituted, and brought in for us, by a most reverend example, by a most useful experiment. There were indeed before—be it said with the peace of the faith—wandering, lukewarm, infrequent, and (so to speak) yawning supplications, which were often blunted by the interposing obstacles of luncheons—chiefly to deprecate either rains or fair weather; to which, to say nothing more, it was not fitting that the potter and the gardener alike should come.

5.14.3. But in these which the aforesaid supreme priest both brought forth and bestowed on us, there is fasting, praying, psalm-singing, weeping. To these festivals of humbled necks and the sighing companies of prostrate citizens I summon you; and, if I rightly measure your spiritual mind, you will now come the sooner, since you are called not to feasts but to tears. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Ruricius, greetings.

5.15.1. The word of office being premised, I commend our bookseller—tested by me not by favour but as a judge—of whom I have proved well and abundantly the good faith in his breast, and likewise the swiftness in his work, toward you, his master and mine and his own in common. This very man, then, carries hither a book of the Heptateuch, written with the highest speed and the highest neatness, although it has been re-read and revised by us also. He brings too a volume of the Prophets, although run through in my absence, yet by his own care and hand cleared of superfluous readings—and not always with the man reading against him who had promised his help; I believe, because his infirmity was an impediment, that he should not fulfil what he had promised.

5.15.2. It remains that your exhortation or your pledge should reward the servant, thus either studying to please or deserving, with a fitting grace; which, at any rate, if it is paid for such labour, will begin to look to your own recompense. But since I beg this from favour alone, do you look at what he deserves, of whom it is agreed that he seeks rather his master's affection than a reward. Farewell.
Sidonius to his wife Papianilla, greetings.

5.16.1. The quaestor Licinianus, coming from Ravenna, as soon as he touched the soil of Gaul, the Alps being crossed, sent a letter ahead of his coming, in which he indicates that he is the bearer of the imperial codicils, at whose arrival the patrician honour accrues to your brother Ecdicius too—in whose titles you rejoice equally as in mine—most swiftly, if you consider his age; most slowly, if his merits; for he long ago paid the suffrage for entering upon this dignity, not in the scale but on the sword's edge, and he himself, a private man, enriched the public treasury, not with moneys, but with spoils.

5.16.2. This, however, the holy Julius Nepos—supreme Augustus alike in arms and in character—did, in that the good faith of his predecessor Anthemius, pledged to your brother's toils, he discharged the more praiseworthily the quicker; since this man fulfilled what that one most often promised. Whence it comes that henceforth, for the commonwealth, every best man can and ought, if there is any strength in anyone, to spend it—being secure, and hence eager—since, even when an emperor is dead, the principate always repays whatever the prince has pledged to the devotion of the labouring.

5.16.3. Meanwhile you, if I well gather your affection, on learning these things take great solace amid the greatest adversities, nor does the terror even of the neighbouring siege swerve your mind from the path of common joys. For I know well that you were not so gladdened even by my own honour, which by the law you share, since, although you are a good wife, you are a most excellent sister. On which account, by Christ our God being propitious, I have hastily inscribed with congratulatory letters the enlarged titles of your line, at once absolving your solicitude and your brother's modesty; who would indicate nothing of his own dignity—and if perchance you did not know him to be modest, you would not on that account judge him impious.

5.16.4. But I enjoy not so much your insignia—which you have hitherto awaited, the more freely the more impatiently (although these too greatly)—as your concord; which I wish in future to be equal for our children and his, demanding by our common prayers that, as we, having attained the prefectorian rank for each of our families, have by divine favour rendered it patrician too, so they may make the patrician rank which they receive into a consular one.

5.16.5. Roscia salutes you, our common care; who, in the most indulgent bosom of her grandmother and aunts—what rarely befalls grandchildren to be reared—is yet brought up with severity. By which, however, her tender age is not weakened but her character is formed. Farewell.
Sidonius to his friend Eriphius, greetings.

5.17.1. You are, my Eriphius, ever yourself, and never does the hunt, the city, the country call you away so much that you are not, by the way, held by the pleasure of letters; and it comes by this zeal that you do not even disdain our writings, who, as you write, smell to you of the Muses. Which sentence, however, is amply proved to lack truth, and which it also appears comes either from jest, if you are merry, or from love, if you are serious; but for the rest it recoils far from what is just, when you assign to me things that would scarcely be fittingly accommodated even to Maro, scarcely to Homer.

5.17.2. Let us leave these things, and converse of that whence the occasion arose. You bid verses be directed to you which I granted to the prayers of a most distinguished man, your father-in-law; who, mingled in the fellowship of his equals, lives with manners alike ready to command and to obey. But since you desire to know both the place and the cause, that you may the more easily understand a very small matter, lay it rather to my fault that the preface will be more talkative than the work.

5.17.3. We had come together at the sepulchre of holy Justus (but infirmity was an impediment to you, that you were not then present); the procession had been before dawn, the solemnity the yearly one, the people huge, of either sex, whom the most capacious basilica could not hold, however girt with spreading covered galleries. The worship of the vigils being performed—which the monks and the clergy, psalm-singers, had celebrated together with alternating sweetness—each of us withdrew in different directions, yet not far off, since at the third hour we were to be present, when the divine service was to be performed with the priests;

5.17.4. exceedingly out of breath, indeed, from the press of the place and the crowds, and from the numerous lights brought in; and at the same time the night, still close upon summer, had scorched us, shut in under a roof, with its vapour, even though now, with the first chill, the autumnal Dawn was nonetheless growing cool. And so, when the various bodies of the orders were dispersed here and there, it pleased us, with the chief of the citizens, to come together at the tomb of the consul Syagrius, which was not separated even by a full bowshot. Here some of us had sat down under the shade of a grown vine, which, the stems being raised high and hanging trellis-wise, the foliage drawn over had woven; some on the green turf, but fragrant with flowers.

5.17.5. The talk was sweet, jocular, bantering; and besides—which was the most blessed thing—no mention of the powers or of the tributes, no speech that could be betrayed, no person who would betray. Anyone, certainly, could have related a tale worthy of relating and worthy in its sentiments: it was listened to most ambitiously; nor for that reason was the narration the less distinct, that gladness was mingled with it. Amid these things, to us long languid from leisure, it seemed good to do something.

5.17.6. Presently, two parties being formed—as the age allowed—amid the acclamations demanding it, there is brought forth to these the ball, to those the dice-board. Of the ball I was the first standard-bearer, which, as you know, is held my companion no less than the book. On the other side my brother Domnicius, a man of the highest grace, of the highest charm, had taken the dice and was shaking them, by which, as by a trumpet, he called the gamesters to the dice-tower. We, with a troop of scholars, played abundantly, so much as our limbs, dulled by the torpor of stationary labour, might be invigorated by wholesome running.

5.17.7. Here the illustrious Philomatius—as is that phrase of the Mantuan poet, "daring himself too with his hand to try the labour of the young men"—steadfastly mingled himself with the bands of the ball-players, for he had done this beautifully, but when his years were still younger. Who, since he was frequently thrust from the place of those standing by the impulse of one running in the midst, now too, received into the field, neither cut off the path of the ball flying past before him or thrown over him, nor avoided it, and, often bent forward through a tumble, scarcely gathered himself up again from the ruinous swerve, was the first to remove himself from the noise of the game, sighing, his inwards growing hot. For frequent pains, the fibre of his little liver swelling, pricked the exercised man.

5.17.8. I straightway stopped too, about to do, by the fellowship of resting, a deed of charity, lest the brotherly weariness should suffer shame. So, as we sat down, sweat soon admonished him to ask for water for his face: it was brought to him as he asked, and likewise a towel heavy with nap, which, polished by yesterday's washing, chanced to be swaying under the very double-leaved doors of the little house, from the porter's upright rope, pulley-wise.

5.17.9. While at leisure he dries his cheeks with it: "I should wish," he said, "you would bid some quatrain of like office be written for me on the cloth." "Let it be," I said. "But," he said, "let it hold my name too in the metre." I replied that what he had asked were things possible to do. He himself too said: "Dictate, then." Then I, smiling: "Know at once that the Muses are stirred, if I am at leisure with their choir not without witnesses." He answered vehemently and most urbanely—as he is by nature a fiery man and a certain inexhaustible fount of eloquence: "See, lord Sollius, lest Apollo perhaps be the more stirred, that you alone solicit his foster-children to secrets." Now you can know what applause a sentiment so sudden, so charming, stirs up.
5.17.10. And, delaying no longer, presently his scribe, who held the tablet at hand, being called to me, I composed the following epigram:
