For that, as I judge—I who lead your mind to be preferable to your limbs—has no equality, that the reasoning of an intellectual soul, knowing the true and the false, has raised our state above the beasts; and if those men, who look upon their friends mockingly, not so much with judgement as with the eye, should for a moment remove its dignity, let them say, I pray, what in the form of man they think sufficiently pre-eminent, what worthy of regard.

7.14.5. His height? As though this were not often more fittingly suited to beams. Or his strength? Which reigns more vigorously in the sinews of a lion's neck. Or the beauty of his features? Which clay often more skilfully fixes in images, and wax in pictures. Or his swiftness? Which is more competently ascribed to dogs. Or his vigilance? With which even the owl contends. Or his voice? To which the ass would not yield in clearness. Or his industry? With which, after its own measure, not even the ant fears to be compared.

7.14.6. But perhaps they prefer the power of seeing: as though the sight of eagles were not more eminent. They prefer the efficacy of hearing: as though the bristly swine did not surpass us in hearing. They prefer the subtlety of smelling: as though the vulture did not precede us in scent. They prefer the discernment of tasting: as though we did not here yield much even to the ape. What shall I say of touch, the fifth sense of our body? Which the philosopher and the little worm claim for themselves indifferently. I say nothing here of the alluring appetites, which, in coition, the bowed-down pleasure of human flesh shares with the beast's impulse.

7.14.7. See what misery they prefer and cultivate, who, puffed up, insult me because you are known to them by sight alone. But I always see that Philagrius whose face, if I saw it silent, I would not see as Philagrius. Whence that common saying, which a certain man uttered, in a different case but with a like opinion: "The Roman people did not recognize the son of Marcus Cicero when he spoke." For by universal judgement the dignity of knowledge, virtue, prerogative are renowned, to whose highest summit one ascends by the steps of merits.

7.14.8. First, even the bestial body, if it is now perchance formed, transcends in dignity the unformed matter; next, before the formed is set the animated body; thirdly, the human mind precedes the soul of the beast, because, as the flesh is inferior to life, so life to reason, of which our substance God the Maker made master, but the beast's incapable; yet so that in the state of the human mind a twofold condition prevails; for as souls that reason in a human way, but are dull and rather sluggish, are trodden down by the talent of the prudent and the keen, so, if there are any that flourish by natural wisdom alone, these easily concede that they are surpassed by the merits of the skilled.

7.14.9. Observing the difference of these grades, I always behold with the eye of the heart that Philagrius, to whom my mind makes me potentially known by likeness of character; for, although you please all good men, no one has been more able to look upon you within than he who strives to imitate you without. Indeed, in what manner I become a follower of your pursuits, will be disclosed in the following part of the page.

7.14.10. You love, as I have learned, the quiet; I, even the indolent. You avoid the barbarians, because they are thought evil; I, even if they are good. You give diligence to reading; I too suffer my own sloth to harm me little in that part. You yourself fill the person of a religious man; I, at least the image. You do not desire the goods of others; I even count it as gain if I do not lose my own. You delight in the company of the learned; I call any crowd, however great, lacking in literary art, the greatest solitude.

7.14.11. You are said to be most cheerful; I too define that all tears perish which anyone has shed, except as often as he supplicates God. You are reported to be most humane; no guest has shuddered at our little table, as at the cave of Polyphemus. The highest clemency is attributed to you toward your servants; nor am I tortured, if mine, as often as they sin, are not as often tortured.

7.14.12. You think one ought to fast on alternate days? It does not irk me to follow. To dine? It does not shame me to be the first. For the rest, if it is granted me, by the gift of Christ, to be seen by you, I shall so rejoice as one from whom no lesser things have been withdrawn concerning you. Moreover, what greater things are in you, I now know well enough. On account of which it can the more easily come about that, even if at some time, set before you, I look upon your face, some fresh joy concerning you, rather than opinion, accrues to me. Farewell.

7.15.1. As often as I come to Vienne, I would wish, at the greatest price purchased, that the dwelling of the city held you and our common brother as settlers the more—you who are joined to me not by love only but also by profession. But that one eludes my reproach under the pretext of his frequented suburban estate, by which it comes about that he is to us neither present himself nor accountable; and you have wherewith meanwhile to excuse yourself, that a possession scarcely recovered now possesses you long. Whatever it is, come now, henceforth to obtain a departure on this condition, that you either return in turn or stay longer. For however much, set in the country, you make your husbandmen industrious, then truly will you make your own land fruitful, if the church, which you cultivate much, you cultivate more. Farewell.

7.16.1. You do, my only patron in Christ, a thing alike of your love and of your custom, in that you soothe the cares of a wandering friend by consoling letters. And would that you always so remember me, that the very anxieties, chained together by a succeeding anguish, which as an exhorter you make thin, you may, as an intercessor, cut off!

7.16.2. For the rest, I think your freedmen, the business you had enjoined being despatched, are returning; who, it is agreed, performed the matter so vigorously that they did not even need to be helped. Through them I have sent the nightly cowl, with which you may worthily cover your limbs, worn out by fasts, between praying and lying down—although the shaggy garment is sent not opportunely, the winter being ended and the seasons of summer now drawing near. Farewell.

7.17.1. You bid me, my lord brother, by the law of friendship, which it is a sin to wound, to set my long-idle fingers upon the anvils of the old workshop, and to inscribe for the holy Abraham, his day fulfilled, a funeral dirge in mournful verses. Quickly will I comply with what is enjoined, both drawn by your authority and chiefly forestalled by the devotion of that most distinguished man, the count Victorius, whom by secular right I honour as a patron, by ecclesiastical right I cherish as a son, as a client, and love as a father; who sufficiently showed what and how great a care burned within him toward the servants of Christ, when, bending about the couch of the dying bishop, no less than about his limbs, and made one colour with grief, growing pale at the death close above his face, he showed by his indicative tears what he wished for the man.

7.17.2. And since he himself snatched for himself the greatest parts of burying the body, bestowing the whole apparatus of the abundant expense that befitted the bishop to be buried, we confer, at least to the obsequies, the words that remain, about to scratch with the impress of the engraving pen nothing other than a testimony of mutual love; for the rest, the character, deeds, and virtues of the man will be most unworthily weighed by the meanness of my words.
Abraham, worthy to be joined to the holy patrons,
whom I would not tremble to call your colleagues:
for so they go before that you may soon follow them;
a share of martyrdom gives a share of the kingdom.
Born by the Euphrates, having suffered prison for Christ
and bonds loosened only by a five years' famine,
escaped from the truculent king of the Susian shore,
you hasten alone all the way to the western land.
But the signs of his powers follow the confessor,
and to evil spirits you bring, fugitive, their flight.
Wherever you come, the throng of Lemures cries that it yields:
you, an exile, bid the demons go into exile.
You are sought by all, yet no ambition takes you;
the honour thrust upon you is more burdensome.
You flee the uproars of Rome and Byzantium
and the walls broken by arrow-bearing Titus.
The wall of Alexander and of Antioch holds you not;
you spurn the Byrsa-roofed house of Dido,
you scorn the populous fields of marsh-dwelling Ravenna
and those that take their name from the wool-bearing sow.
This corner pleases you, and a poor man's retreat,
and a hut whose roof was pressed low with straw.
Here you yourself build a temple venerable to God,
having yourself first been made by your body a temple of God.
Here ended the course of your life and your journey:
a double crown remains for your toil.
Now the thousands of the holy paradise stand around you;
now Abraham, your fellow-pilgrim, holds you;
now you enter the homeland, but the one from which Adam fell;
now you may go to the fount of your own godhead.

7.17.3. See, as you had enjoined, the rites that remain we have paid in full to the buried man; but if in turn it is fitting for brothers, friends, and fellow-soldiers to comply with the commands of charity, in your turn, I pray, do you too, by the institutions in which you excel, undertake to console his disciples, and swiftly form the wavering rule of the abandoned brothers according to the statutes of the fathers of Lérins or of Grigny; of which discipline, if any are rebels, do you yourself chastise; if any are followers, do you yourself praise together.

7.17.4. The holy Auxanius is indeed seen to be set over them; who, as you know, being somewhat more than is just both weak in body and modest in disposition, and thereby readier to obey than to command, requires that you be asked that he himself come as master of the monastery under your own mastership, and that, if any of the younger ones should despise him as unskilled or faint-hearted, he may feel, through you alone, that both are not contemned with impunity. Why many words? Do you wish to learn in a few what I want? I ask that brother Auxanius be abbot over the congregation, but you over the abbot. Farewell.

7.18.1. From you the beginning, with you it shall end; for I have sent the requested work, the copies hastily chosen, which on this account came few into my hands, because, while I meditated nothing about the writing of this little book, things hitherto unkept cannot be found. Indeed these few, which are also slight, I quickly finished, although my mind, once spurred, did not yet cease to wish to write—keeping diligently this kind of moderation, that the text of the letters should not be drawn out, if the number were shortened.

7.18.2. At the same time I judged that the book, which you, a most delicate reader, would desire, would be both handy enough and not a little excusable, if—since the lightness of the senses and the structures could offend you—you were at least the less burdened by the bundles of parchments. I commend, therefore, the various motions of our breast to your judgement, by no means unaware that the mind lies as open in a book as the face in a mirror; for I have composed some things by exhorting, very many by praising, and some by advising, a few by mourning and not a few by jesting.

7.18.3. And if anywhere you have read me as somewhat too vehement against certain men, know that I wish you to understand—the right hand of Christ aiding—that I shall never endure a servitude of the spirit, holding it most certain that the judgement of men upon these characters is twofold; for as the timid call me rash, so the steadfast call me free; among which I myself decide that his person lies low enough, whose opinion must needs lie hidden.

7.18.4. I return to my purpose. Meanwhile, if you take any breathing-space from the continuation of sacred reading, you may be diverted by these trifles. Nor will the matter, as being boundless, cause distaste, because, since the several causes are finished almost in single letters, the eye, quickly recognizing the things on which it is bent, will cease to read before it ceases to wish to read. Farewell.

8.1.1. You do well (this is your way; persevere in it), a man most worthy of the praise of all good men who dwell anywhere, in that you flatter the glory of your friends wherever there is room. Hence it is that you ask even the Arvernian writing-cases to be aired out, although we supposed it would suffice you if we had brought forth something by the earlier publication. So we will comply with what is enjoined, yet prolonging the work of the pen only so far that the series of letters—begun, of course, from the beginning of the volume—may at the very end be drawn out by the sum of a number still small, namely so as to crown the finished work with a kind of fringe upon its own margin.

8.1.2. But more care must be taken lest, on account of the additions to a volume already made public, we should perhaps late fall foul of certain fault-finders, whose tongues, naturally sharpened on the whetstone of envy, not even the artful maxims and well-wrought eloquence of Demosthenes and Cicero could escape—of whom the earlier orator endured Demades, the later Antonius, as his detractors; and these men, though envious with a famous malice and an obscure diction, have nonetheless run down to the knowledge of posterity through their hatred of virtues.

8.1.3. But since you exhort me, let us loose our sails to the storms revisited, and we who have, as it were, crossed seas, let us sail across this as though a pond. For I have sufficiently resolved that, as diligence is to be applied in the writing, so steadfastness is to be kept in the publishing; and indeed there is no middle course: for either the least is to be feared from these things, or one must be wholly silent in all. Farewell.

8.2.1. I believed, most skilful man, that I should commit a sin against learning if I delayed to pursue with praises that which you have prevented from being abolished—I mean letters, of which, as of something already in a manner buried, you are celebrated as the reviver, the patron, the champion; and through you, one master, in this storm of wars, Latin shores have kept their harbour, though arms have suffered shipwreck.

8.2.2. Therefore our contemporaries and our posterity universally ought, with fervent prayers, now to consecrate you—a second Demosthenes, a second Cicero—if it be allowed, with statues, now with portraits; you, by whose teaching they have been formed and instructed, will, in the very midst of an unconquered though foreign nation, retain the tokens of their ancient birth: for now that the grades of dignities are removed, by which each highest man was wont to be distinguished from each lowest, the only mark of nobility henceforth will be to know letters.

8.2.3. But us above the rest the benefits of your teaching bind, who, accustomed to write something and labouring at what those to come may read, shall have at least a competent throng of readers proceeding from your school and instruction. Farewell.

8.3.1. The Life of Apollonius the Pythagorean—not as Nicomachus the elder copied it from the draft of Philostratus, but as Tascius Victorianus from that of Nicomachus—I have sent, because you had bidden it; which, while I hastened to obey, a translation turbid, headlong, and uncouth quickly cast out into a hasty copy. And do not turn it to my discredit, as though a thing long elaborated, believe me: for while the delay of the Livian walls held me shut in (the end of which inconvenience, after the help of Christ, I owe to you), my mind, sick with cares, had not the strength to run through, even by snatches, what was to be rendered, distracted now by nightly sighs, now by daily duties.

8.3.2. To this add that, when the dusk-bringing hour had recalled me, worn out from my watches, to my lodging, scarcely was a little rest granted to my drooping eyes; for at once there was an uproar, which two certain old Gothic women, neighbours to the open court of my chamber, would raise—than whom nothing will ever be more quarrelsome, more bibulous, more given to vomiting. Indeed, when first there was some leisure on my return, this unpolished and half-raw book—a book, as they say, still new like must—mindful more of your desire than of my own duty, I have offered.

8.3.3. Wherefore lay aside for a while the Pythian laurels and Hippocrene, and those modes of song most intimately familiar to you alone, which yet, with learned persons such as you are yourself, are sweated out not so much from the fount as from the brow. Suspend that too most renowned river of pleading, which is poured into your breast not only as your nation's but as your household's, transmitted through the succeeding ages from your forefather Fronto. Lay aside for a very little your most celebrated declamations, which you compose in the king's stead—by which the renowned king himself now strikes terror into the hearts of nations beyond the sea, now, from a position of superiority, binds a treaty as victor with the barbarians trembling at the Waal, now, along the boundary of his advanced lot, as he curbs peoples under arms, so curbs arms under laws.

8.3.4. Strip yourself somehow from your most continual cares, and steal your leisure from the burdens and motions of the court. You will then recognize the history you demanded, opportunely and competently, if with our man of Tyana you now travel to Caucasus and the Indus, now to the gymnosophists of the Ethiopians and the brahmans of the Indians—wholly given to the reading, and yourself in a manner a wanderer.

8.3.5. Read of a man—peace be first granted to the catholic faith—in very many things like yourself: that is, courted by the rich, yet not courting riches; desirous of knowledge, continent of money; abstemious among feasts, linen-clad among the purple-robed, censorious among the alabaster vases; thick-coated, rough, shaggy in the midst of perfumed nations, and among the satraps of kings tiara'd, scented with myrrh, smoothed with pumice, anointed with malobathrum, precious with a venerable squalor; and since he contributed nothing of his own from a beast for food or clothing, he was on this account to the kingdoms through which he wandered not so much an object of suspicion as of awe; and, with the fortune of kings obsequious to him in all things, demanding only those benefits which he was more wont to bestow when offered than to take.

8.3.6. Why many words? If we measure and assess truly, it may chance that the writer of the philosopher's life approached, equal to the men of greater times; certainly an equal to my age has fallen to me as a reader, through you. Farewell.

8.4.1. Will that field of yours, the Octavian estate—and not so much yours as your friends'—ever, by God's will, my lord, see us together? It, near to the city, the river, and the sea, feeds guests with feasts and feeds you with guests; and besides this, it is, to the eyes of the beholders, fair in its situation: in the first place, in that the dwelling rises with walls skilfully placed for architectural harmony; then it gleams far and wide with a chapel, with porticoes, and with conspicuous baths; to this add that, with fields and waters, with vineyards and olive-groves, with vestibule, plain, and hill, it is most delightful; and now, above its provision and its plentiful furniture, it is largely stocked with the treasures of a library, where, while you yourself bend no less to the pen than to the plough, it is hard to discern whether the master's land or his mind has been the more cultivated.

8.4.2. Therefore here, as far as I recall, swift iambics, sharp elegiacs and well-rounded hendecasyllables and other songs, redolent of the flowers of music and of thyme—now to be sung by the people of Narbonne, now by those of Béziers—you laboured into being, doubtful whether more swiftly or more beautifully, about to enlarge your favour with your equals and your fame with posterity. Certainly so it seemed to me, as often as your verses were brought, still as it were warm from the anvil of meditation; for though I write not well, I judge well.

8.4.3. But, as must be confessed, an earlier age might justly be at leisure—or, what is truer, was occupied—with such studies; now it is time for serious things to be read, serious things to be written, and for thought to be given to eternal life rather than to memory; and to remember overmuch that, after our death, not our little works but our works are to be weighed. Which indeed I do not say of the present as though you did not accomplish both that are to be praised, or, if cheerfulness still endures in your speech, censure were not kept in your action; but that, as one who by Christ's favour is secretly holy, you may now be openly venerable for your religion, submitting alike neck and heart to the healthful yoke, and that your tongue keep watch upon heavenly things as their herald, your soul upon their maxims, your right hand upon offerings—chiefly, however, your right hand upon offerings, because whatever you scatter to the churches, you gather for yourself; to which exercise of virtue this above all can kindle you, that, set amid riches of whatever kind, which fools falsely call goods, if we give anything, it is our own; if we have anything, it is another's. Farewell.

8.5.1. You too shall go into our pages, pillar of friendship, Fortunalis, illustrious glory of the Iberian regions; for your familiarity with letters is not so small that it should not be fitting, through these very letters, that something of you survive after you. There shall live at once, shall live for posterity, the glory of your name.

8.5.2. For if there is in my pages any grace, reverence, or trustworthiness whatever, I wish a future age to know that nothing is firmer than your faith, fairer than your form, juster than your judgement, more enduring than your patience, weightier than your counsel, more cheerful than your feast, more pleasant than your converse. This too, above the rest, it will recognize: that the heralding of your praises came from the contrariety of fortune; for it is well-nigh the case that a thing is the more eminently esteemed which adversities proved you steadfast, than if prosperity were concealing you happy. Farewell.

8.6.1. Gaius Caesar the dictator, than whom, they say, none administered military affairs with more generalship, the studies of composing and of constant reading claimed by turns for themselves. And although, in the person of one and the same man, the leading man of his time, the care of camp and of oratorical science contended with well-nigh equal glory, yet he never deemed himself sufficiently placed at the summit of either art, before, by the testimony of your man of Arpinum, he was preferred to all other mortals.

8.6.2. Which has likewise befallen me too—if it is permitted to compare small things with great—after my measure, though by a most dissimilar likeness; and it was fitting, before all, that you first of all should learn of it, because my glory is as much your care, and my modesty very much. Flavius Nicetius, a man most illustrious by birth, of the rank of spectabilis, illustrious by his merit, and well-nigh the greatest of the men of our homeland in prudence and skill alike, extols, as far as I have learned, the volumes of my present little work with immense heralding; declaring, besides, that I have surpassed very many of the young and not a few of the old in various kinds of composing and of soldiering—I being still green in age.

8.6.3. Indeed, as far as it can be done without boasting, I rejoice in the authority of a most excellent man, if he is sure; in his love, if he is mistaken: although who, challenged now to the deeds of his forefathers, will be most inert? Who, too, will be most speechless at words? For the Ruler of the ages engendered the virtues of these arts rather in the ancient times of the ages, which—through the age of a world already growing old, the seeds, as it were, wearied and drained of marrow—show at this time something small, and that in only a few, to be admired and remembered.

8.6.4. Of this man, however—although he is the head of all studies and letters, because I have always cherished his person—I fear his opinion, uttered with too weighty an affection, beyond what truth holds. Nor on this account would I deny that I have often stood by his brilliant pleadings, of which, though I seem to render a mutual return, it is right that I be made mindful, at least in part and in passing.

8.6.5. I heard him as a young man, and then but lately a boy, when my father, prefect of the praetorium, presided over the Gallican tribunals; under whose magistracy, of course, the consul Asturius, robed in the trabea, had opened the doors of his votive year. I clung to the curule chair, if not concealed by my place in the order, certainly not seated by reason of my age, and, mingled with the troop of the cloaked assessors, I was next to those nearest the consul. So, when first the brief largess (and it was not brief) had been completed and the fasti given, it was acclaimed by all the assembly of Gaul to the leading advocates that, the festivity being forestalled, they should grace the hours before dawn—they who awaited the late day in silence—with a fitting praise of the merited fasces.

8.6.6. The conspicuous men at once looked round for Nicetius; who, sought not gradually and one by one, but tumultuously and all at once, modestly cast down his face and blushed, with a kind of preface of bashfulness. And on this account modesty, before eloquence, gave him the greatest "Bravo." He spoke in order, gravely, ardently, with great keenness, greater eloquence, the greatest discipline; and that palm-bordered robe, drunk with Tyrian dyes, amid its rustling fringes, he made the more comely with a speech more painted, more golden.

8.6.7. Through that very time, to speak in the manner of the Decemvirs, the law concerning the prescription of thirty years had been promulgated, by whose peremptory rubrics every suit abolished was bounded, drawn out to the sixth lustrum. This law, before unknown within Gaul, the orator of whom we speak first introduced into the proceedings, published at the tribunals, set forth to the parties, added to the records—with a full assembly, the bench seldom sitting, with few decisions, with many praises.

8.6.8. Besides these things, on other occasions I observed his learning unnoticed—in the way by which a man is more quickly learned—at the time when the prefecture which governs the provinces with its fasces was governed by Nicetius' counsel. Why many words? I heard nothing that I would not wish to be my own, nothing that I did not admire.

8.6.9. On account of all these good things set in the man, I rejoice that, at the marks of a censor, he is celebrated by the voice of all. For his opinion of me, in either direction, weighs greatly; which, if we find it true, is as much a favour to my security as it would be, opposed, a cause of fear. For the rest, it stands fixed and settled with me, according as I shall come to know the matter to the full, either by silence to slacken the reins or to tighten the bridle on my chatter. For if I am confirmed by the assent of the aforesaid, I shall be more talkative than Athens; if not, more silent than Amyclae itself.

8.6.10. But of my comrade and of myself enough has been said. You, now, amid these things, what of your affairs? Which it is no less at my heart to know in turn—do you hunt, do you build, do you play the countryman? Or any one of these alone? Or each in turn? Or all alike? But whether you follow Vitruvius or Columella, or one or both of them, you do most becomingly; for you can do either in the way that he who is best does it—that is, as some first-rate husbandman and architect.

8.6.11. For the rest, that you may flatter yourself as little as possible on the office of huntsman, I particularly enjoin. For you call the boars in vain to your hunting-spears, whom you have been wont rather to start than to set in motion with your most merciful hounds, of which you abound—and indeed alone. Be it so, let it be worthy of indulgence that your whelps shrink from approaching beasts terrible and corpulent: but I know not how you excuse this—that they pursue the roes, the flat-nosed flock, and the does alike, prone to flight, with downcast spirits, breasts erect, sparse steps, frequent barkings.

8.6.12. Wherefore, for the rest, more fruitfully with nets and toils, a stationary applauder, you beset the rocky crags and the woods fit for shading lairs, and—if there is any shame—you forbear to beat the open plains in your runnings and to lie in wait for the little hares of Oléron; whom it is not worth while to disturb (since they would be overcome though you seldom give chase) by leashes led openly—unless perhaps, while our Apollinaris comes between you and your father, it will be done more rightly that they be exercised.

8.6.13. Jesting apart, let me at last know what concerns you, what concerns your household. But behold, while I now wished to close a letter which has long chattered, a sudden messenger from the Santones; with whom, while in regard to you we draw out some hours in conversation, he constantly affirmed that you had lately sounded the trumpet in the fleet, and that, amid your duties, now of a sailor, now of a soldier, you rove along the winding shores of the Ocean against the curved skiffs of the Saxons, of whom you may think that, however many oarsmen you see, you behold so many arch-pirates: so do they all at once command and obey, teach and learn brigandage. Whence now even a very great cause has arisen for warning you to take the utmost heed.

8.6.14. The enemy is more truculent than any enemy. Unforeseen, he attacks; foreseen, he slips away. He scorns those who oppose him, he overthrows the unwary; if he pursues, he intercepts; if he flees, he escapes. To this add that shipwrecks exercise them, they do not terrify; with the perils of the sea they have a certain not acquaintance only, but familiarity. For since any storm renders the secure ripe to be caught, and forbids those who would catch them to be seen, in the midst of waves and broken reefs they take joy in the hope of a surprise and gladly run risks.

8.6.15. Moreover, before they loose their sails from the continent toward their homeland, and pluck up their biting anchors from the hostile shoal, it is the custom of those returning to slay every tenth captive by drowning and crucifixion—sadder for this, by a superstitious rite—and over the gathered crowd of those about to perish, to scatter the iniquity of death by the equity of the lot. By such vows they bind themselves, by such victims they discharge them; and, purified by sacrifices of this kind not so much as polluted by sacrileges, the perpetrators of an ill-omened slaughter deem it a religious thing to exact tortures rather than ransoms from a captive's head.

8.6.16. Wherefore I fear many things, suspect various ones, although on the contrary great things urge me: first, that you accompany the standards of a victorious people; next, that I allow it less lawful for chance accidents to assail wise men, among whom you are rightly reckoned; thirdly, that for comrades joined by faith, parted by abode, even safe things frequently strike grief, because fear the more readily augurs every sinister thing concerning distant and doubtful actions.

8.6.17. But you will say that the things at which I shudder are perhaps not so greatly to be cared for. That indeed is true; but neither is this false, that for those whom we love more, we fear more. Whence nonetheless, I pray, for your sake remove as soon as you can, by a prosperous report, the anguish arisen in my senses. For I can never anew be bent to this, that, concerning friends abroad—since, indeed, the trumpet and the military watchword wear them down—until I learn the favourable, I should not fear the adverse.

8.6.18. Varro the logistoricus, as you had asked, and Eusebius the chronographer I have sent; whose polish, if it reach you—if, amid your watch-cares, as in camp, you have at least some leisure by lot—you will be able, after you have wiped your arms, to remove from your mouth too the rust of speaking. Farewell.

8.7.1. Where now, I would have you say, in the world do they hide, who often flattered themselves on the masses of their heaped-up means and on the piled-up stacks of silver now blackening? Where, too, is the prerogative of those who, against the natural gifts of their juniors, swelled on the mere occasion of their precedence in age? Where are those whose kinship is recognized by no greater token than enmity?

8.7.2. Surely, when first there was room for good deeds, and at last there was weighed at the balance of the imperial judgement not a pound of coins but of characters, there remained those who most proudly thought that they were to be assessed by their fortune alone, and who, brooding thus on their vices as on their riches, wish another's person to be seen to have risen out of vanity, when they are unwilling to be branded with covetousness, that their own substance has grown; in which, however, exercised in the wrestling-school of detraction, they are wasted away, as if by oil, so by the infused venoms of their rivalries.

8.7.3. But you, amid these things, all hail—you who, enlarged with the titles of the prefecture, although hitherto you were reckoned of an illustrious lineage, have particularly, no less actively, laboured that your posterity might be the more gloriously numbered from you. For nothing is, by the opinion of every good man, more nobly born than he, whoever he is, who, with a steadfast and combined effort of mind, body, and means, exercises himself to this end—to be preferred to his own forefathers.

8.7.4. For the rest, I ask God that your sons may match you, or—what it more befits you to wish—surpass you; and that whoever cannot endure to love one advanced, seething to the marrow, may always exact from himself the penalties of his own envy; and, since he will never have any causes of pity in you, may have causes of envy; for justly, under a just prince, that man lies low who, by himself least and only by his possessions greatest, lives small in spirit and very great in patrimony. Farewell.

8.8.1. Tell me, flower of the Gallican youth, how long at last, busied with rural works, will you disdain the city? How long will the implements of grain claim for themselves, against right and divine law, hands once worn smooth by the throws of the dice? How long will your Taïonnacus weary you, a farmer of patrician stock? How long will you, not as a knight but as a herdsman, bury the spoils of the maned meadow in the wintry fallows? How long will you lay down the weight of a blunt mattock not before the headlands are dug through?

8.8.2. Why, a rival of the Serrani and the Camilli, since you guide the plough-handle, do you make a show of not wishing for the palm-bordered robe? Forbear only to play the countryman to the envy of nobility. If you cultivate your field moderately, you possess it; if too much, you are possessed by it. Give yourself back to your father, give yourself back to your homeland, give yourself back even to faithful friends, who are rightly placed among the affections. Or if the life of the dictator Cincinnatus alone delights you so, first bring along a Racilia to yoke the oxen.

8.8.3. Nor would I say to a wise man that domestic matters are not to be cared for, but with that moderation by which he considers not only what he ought to have, but what he ought to be; for if, the other arts of noble pursuits being repudiated, the nettle of propagating his estate alone solicits you, although you recall your name derived from the trabeae and the ivoried curule chairs and the gilded litters and the purple-dyed fasti, you will assuredly be found such a man that a censor ought not so much to honour you, industrious as you are because hidden, as a tax-assessor to burden you. Farewell.

8.9.1. As soon as I came to Bordeaux, your courier presented me a letter full of nectar, flowers, and pearls, in which you blame my silence and demand some of my verses for your verses—which are wont to be poured forth for you, ringing with a varied voice through the musical hollow of your palate, as if from many-holed pipes. But this you now do, abusing the royal munificence enough, secure after your gifts; because perhaps you do not recall that satiric saying about the satirist: "He is full when Horace cries euhoe."

8.9.2. Why many words? You rightly bid me sing out of leisure, because it now delights you to dance. Whatever it is, I obey nonetheless, and that not only not under compulsion but even of my own accord; only do you somehow moderate the Catonian judgement of your supercilious brow. For you know well the cheerfulness of poets, whose talents are wrapped in griefs as little fishes in nets; and if anything is harsh or sad, the tenderness of poetry does not at once unloose itself from the bond of the anguish that has befallen it. For I have not yet obtained anything from my mother-in-law's inheritance, even for the use of a third part at the price of half.

8.9.3. Meanwhile do you see how the theme of the epigram you demand will please you; me, however, my anxiety by no means permits to have one thing now in my business, another in my song. That indeed you would do beyond justice, if for the present you should, as it were, compare our writings in turn: I act the toiling man, you yourself act the happy one; I act still an exile, you yourself act already a citizen; and on this account I sing unequal things, because I ask for like ones and do not obtain equal ones.

8.9.4. But if by any chance you should receive, with a more indulgent nod, these trifles which I have written amid the torments of my mind, you will persuade me that they were like the songs of swans, whose tuneful clangour is in their pains; like too the lyric string more violently stretched, which the more it is twisted, the more musical it is. For the rest, if verses devoid of leisure or cheerfulness cannot be approved, you too, in the page which I have woven below, will find nothing to please you.

8.9.5. To these add still this, that, for matter which has fallen not to a hearer rather but to a reader, the delivery of an absent author in nowise helps; for after the work is sent, there remains nothing which a poet, even the most vocal, may do, whom distance of place does not permit even to do this—what the choirs of pantomimes are wont to do, who by good singing commend things ill written.
Why do you try now to stir to song Cirrha, or the Hyantian Muses,
or the learned waters of the Heliconides,
carved out by the stroke of the neighing winged steed,
O Lampridius, glory of our Thalia,
and so again and again compel me to write,
as if I had brought the Delphic instruments to your Delian,
and, a new Apollo, should drive the tripod, cauldron, lyre, quiver,
bows, and griffins, and shake from the double foliage
on this side the berries, on that the clusters?
You now, Tityrus, your fields recovered,
roaming through myrtles and the plane-grove,
strike the lyre, and as you sing together
your lips and quill ring back the measures to you,
astounding harper in string, voice, and metre:
but us, set here and seen but once,
the monthly moon already beholds twice over,
nor has the lord himself much leisure,
while the subjugated world seeks his answers.
Here we see the dark-blue Saxon,
accustomed to fear before only the sea, now the land;
along the outermost edges of whose crown
the razor, not content to keep its own bite,
narrows the margin of the hair,
and so, the locks cut to the skin,
the head shrinks and the face is added.
Here, the back of his head shorn, the aged Sygambrian,
after you are conquered, draws back
new hair to his old neck.
Here the Herul wanders with grey-green cheeks,
dwelling in the lowest recesses of the Ocean,
nearly one colour with the weedy deep.
Here the seven-foot Burgundian often,
with bent knee, supplicates for peace.
Under these patrons the Ostrogoth flourishes,
and pressing in turn the neighbouring Huns,
because they are subject to him, hence grows proud over those.
Hence, Roman, you seek your safety,
and against the throngs of the Scythian region,
whatever tumults the Parrhasian bear bears,
Euric, your hands are entreated,
that, strong through his settler's warfare,
the Garonne may defend the slender Tiber.
Here the Parthian Arsaces himself prays
that he may hold the height of the Susian court
under a tributary treaty.
For because he perceives that arms rise hence
against the Bosphoran regions with great preparation,
sorrowful Persia, at the sound of war,
scarce thinks the Euphrates' bank to be defended;
who, though he feign that the stars are kindred to him,
and swells with his nearness to Phoebus,
yet here, mortal, fills the air with his supplication.
Amid these things we wear away empty delays;
but you, Tityrus, forbear to provoke me;
for I do not envy, and rather marvel that I,
while I deserve nothing and spend my prayers in vain,
have begun to be a Meliboeus.

8.9.6. There is the poem, which you may review at your leisure, and, gazing at my sweat and dust, like a charioteer already crowned from the platform. For the rest, there is no reason you should suspect that I will repeat a like kind of service, even though you be delighted with the present one, unless I myself first cease to prophesy losses rather than songs. Farewell.

8.10.1. That letters are alike of use and at heart to you I greatly rejoice; for what flame of meanings or wave of words accompanies your pen I would more freely assert, did you not, while you study not a little to praise me, forbid yourself to be praised at all. And although in your letter charity preserves its sweetness, nature its eloquence, skill its discipline, yet in the choice of matter alone you have erred—although this very thing can be proclaimed in your intention, that you seem to have erred in judgement. You apply huge titles of heraldings to my character; but if you had taken any account of my modesty, it would have been fitting for you to think of that saying of Symmachus: "As true praise adorns, so false chastises."

8.10.2. In which place, however, if I measure your mind well, beyond the affection which you show as the greatest, you have also done this with art; for it is the custom of eloquent men to prove the faculty of their talents by the difficulties of their tasks, and there to fix their skilled pen, like a kind of ploughshare of a fertile breast, where the argument of a barren matter, like the dry clod of a lean turf, starves. The world gushes with like examples: the physician is known in desperation, the helmsman in a tempest; the fame of all these the preceding perils extol, which assuredly lies hidden, unless it find where it may be proved.

8.10.3. So too the great orator, if he undertakes a narrow business, then more applaudably makes manifest his ample talent. Marcus Tullius, in his other pleadings, conquered the rest; in defence of Aulus Cluentius, he conquered himself. Marcus Fronto, while he was eminent in his other orations, in the Pelops preferred himself to himself. Gaius Plinius, on behalf of Attia Viriola, brought home more glory from the centumviral platform than when he delivered before Marcus Ulpius, the incomparable prince, a comparable panegyric.

8.10.4. So too you yourself have done, who, while you wish to exercise your knowledge, have not feared that even my conscience would be a hindrance to you. Nay rather, by supplicating, heal my languors, and do not, by the snare of an ill-flattering eloquence, weigh down the frailty of a soul still sick with the burden of false glory. Indeed, since with you, though your speech is beautiful, your life is more beautiful, you indulge me more, if for my sake you would rather pray than plead. Farewell.

8.11.1. What do your people of the Nitiobroges, what your people of Vesunna do, among whom, in claiming you for themselves on either side, a holy contention always arises? One people holds you by patrimony, the other even by matrimony; and while this holds you by origin, that by marriage, better is this, that both hold you by judgement—you, however, by the gift of God happy amid these things, over whom, to be the longer engaged and possessed, it is worth while that the votive zeal of the peoples should clash!

8.11.2. But you, having disposed your presence to both, parted by turns, now restore to those a Drepanius, now to these an Anthedius. And if rhetorical instruction be demanded of you, these do not require a Paulinus, those an Alcimus. Whence I marvel the more at you, whom daily the riddling of so manifold a library, aired out, wearies, that you demand of me some of the old ditties. I obey indeed, although the recollection of jests seems unseasonable at a time of grieving.

8.11.3. The orator Lampridius is now first known to me to have been slain; whose death would consume my love with the highest anguish, even had not a violence inflicted snatched him from human affairs. He once, as jests among friends, called me Phoebus, himself having received from me the name of the Odrysian bard. Which it suits to be told beforehand, lest the figured names obscure the poem set below. To him, at a certain time, visiting Bordeaux, I sent, as it were with the Muse going before, a billeting page. I think this is more freely offered than if, composing something mournful upon the death of one departing, I, who did not please by my eloquence, should displease by my matter.
Phoebus' reminder to his too-beloved and special Thalia.
Lay aside a while your quill, foster-child,
and bind your scattered hair with a green fillet,
and let the readier ivy gird up for you
the wrinkles of your trailing robe.
Beware to wear the comic sock, nor, as it was wont,
let your high foot swim in the loose buskin;
but take care to bind such sandals
as Harpalyce, or as that maiden bound,
who cut down with the sword her vanquished suitors.
So will you go better with flying leap,
if the bandaged steps of your bare toe
guide you over the surface, with firm and quickened gait,
and the chain, bent back by the meeting loops of the bindings,
rise to your leg through the arch.
Remember, nimble in this guise, to visit
my Orpheus, who daily
softens stones and oaks and horny fibres,
tuneful, by his sweet-speaking art;
whom now the Arpinate enriches with thundering tongue,
now the pen of Maro,
or that with which you bless Latium, Horace,
a better lyrist than Alcaeus himself;
and now he swells the epic of tragedies,
now jesting comedy tempers him,
now satires inflame him, and the declamation
of tyrannical controversies.
Say: "Phoebus comes, and after his post-horses
beats the sail-winged Garonne with oars;
he bids you come to meet him, but with lodging
made ready at once beforehand." And to Leontius,
whom old Livia gives from the ancient senate,
say: "He will be here even now." And see Rusticus,
witty enough in his very name.
But if they refuse their roof as occupied,
go straightway to the thresholds of the bishops,
and, holy Gallicinus' hand kissed,
ask the loan of a small roof,
lest, if I am abandoned, my home denied,
mourning I go to the dripping taverns
and, holding both nostrils shut again and again,
groan because of the smoking kitchens,
where in the thyme-bearing dishes
the red sausage smells among twin berries,
or the clouds of the pots, their vapour joined,
smoke with the crackling pans.
Here, when the festal day has begun to rouse
the hoarse songs and to clatter the pleasurable
complaint of the buffoons,
then, then, stirred by the Muse of a wine-soaked host,
songs more worthy of you
I, a barbarian, would whisper more than they.

8.11.4. O abject necessity of being born, wretched of living, hard of dying! Behold to what point the wheel of the volubility of human affairs is led. I loved the man, I confess, well enough, though he was entangled by certain—yet pardonable—errors, and mingled lesser things with his virtues. For he was often roused by light causes, but lightly; which I nonetheless studied rather to persuade was nature rather than vice; and I urged the better view, so that the wrath which reigned in the man's breast as in its native matter, because it had been infected with a blemish of cruelty, might at least under the pretext of severity be cleansed of its spot. Besides, though frail in counsel, he was most firm in faith; most incautious, because credulous; most secure, because doing no harm. No one was so his enemy as could wring from him a curse; and yet no one so his friend as could escape his reproach. Difficult of approach, though easy when inspected, and to be borne indeed, but bearable.

8.11.5. For the rest, if you measure his orations, he was keen, well-rounded, well-ordered, vigorous; if his poems, tender, of many metres, witty, an artist. For he made verses thoroughly exact, with a marvellous variety both of feet and of figures: hendecasyllables smooth and without knot; hexameters resounding and buskined; elegiacs indeed now echoic, now recurrent, now connected by anadiplosis at end and beginning.

8.11.6. Hither, as the work he had seized counselled, he varied his ethical diction according to the quality of person, time, and place; and that not with words of any sort, but with grand, beautiful, elaborated ones. In controversial matter he was strong and brawny; in satire careful and biting; in tragedy savage and tearful; in comedy urbane and multiform; in fescennine verse blooming with words, seething with wishes; in bucolic watchful, sparing, song-full; in georgic so playing the rustic much, that he was in nothing rustic.

8.11.7. Besides, as for epigrams, he pleased not by abundance but by sharpness, which were finished neither shorter than a distich nor longer than a tetrastich; and these, though you saw not a few peppered and many honeyed, you saw all salted. In lyrics, however, following Horace, he was now borne swift in the iambic, now grave in the choriambic, now winding in the alcaic, now swelling in the sapphic. Why more? Subtle, apt, well-furnished, and most eloquent wherever his mind carried his pen—so that one might rightly judge him, after the Horatian and Pindaric swans, about to fly forth on the wings of glory.

8.11.8. To dice and ball he was not equally given; for while with the dice he was occupied to his labour, with the ball only to his pleasure, he gladly wearied others, and—what is more sweet—was the more gladly wearied himself. He wrote assiduously, although more frequently he wished to write. He also read the authors incessantly, the ancients with reverence, the recent without envy, and—what among men is most difficult—he yielded to none with difficulty the praise of talent.

8.11.9. This indeed was not only blameworthy in the man, but fatal, that he once consulted the astrologers about the end of his life—citizens of African cities, whose mind, like their region, is the more ardent; who, the constellation of the inquirer being inspected, named alike the year, month, and day which—to use a term of the mathematic art—he would have as climacteric, inasmuch as to them, the theme being offered, the scheme as of a bloody nativity had lain open; because, of course, in the year of the friend's birth, whatever gentle globe of the planetary stars a prosperous rising had raised into the zodiacal intervals, this, at its setting, the reddening with learned fires—whether disjoined Mercury over the diameter, or retrograde Saturn over the square, or restored Mars over the centre—had exasperated.

8.11.10. But of these things, if any or in any way they are—although they are utterly false and therefore deceiving—if anything more fully and plainly, better face to face; though you yourself too study arithmetic and, with your diligence, anxiously unroll Vertacus, Thrasybulus, Saturninus, as one who always meditates nothing but the arcane and the lofty. Meanwhile, for the present, nothing was done conjecturally, nothing by riddles, since the time and the manner of his foretold death entangled this our rash inquirer into the future, who long shuffled in vain.

8.11.11. For at home, pressed and strangled by the hands of his slaves, his breath stopped, his throat constricted, he perished—not to say by the end of Lentulus, Jugurtha, and Sejanus, certainly by that of Numantine Scipio. In this slaughter these things were the less sad, that the crime itself, with the author of the parricidal deed, was discovered at daybreak; for who is so far from the sense of men, who so blinded in both eyes, as not, the corpse of the dead man inspected, at once to gather the signs of a life wrung out?

8.11.12. For at once the livid skin, the protruding eyes, and, in the buried face, traces no less of wrath than of grief, were the proof. The earth indeed was found wet with the falling gore, because after the deed the brigands themselves had turned the dead man's face to the pavement, prone, as though an overboiling flux of blood had emptied him. But, the man at once seized who had been the kindler, instigator, and standard-bearer of that very faction, and the other accomplices oppressed and separately examined, the terror of torments dragged the truth of the crime from unwilling breasts.

8.11.13. And would that, while he imprudently, trusting, consulted vain things, he had not deserved to meet this end! For whoever shall have presumed to pry into the forbidden, the secret, the prohibited, I fear that he will swerve from the rules of catholic faith, and be made worthy to have adverse things answered concerning his state, while he seeks the unlawful. Vengeance indeed followed the dead man, but these things rather profit those who are to live. For as often as a murderer is punished, it is not a remedy but a solace to be avenged.

8.11.14. Love has impelled me to go on rather far, whose anguish I could not breathe out in silence. You meanwhile, if there is anything there worthy to be known, indicate it quickly, writing at least for this, that the reading may lighten my mind, heavy with sadness. For there was much grief, and rightly, to my confused breast, when I committed these things to the page alone. For nothing else at this time does it please me to write, speak, or revolve by hand, speech, or counsel. Farewell.

8.12.1. Does the city of Bazas so much possess you—a city set not on turf but on dust—does the Syrtic field and the wandering soil and the sands flying in the wrangling winds so much possess you for themselves, that you, demanded by great prayers, parted by small spaces, awaited for many days, neither powers, nor friendships, nor oysters fattened in their preserves can draw to Bordeaux? Or do the uncertainties of the roads hold you in suspense in the wintry seasons; and, because the Bigerric whirlwind is wont to confuse the tokens of the shifting causeways, do you fear a kind of pedestrian shipwreck on an earthly journey?

8.12.2. Where, we ask, has Calpe, lately subdued by your steps, so quickly departed from your mind? Where the tents fixed in the western bounds of the Gaditanians? Where that same limit of wandering for my Trygetius which once was Hercules'? Do you so much differ from your very self, that you have wholly yielded to the laws of sloth—you, in whose roaming through the secrets of fabled regions the work of toil failed sooner than the intent of fatigue?

8.12.3. And after these things you tread so sluggishly the harbour of Alingo, as if you had now to set out to the Danube frontier against the raiding Massagetae, or as if even now the pools of the Nile's water, feared by the native crocodiles, were to be crossed by your ship. And since you are not so retarded even by the interposition of twelve miles, what, do we suppose, would you have done with the army of Marcus Cato in the Leptitan Syrtis?

8.12.4. But however you tremble at the mere names of the winter months, so mild is the face of the sky, so warm, so clear, and it has breezes rather than winds, so that the season cannot retain you more strenuously than the mildness can invite you. But if you spurn the summoning letter, I believe you will not resist even verses—coaxing impellers and, as far as I suspect, strenuous executors of my desire, whose camp will be moved against you after two days.

8.12.5. Behold, my Leontius, easily first of the Aquitanians, behold Paulinus, now but little inferior to his father, to the place I named above, through the ebbing currents of the Garonne, will come to meet you not only with a fleet but even with the river. Here, in measured rowing-chant, the rowers among the benches, the steersmen among the stern-ornaments, will sing your praises. Here a couch built up with cushions, here a board strewn with two-coloured counters, here frequent dice, about to rebound from the ivoried steps of the towers, await you; here, lest the rolling bilge-water wet your dangling foot, the curved bellies of the firwood timbers will be platformed with a woven texture; here, by the lattice bent over the awnings, you will avoid the treachery of a wintry calm.

8.12.6. What more can be spent upon your delicate idleness than that you find you have arrived, when you scarce feel that you are coming? Why do you mutter? Why do you delay? The very creeping snails, with their native houses, seem to me about to outstrip your arrival. There is besides for you a most copious larder, abundantly stuffed with heaped-up dainties, if only there be a spirit equal to the spending in airing them out.

8.12.7. Why many words? Come either to be fed or to feed; nay, what is more pleasing, to do both; come with your inland equipment to war down and subjugate these gluttons of the Médoc furniture. Here let the Adour fish insult over the Garonne mullets; here let the throng of cheap crabs yield to the supplies of the Labourd lobsters.

8.12.8. You, however, though you are to fight against the rest in this kind of battle, if you think anything is to be conceded to my judgement (for it is not unjust to trust one who has experience), will make our senator, my host, exempt from this conflict; whose feast and roof, if you enter under them, you would deem the dishes of Cleopatra and lavish quarters. For although both he himself and his homeland contend over this pursuit, it was long ago a settled opinion that he surpasses the rest of the citizens, though that town too surpasses the rest of the cities. Farewell.

8.13.1. We rejoice, most blessed Bishop, that many kinds of virtues are heaped up in you by the supernal gift; since you are said to act the nobleman without pride, the powerful man without envy, the religious man without superstition, the lettered man without ostentation, the grave man without ineptitude, the witty man without effort, the steadfast man without harshness, the affable man without seeking popularity.

8.13.2. Besides, to these goods fame heaps this most excellent thing, that it asserts you to transcend all these so many graces by the topmost height of your charity—fame, I say, which, when it sings of your praises, says much and keeps back more. For to those set farther off it can assign the design of your actions, not their number; by the relation of which, kindled, I of my own accord first run forward, as becomes one far inferior, to discharge my duties; nor do I fear to be charged with garrulity at any time, who could hitherto be blamed for taciturnity.

8.13.3. I commend Promotus, the bearer of this letter, indeed already known to you before, but lately made, by your prayers, our fellow-tribesman; who, though by race a Jew, has nonetheless chosen rather to be reckoned an Israelite by faith than by blood, and, aspiring to the citizenship of that heavenly city, and disdaining the killing letter for the quickening spirit, contemplating alike the rewards set before the just here, and foreseeing here that, unless he made his desertion to Christ from circumcision, he would through eternal ages suffer everlasting torments, chose that his homeland should be reckoned to him Jerusalem rather than Hierosolyma.

8.13.4. These things known, let the spiritual Sara receive into her maternal arms the now truer son of Abraham as he draws near; for he ceased to belong to Hagar the handmaid when he exchanged the servitude of legal observance for the liberty of grace. For the rest, what cause of coming hither he himself had, he will be able more profitably to explain by present narration; but to us, for the reasons I have written above, he is held most dear—which I therefore signify, because he commends each man most effectively who has laid open the pure causes of a just commendation. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

8.14.1. Long since, venerable Bishop, though your face has not yet been beheld by sight, yet your conduct has been inspected. For the praise of holy merits, when diffused, is not content to be bound within final spaces. Hence it is that, because a measure is not set to a good conscience, neither is a term found to a good repute.

8.14.2. Deem what I say false, unless a competent witness has come to my profession—a head once conspicuous enough in that monastery of Lérins, a fellow-monk of the Lupi and the Maximi, and aspiring to follow in the woodland glades of parsimony the Memphitic and Palestinian archimandrites. This is the bishop Antiolus, by whose account I anxiously studied to learn who was your father, and who and of what sort you brothers are, by what prerogative of character you both discharge the highest pontificate; and I remember rejoicing that I have learned it.

8.14.3. To which father once—namely, having you—scarce would the house of Aaron, the ancient bishop, deservedly be compared; whom, though the right hand of his law-giving brother first lost in the midst of the eremite people by the oil of sanctification, calling his sons to the duties of a like office, yet the felicity of that man over Ithamar and Eleazar was discoloured by Nadab and Abihu, smitten with the thunderbolts; whose souls, however slain, we believe to be absolved, yet we know their persons to have been punished.

8.14.4. But you, about to touch the page of the altar, offer nothing, as I hear, of strange fire, but, with the accompanying victims of charity and chastity, burn the most fragrant incense in the censers of the heart. To this, as often as you bind the yoke of the law upon the necks of the proud by the bonds of preaching, then you spiritually immolate bulls to God; as often as you drive those polluted by the stench of a luxuriant conscience to the sweet odour of chastity by the goads of correction, Christ reckons that you have offered him the violence of he-goats.

8.14.5. As often as, at your exhortation, in any pricked man the soul, penally recalling its faults, sighs, who would doubt that you have, by a mystic sacrifice, offered up the pairs of turtle-doves or the two young pigeons, which assign the double substance of each of our men as much by number as by groaning? As often as anyone, at your warning, shall have scorched his fat body and the seething suet of his swollen belly, to be boiled down by the frequent fire of fasts, it is doubtful to none that you then consecrate the fine flour fried in a certain frying-pan of continence.

8.14.6. As often as you persuade someone who sets aside the figments of a faithless mind to answer to sound doctrine, to believe the faith, to hold the way, to hope for life, who would doubt that, in the amendment of this converted man—who is now free from heresy, free from hypocrisy, free from schism—you consecrate the most purified bread of the show-bread with the unleavened cakes of sincerity and truth?

8.14.7. Lastly, who would not know that whatever in the days of the law was figuratively immolated in bodies, all that you, in the time of grace, manifestly offer in characters? And therefore I render abundant thanks to God, that according to the quality of your page I easily recognize that the aforesaid bishop, when he said great things of you, kept silent about greater; wherefore no one would doubt that you, who are good when judging, and better when reading, are best when seen.

8.14.8. Megethius the cleric, the bearer of your eloquence, his business prospering as he wished, since he brought the gifts of your letter, carries back my compliances; whom we have at least helped by our wish, because by the deed perhaps we cannot. Through him I earnestly beseech that you both, brothers, may irrigate our thirst frequently with lettered letters—you the more frequently. But if the difficulty of the intervening journey resists our wishes, at least sometimes supplicate for your suppliants; and it is the greater thing if you deign to grant us salvation by rare intercessions rather than dignity by frequent addresses. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

8.15.1. While you wish the holy Anianus—the greatest and most consummate bishop, equal to Lupus and not unequal to Germanus—to be celebrated with the highest praises, and desire that the character, merits, and virtues of so great a man be fixed in the hearts of the faithful—to whom even this is given for glory, not without justice, that he died with you as his successor—you had demanded of me that I should promise you to make known to posterity, with my pen, the war of Attila, in which, namely, were contained the siege, the assault, the breaking in but not the plundering of the city of Orléans, and that famous prophecy of the bishop heard from heaven.

8.15.2. I had begun to write; but, the burden of the undertaken work perceived, it irked me to have begun. On account of this I have trusted to no ears what I had first, by my own censure, condemned. It will be granted, as I hope, to your prayer and to the merits of the highest bishop, that on whatever occasion, and indeed a swift one, we may serve his heralding. For the rest, you, a just creditor, will laudably have indulged this to the imprudence of a rash debtor, that what seems to me insoluble may seem to you too irreclaimable. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

8.16.1. I had promised Petronius, an illustrious man, that I would despatch the present little work in a few letters; whose ears I have not spared, while I spare yours; for I preferred that the labour of correction should regard him, the honour of publication you, and that this volume should come into your hands at another's risk, by my compliance. The promise is fulfilled; for if your skill should inspect the marks of the headings collected onto the parchments, already, unless I am mistaken, a copious copy knocks at you; already one comes to the margins of the rollers; already it is time, as the satirist says, for our Orestes to be finished even upon the back.

8.16.2. Here I have not, in the manner of the old study, summoned a feigned Terpsichore, nor, beside the gushing of the Aganippic fount, have I drawn my pen through dewy banks and mossy pebbles. And would that here nothing soft, nothing greedy, nothing borrowed from the crossroads were found! For to a ripe reader, such as you are yourself, not so much a boneless, tender, nerveless diction pleases, as one a little old-fashioned, brawny, and as it were masculine. But let these things be reserved for better men; it suffices me, if you quickly forgive that we are slow.

8.16.3. Besides, if the illustrious man had demanded that something more amply be written in addition, we should have fallen into great delays. For through our little cupboards and chests there remained nothing worthy of being brought forth. Whence learn that, though we have not yet begun to be silent, we have certainly begun to wish for silence, from a twofold cause: that, if we please, the few may incite the pleasure of those about to read; if we are refused, the many may not excite distaste; since in this style there is not urbane wit, but rustic simplicity.

8.16.4. For whence to us that grim and most ancient kind of speaking? Whence those Salian or Sibylline words, or those fetched from the Sabines all the way from Cures, which, the masters for the most part keeping silence, some fetial or flamen or aged riddler of legal questions would more readily lay open? We have composed our little works in a speech dry, slender, and certainly for the most part common, of which on this side the honour is rare, that the use is frequent; on this side the grace is difficult, that the invention is easy.

8.16.5. Indeed I profess boldly that, as here there is nothing keen, nothing eloquent, so there is nothing set down that is not finished, not according to a model. But why these things with more words? My diction—which suffices me—pleases my friends, in whom, however, I embrace either case: whether they do not deceive me by their examination, or are deceived by their charity. And God, for what remains, I ask, in time to come, that those who follow may either be deceived likewise or pass judgement. Farewell.

9.1.1. You require, my lord son, that, the boundary of the earlier letters broken through, our pen run forward into further matter, not content to be enclosed by the privilege of the number aforesaid. You add also causes by which this ninth book should grow upon the eight earlier volumes: namely, that Gaius Secundus, whose course you pronounce us to follow in this work, bounds his epistolary work with like headings.

9.1.2. What you bid is not unworthy of approval; although this very thing which you piously enjoin proves arduous and not opportune for whatever little praise has now once been won: first, because there is a late conjoining of the present increase to a little work already published; next, because, before any judges whatever, unless I am mistaken, it is most unseemly that, for one matter, a single beginning and three epilogues should be found.

9.1.3. Likewise too I know not how it can be made pardonable that our garrulity will not endure to be restrained even after the term has been announced—unless because perhaps the measure which can be set to pages cannot itself be set to friendships. Wherefore it befits you to be in a kind of watchtower, as it were, for guarding my reputation, and to make manifest to the curious the reason of this deed, and what all the best men think on this point, to lay open to me by a most frequent reply.

9.1.4. Moreover, if, when I am compelled to chatter, you yourself persist in keeping silent, it is not over-unjust that you too should be punished in turn by the retaliation of our silence. So do you first, you above all, forgive the task you impose and the service. But we, if any copy fall into our hands, will quickly add it to the margins of the eighth book.

9.1.5. Although your Apollinaris, who has zeal in all other things, in this at least is most negligent, since he is held by very little reading, whether compelled or willing—yet, as far as it seems to me, I would not refuse to be joined to those fathers to whom, by their zeal, wish, and fear, it is laboriously, though with difficulty, persuaded that something praiseworthy is enough in their sons, and with more difficulty enough. Farewell.

9.2.1. The bishop Albisus and the deacon Proculus—on this account to be pronounced our masters of conduct, because they deserve to be your disciples—have brought letters, with whose sacrosanct address you have gifted me; which letters, however, impose on me very much honour, more burden. Whence too I rejoice at their blessing in such a way that I am confounded by their injunction, since, wholly disturbed, I do not even in part obey. For you bid things as diverse as they are excessive, and decree that a work be unfolded which is as hard for my extremity to complete as it is imprudent to begin.

9.2.2. But if I measure well the amplitude of the proven piety in you, you have laboured more that the affection of your heart, rather than the effect of our work, should be made public. For when Jerome the translator, Augustine the dialectician, Origen the allegorist bring forth for you, in a wholesome harvest of doctrine, the heavy ears of spiritual meanings—shall now, forsooth, the dry stubble of a fasting tongue crackle for you from my part? In this manner you would also rightly join the hoarse geese to the songs of swans, and the chattering whispers of base sparrows to the measured plaints of nightingales.

9.2.3. What of this—that it would even thus be done arrogantly and unseemly, if I should undertake the weight of the enjoined task, a new cleric, an old sinner, of light knowledge, heavy conscience—namely so that, if I sent anything written anywhere, my person would not even then be absent from the laughter of the judges, when it had been absent from their sight? Do not, I pray, my Lord Bishop, demand too much that my modesty, suckling somehow as it is, be disfigured by the rashness of beginning this work; for so great is the envy of detractors that the matter you send would more swiftly obtain disgrace when begun than approval when finished. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.3.1. Your eloquence keeps its custom, as does your piety; and on this account we greatly esteem your speech, because you write eloquently; your affection, because you write willingly. For the rest, at present, pardon first asked and obtained, I think it most cautious and most wholesome—especially through these cities which, much segregated by their situation, are cut off, while the routes are suspect through the movements of the nations—to renounce a more frequent pen, and, the assiduity of mutual converse being deferred for a while, to undertake rather the care of keeping silence. Which, among persons bound by intervening affection, although it is most harsh and most bitter, is yet not brought about by causes of any sort, but by very many sure and necessary ones, each of which proceeds from a different origin.

9.3.2. Of these this will be numbered first in the reckoning: that no courier passes the guards of the public causeways uninterrogated; who, though there is no danger, inasmuch as he is free of crime, is yet wont to suffer very much difficulty, while a wakeful searcher tracks out every secret of the bearers. And if perchance their answer should waver ever so little from the questions, what is not found written is believed to be commanded by word of mouth; and through this the one who is sent generally suffers injury, the one who sends, odium—and more in this time, in which the treaties of kingdoms long ago established between rivals are again rendered doubtful through discordant conditions.

9.3.3. Besides this, my very mind lies wounded by domestic losses on this side and that; for, by the image of duty or, what is truer, the necessity, driven from my native soil, here relegated, I am broken by various anguishes in every direction, because I suffer here the inconveniences of a stranger, there the losses of an outlaw. Wherefore to pay you now letters a little more polished is either unseasonably asked of me or impudently undertaken by me—letters which, whether pleasant in their jesting or cultivated in their style, it belongs to the happy to exchange. Moreover, a pleasant speech, when the mind is in mourning, is a kind of barbarism of conduct.

9.3.4. Nay rather, endow a soul ill-conscious of itself, and trembling hourly at the recollected debts of a penal life, with those most frequent and most powerful supports of your prayers—you who are skilled in the prayers of the islands, which you have transferred from the wrestling-school of the eremite congregation and from the senate of the Lérins cell-dwellers into the city too, over whose church's holy things you keep watch—in nothing changed from an abbot by being a priest, since under the pretext of a new dignity you have not relaxed the rigour of the old discipline. By these prayers, then, as I said above, most efficacious, obtain that the Lord be our portion, and that, enrolled in the troops of our fellow-tribesmen the deacons, we may not remain earthly, we for whom no earth remains, and that we may begin to be exiles, as from the gains of the world, so too from its faults.

9.3.5. The third cause, or even the greatest, why I have forborne to write to you, is that I immensely fear that tropological and figured kind of composing in you—most eminent and many ways polished with words—which the letter we received from you shows: although long ago I, a hoarse applauder, have heard your sermons, now sudden, now, when reason demanded it, laboriously elaborated—then especially when, at the weekly festivals of the dedicated church of Lyon, at the request of your sacrosanct colleagues, you were entreated to preach. Where, while you discoursed of something midway between the spiritual and the forensic rules—since you are most learned in both disciplines—we surrounded you, our minds alike erect and our ears bent, here doing too little for our desire, because you had satisfied our judgement.

9.3.6. For these causes I have tempered my pen and will temper it, speaking briefly that I may obey, about to be silent long that I may learn. For the rest, it is your part, my Lord Bishop, to bend yourself sufficiently to works that will live, of wholesome and singular doctrine; for whoever listens to you teaching and disputing learns to do praiseworthy things more than to speak. But now, for what remains, grant with pardon a page that plays the rustic and complies with you, in which, on my own authority, if it be compared with your letters, there is a most infant style. But whither, stupid that I am, do I allege these things? For to deprecate ineptitudes overmuch is itself most inept—in which, if you, the unmixed arbiter, unloose the matter to the full, you will laugh at very many things, blame more. But this too I embrace, if, for the charity in which you abound, you are not everywhere most continent of judging—that is, if your opinion should annul anything upon these pages. For then I shall the more surely rejoice that you have approved the rest, if I learn that you have crossed out some. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.4.1. Our traveller and courier wears the tracks of his accustomed journey, often retracing the space of road and of regions that separates our towns. Wherefore it befits us too to follow the duties of a diligence once proposed, which we ought to redouble, with a certain intentness of mind, both with the other travellers and especially when Amantius runs between, lest perchance he himself should seem to demand letters from custom more than we to dictate them from love, my Lord Bishop; and therefore remember more those of your own, among whom we presume to be reckoned, and who, as we are raised by your prosperities, so are cast down by your adversities.

9.4.2. For that you have lately, by the necessity of certain brothers, endured many anguishes, has come, by a tearful report, to us who weep. But you, flower of priests, gem of bishops, strong in knowledge, stronger in conscience, spurn the threats and waves of the world's storm-clouds, since you yourself have frequently taught that one comes to the promised banquets of the patriarchs, or to the nectar of the heavenly cups, through the goblets of earthly bitternesses.

9.4.3. Willy-nilly, whoever attains the kingdom of the despised Mediator follows his example.
