However much the affliction of the present life may pour out for us the bowls of anxieties, we endure small things, if we recall what He drank at the gibbet who invites us to heaven. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.5.1. Although we dwell, perchance, in a seat a little more separated than our common mind could wish, yet our diligence would not, as far as it concerns the discharge of duty, be hindered by the obstacle of the intervening journey, were it not that, divided by kingdoms, we are recalled, by the law of our different lots, from a more frequent exchange of speech; which lots now at least—because, after the pact of peace entered into, they will be allied with faithful minds—our letters will begin to pass frequently, since they cease to be suspect. Accordingly, my Lord Bishop, join with your sacrosanct brothers prayers that will alike supplicate Christ, that, deigning to prosper what we do, and tempering the disputes of our dominion and checking arms, He may endow them with innocence, us with quiet, and all with security. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.6.1. Your holiness availed before Christ, by the effect of its intercession, on behalf of our most beloved one (why should I speak the name, the person? you will recognize all)—of whose youthful looseness you often used now to complain openly before witnesses called in, now to groan in silence. So lately, the company of a most shameful handmaid being broken off, to whom, bound by obscene habit, he had wholly given himself over, he by a sudden correction of himself took counsel for his patrimony, his posterity, his fame.

9.6.2. For, emptied through the losses of his estate, as soon as he began to understand and reconsider how much of his little goods, from grandfather and father, the costliness of the domestic Charybdis had licked away, though coming to his senses late, yet at last, as it were, he bit the bridle and shook free his neck, and, fixing in his ears, as they tell, the wax of Ulysses, fled, deaf against the vices, from the blandishments of the harlot shipwreck, and—as was fitting—the praiseworthy man took to wife, untouched, a girl as supreme in character and birth as she was foremost in fortune.

9.6.3. This indeed would be glory, if he had so left his pleasures as not even to be joined to a wife; but, even if it chance to migrate from error to good character, it is the lot of few to begin with the greatest things, and for those who have long indulged themselves in everything, straightway to cut off everything and all at once.

9.6.4. Wherefore it is your part to obtain as soon as possible, by diligent prayer, the hope of children for the wedded pair; the consequence will be that, one or another son being born (and I have said too much), he may henceforth abstain from things lawful, who presumed upon things unlawful. For the spouses themselves, although wedded but lately, conduct themselves with such character, with such modesty, that truly you would recognize, if you saw them but once, that there is very much that distinguishes that most honourable wedded love from the figments and allurements of concubinage. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.7.1. A certain man, going from Auvergne to Belgica (the person is known to me, the cause unknown; nor does it matter), after he had come to Reims, wheedled out of your scribe or bookseller—won over, be it by a price, be it by a favour—a most copious draft of your declamations, willy-nilly. He, returning to us and exceedingly boastful, since so many volumes had been obtained, whatever he had brought (though we were ready to buy it), yet, as a citizen (nor was it unjust), pressed upon us as a gift. It was at once my care, and that of those who study, since we deservedly wished to read, to hold very much, to transcribe all.

9.7.2. By the assent of all it was pronounced that few like things can now be composed. For there is one rare, or none, to whom, as he meditates, there stands by abundantly an equal arrangement through the causes, a placing through the letters, a composing through the syllables; to this, opportunity in examples, trustworthiness in testimonies, propriety in epithets, urbanity in figures, force in arguments, weight in meanings, a river in words, a thunderbolt in clausulae.

9.7.3. The structure, indeed, strong and firm, and knit by the cuttings of most witty conjunctions with indissoluble caesuras, yet nonetheless slippery and light and in all ways well-rounded, and such as fittingly speeds the reader's tongue unimpeded, lest, suffering rough junctures, it stammer as it is rolled through the vault of the palate; in fine, wholly liquid throughout and ductile, as when a finger, with no driven nail, glides over crystalline or onyx surfaces, since no tenacious fracture, caught by chinky obstacles, holds it back.

9.7.4. Why more? There exists at present no oration of any living man which your skill could not pass and outstrip, not without labour. Whence too I almost suspect, my Lord Bishop, that on account of your overflowing and ineffable eloquence (pardon be granted to the saying) you are proud. But although you shine with a good thing, as of conscience so of a most well-ordered diction, you should nonetheless by no means flee from us, who praise things well written, even if we do not write things to be praised.

9.7.5. Wherefore cease henceforth to decline our judgements, which threaten nothing biting, nothing reproachful. Otherwise, if you delay to make our sterility fruitful with eloquent colloquies, we shall lie in wait for the markets of pilferers, and the cunning hand of housebreakers shall, of its own accord, plunder your writing-cases, we conniving and abetting; and you will then begin in vain to be moved, despoiled by theft, if now, when asked, you are not moved by duty. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.8.1. Although we did not expect, yet did desire, your letters, the old courier delivered them—found fit, to whom the duty may rightly be entrusted again, since he delivered the first so well. Therefore, gifted with a second address, or rather a blessing, I too in turn pay back another "Hail," combining compliances equalled in number, not in merits.

9.8.2. And since, my Lord Bishop, we now live with minds joined but regions disjoined, and are forbidden by the situation of our separated dwelling to enjoy the mutual sight of one another, pray that, by a longed-for and religious departure, the anguishes and burden of the present life discharged, when the holy day of judgement shines forth with the resurrection, we may be joined to your throngs, to serve them—even under the occasion of a Gibeonite servitude; because, according to the heavenly promises, which pledged that the sons of God should be gathered from the nations, if pardon console us who are guilty, while glory awaits you who are blessed, we shall be divided, though by the difference of our deeds, yet not by the distance of our places. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.9.1. You have complained, most sacred man, that we both keep silence too long; I recognize the zeal of your part herein, but I do not recognize the guilt of ours. For, long ago bidden to chatter, I did not keep silence, with letters running on ahead—which, however, to be perused, when they had come to Riez, you, who were then at Apt, most aptly were absent for. And that was greatly votive and most longed-for by me, that the enjoined letter should neither be denied as written to friendship nor be subjected, when read, to censure.

9.9.2. Let us pass these things over. You bid a copious page be sent again; to obey, the wishes are at hand for one hastening, the causes are absent; for a salutation, unless the matter actively brings some business, is succinct; and he who extends it with unnecessary words, turned aside from the rule of the Sallustian track, strays—Sallust, who blames Catiline for having had eloquence enough, wisdom too little. Whence, "Hail" said, we straightway say "Farewell." Pray for us.

9.9.3. But it is well, it is well, that, as I was about now and now to fold up my little paper, a matter chanced to occur, in the upbraiding of which, if either my joy or my anger should restrain itself longer, I shall judge myself worthy of the affront received. You have come, master, into my hands (nor do I only exult, but truly I insult), you have come—and indeed such as for a long time now our desires awaited. I doubt indeed whether even unwilling, but certainly like one unwilling, since by your providing—or, if you altogether deny this, your acquiescing—I have been unsaluted by your books, and these, what is much more injurious, when they passed by the Arvernian territory, grazing not only my walls but even my flanks.

9.9.4. Or did you fear that we would envy your sayings? But by God's indulgence we are addicted to no vice less; to whom, if it lay subject from my part as to others, despair of attaining would even so take away the rivalry of contending. Or did you dread my eyebrow, as of a difficult and rigid applauder? And what neck of skill is there so great in anyone, or what dropsy, that it should not pursue your lukewarm things too with the most fervent praises?

9.9.5. Or did you take care to have me disdained and neglected for this reason—that you despised my youth? Which I little believe. Or that I am unlearned? Which I bear the more—yet so that one who knows not how to speak does know how to hear; for even those who have been present at the circus games do not refuse to pass judgement on the chariots. Or did we by any chance fall out, so that we were thought likely to disparage those little books which you had published? But, God presiding, that our friendships are slight, not even an enemy can feign.

9.9.6. To what end these things? you ask. Behold, now I lay it open—both what I rejoice to have tracked out, and at what I am angry that you concealed. I have read your volumes, which the bishop and monk Riochatus, twice a pilgrim of this world, carries back for you to your Britons—he being now, for the present, fortunate rather, who does not grow old, and who, not about to fail the living, will after his burial become, through the very things he wrote, a survivor of himself. So this same venerable man, while he tarried at our town, until the storm of the stirred-up nations should rage itself out—whose huge whirlwind had then bristled up on this side and that—so unfolded the rest of your gifts that he most urbanely covered over the more excellent things he carried, dissembling, by your flowers, the lighting up of my thorns.

9.9.7. But after two months or more, when likewise some of the travellers had betrayed that he had quickly set out from us, secretly carrying treasures of mystic wealth in closed wrappers, I, having pursued him as he departed with swift horses, which could easily outstrip the spaces of the previous day's journey, leapt with a kiss upon the throat of the seized brigand—with human jest, with the gesture of a beast, as when a tigress, robbed, leaps over with flying foot to shake off any of her whelps from the neck of the Parthian ravisher.

9.9.8. Why many words? I embrace the knees of the captured guest, I halt the beasts of burden, I bind the reins, I loose the baggage, I find the sought volume, I bring it forth, I read it through, I excerpt the greatest chapters, breaking them off from the great. And the leaping nimbleness of the scribes granted a certain abridgement to one dictating in haste, who caught with signs what they did not hold with letters. With what tears indeed we were wet, drenched mutually in turn by weeping, then when we were separated from an embrace often repeated, it is long to have told, nor does it matter; for what suffices for a triumphal joy, I returned home laden with spoils of charity and possessed of a spiritual prize.

9.9.9. You ask now what I judge of my spoils; I would not yet betray it, that you might hang the longer in expectation; for I should avenge myself more, if I kept silent what I felt. But now neither do you yourself pride yourself in vain, inasmuch as you understand that there is in you a power of pleading so to compass, that for your reader, whether reluctant or willing, the force of pleasure strikes out the necessity of heralding. Accordingly, receive what we, even having suffered injury, judge concerning your writings.

9.9.10. We read a work most laborious, manifold, keen, sublime, digested by headings, heaped up with examples, bipartite under the scheme of a dialogue, quadripartite under the theme of the causes. You had written very many things ardently, more pompously; these things simply, not rustically; those wittily, not craftily; weighty matters maturely, profound ones carefully, doubtful ones steadfastly, argumentative ones in the manner of disputation, some severely, some blandly, all morally, choicely, powerfully, most eloquently.

9.9.11. And so, following you through so many kinds of narration over the whole broadest field of your composition, I easily perceived nothing in the eloquence of others, nothing in their talents, equally polished. That I feel these things true you sufficiently approve, since not even when offended do I judge otherwise. In fine, the oration of an absent man, as far as we suppose, can grow no more, unless perchance the author, speaking face to face, add somewhat to these things—voice, hand, motion, modesty, the artist . . .

9.9.12. So, endowed with these gifts of mind and of letters, you have yoked to yourself, my Lord Bishop, a wife fair—but one marrying with Deuteronomy attesting; whom you, still a young man, having descried among the hostile bands, and there, in the battle-line of the opposing party, fallen in love with, repulsed by no resisting warriors, with the conquering arm of desire you carried off—Philosophy, namely, who, violently rescued from the number of the sacrilegious arts, her hair of superfluous religion shaved, and her eyebrow of secular knowledge cut off, and the wrinkles of her most ancient garments lopped away (that is, the windings of grim dialectic which veil false morals and unlawful things), now cleansed, has joined her limbs to yours in a mystic embrace.

9.9.13. She, from your earliest years long your handmaid, she your inseparable companion at your side, whether exercising you in the urban wrestling-schools or wont to mortify you in the hidden solitudes, she, the consort of the Athenaeum, she of the monastery, with you renounces the worldly, with you proclaims the heavenly disciplines. Whoever shall provoke you, joined in this marriage, will feel that the Academy of Plato serves in the church of Christ, and that you philosophize more nobly:

9.9.14. first, that you assert the ineffable Wisdom of God the Father, with the eternity of the Holy Spirit; then, besides, that you neither feed your hair nor glory in the cloak or club as in sophistic insignia, nor affect pride from the distinction of dress, pomp in elegance, ostentation in squalor; nor do you greatly emulate this—that through the Areopagite gymnasia or the prytanea there be painted, with bent neck Speusippus, Aratus with bowed, Zeno with contracted brow, Epicurus with distended skin, Diogenes with flowing beard, Socrates with falling locks, Aristotle with arm thrust out, Xenocrates with leg drawn up, Heraclitus with weeping eyes shut, Democritus with laughter and open lips, Chrysippus with fingers constricted on account of the marks of numbers, Euclid with them spread out on account of the spaces of measures, Cleanthes with them gnawed on account of both.

9.9.15. Nay rather, whoever shall have contended will find the Stoics, Cynics, Peripatetics, those heresiarchs, shaken by their own arms, by their own engines too. For their followers, if they shall have resisted the Christian dogma and meaning, soon, you being their master, bound by their own home-bred entanglements, will headlong be netted in their own snares, the hooked syllogisms of your proposition catching the voluble tongue of the prevaricators; while you rather knot the slippery questions with categorical coils, in the manner of keen physicians, who, when reason compels, trust for a remedy against poisons even from the serpent itself.

9.9.16. But this, in these times, is under the contemplation only of your conscience or the power of your doctrine; for who would follow your footsteps with an equal step, to whom alone it is given to speak better than you have learned, to live better than you speak? Wherefore deservedly all good men, and that above all others in your age, will celebrate you as most blessed, whose life has so doubly grown illustrious by your sayings and your deeds, that—since indeed the right hand has now numbered your years—proclaimed by your own age, to be longed for by another, praiseworthy by either deed, you may depart, about to leave yourself to strangers, your own things to those nearest. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.10.1. He has delivered to you my letters whom it would have been fitting to offer me yours; for our brother Caelestius, lately returned to you from Béziers, drew out of me a certain bond of cession concerning the status of our Iniuriosus. Which indeed I wrote, broken no less by your modesty than by your wish; for it was fitting that we, of our own accord, should run to meet your bashfulness as it were with certain feet of compliance.

9.10.2. Wherefore, I too willing, possess the thing granted, but liberally (for, as I suspect, you yourself sought nothing more of this kind of solace); whom by these letters, no less commendatory than restitutory, I now, already appeased, introduce; yet so that he attend you, obey you, follow you, and so that, if he remain with you, he be judged the servant of neither of us; if perchance he depart, he be sought as a fugitive by both. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.11.1. On account of a little book which you thought sent not to you more than through you, I have received a letter of yours written not to me more than against me. To the reproaches I reply for the equity of the cause, not for the equality of eloquence—although who or how great am I now, that I should presume to plead, you charging an innocent man? Wherefore I at once, in the very beginning, supplicate that this fault, however small it is, be forgiven me, confessing the error of diffidence only, not of pride.

9.11.2. For though the rigour of your censure, in letters as in character, is on both sides to be trembled at by me, I confess nonetheless that, in the unbarring of the very volume and work, that charity which you allege was to me more of a burden; nor do I conjecture this beside what is just, since this force is naturally inborn in the minds of mortals, that, if anything be done amiss, friends indulge it the less, the more they love.

9.11.3. I had written a book, as you pronounce, full and laden with a varied congeries of causes, times, and persons: I should have seemed to do a most impudent thing, if all of it had pleased me so much that I trusted none of it would displease you. Here too, whatever the outcome of the judgement should be, I saw that the account of piety would by no means stand whole on my side, if at least the volume had not been previously brought to you, even if it should not seem offered—under this moderation, of course, that, if perchance I should please, you might not be judged to have been passed over by arrogance; if otherwise, not to have been sought out by importunity.

9.11.4. Nor indeed did I believe I should deprecate, with much labour, the corrupted causes of blushing. Likewise I had known that you knew this—that authors, in publishing their works, are befitted by modesty rather than by boldness, and that the boldness of a reciter wrings points from grim censors more slowly than his trepidation does. Otherwise, if there is anyone who, with the prerogative of confidence, publishes abroad the work of a theme before unheard, he begins to owe public expectation more in return, though he has paid much. Besides, whatever you shall have decreed concerning the tenor of this reply, I have preferred to confess the deed simply rather than to deny it craftily.

9.11.5. Another would have said: "I preferred no one to you, I gave no special letters to anyone; he whom you suspected was preferred departed content with the form of a single letter, and that indeed bringing nothing about the present matter: you, complaining that you were passed over, wearied with three most loquacious pages, are stirred rather to nausea, while you frequently linger over the empty words of an insipid reading. Add that even in this, which perhaps you did not note, the account of your reverence and merits was kept—that, just as you among the chairs of the other bishops, so your heading is first in the book. His name sounds scarcely once only, and on a page assigned to himself; yours, besides those allotted to you, frequently lights up others'."

9.11.6. Join to these that, if anything there pleases even casually, you read it through by my counsel, he at some time by your benefit—he who, pressed in vain by envy of my little gift, has not yet, as I suspect, come to the faculty of reading, when you yourself have long ago come to the abundance of transcribing. I say this, as though he were not going to deem the membranes autograph, if at least he should receive even a copy of what you had earlier run through; for in the things which you have handled, neither rarity of punctuation nor frequency of barbarisms will be blamed. Indeed, in the end, openly the very property seems transmitted even to you, to whom the use has been transmitted without the prescription of a fixed time, and who can use the aforesaid little book so long that your memory shall enclose it no more than your little cabinet.

9.11.7. These things, and more than these, perhaps someone would say; but I pass over all, and prefer to pray for pardon rather than to deprecate guilt, if this is believed to be such. The negligence too of the present letters I now neither excuse: first, because, even if I wish, I can write little more elegantly; next, because, the work of the little book finished, my mind, about at last to keep holiday, now disdains to polish what it dissembles to make public.

9.11.8. But yet, since I yield to you sufficiently—and that deservedly (for what is like?)—in all things, since in another kind of virtues you, now for fifty years, have, as often as you have made the attempt, been preferred not only to bishops of your own age but even to the ancient ones, I wish you to know that, although you should shake the stars with your complaints and implore the ashes and embers of our forefathers in testimony of wounded charity, I will not draw back my foot from your conflict, if there is to be a contest about mutual love; because, as in other things, so it is most foul of all to be surpassed in affection—which sure profession, willy-nilly, is repaid to those reproaches of yours (which surpass, indeed, all the honeys of blandishments) not beyond what is just.

9.11.9. Behold, you have a letter almost as garrulous as you were demanding; although they are all, if any anywhere are, most loquacious. For into the audacity of discoursing whom would you not yourself compel? You who—of all men of letters (for of myself I am silent), though they affect to be hidden, so draw forth their talents, as the sun's ray is wont to draw water hidden in the bowels of the earth through the absorbing atoms. By the sting of which light not only the subtle sand or the diggable earth is penetrated, but, if by the pressure of a rocky mountain the vein of hidden springs be concealed, the nature of heavenly secrets, more violent, opens the arcanum of the liquid element. So, holy man, if you have perceived any of the studious to be either quiet or modest, or lurking in the obscure recess of an unknown fame, these the clarity of your eloquence, by an artful conversation, while it compels, also makes public.

9.11.10. But whither a little more than is the custom? Let us return to the cause, upon whose superfluous babbling, since I obey, I pray that you, appeased, impart to me, confessing my errors, the elements of pardon by your indulgence—although, by whatever holy joy and communion is yours, you would rejoice the more copiously, if the defence of my fault rather than satisfaction were borne to you written. Deign to be mindful of me, my Lord Bishop.

9.12.1. A page set out from you came into our hands, which draws much resemblance to the Spanish salt cut in the Tarraconensian ridges. For, to one perusing it, it is bright and salty, nor yet on this very account less honeyed—but speech sweet, and keen in its propositions: for so it delights by its eloquence what it troubles by its command, since, measuring too little what order I follow, it asks of us now new poems. First, from the very outset of my religious profession, I renounced this exercise chiefly, because, of course, it could be accommodated to lightness, if the levity of verses had occupied me, whom the gravity of actions had begun to regard.

9.12.2. Then, besides, it is agreed that every work, if it rest in a long interval, is recovered with difficulty. For who would not know that the greatest grace comes to all craftsmen or arts by use, and that, when accustomed pursuits are not frequented, arms in bodies, talents in arts grow black with rust? Whence too is that—that the bow, when seized late or seldom, rebels the more against the hand, the ox against the yoke, the horse against the bridle. Besides, the modesty that is the companion of our sloth inclines my opinion to this—that I am as much ashamed to compose a new poem, after I have run through three Olympiads in silence, as I am loth.

9.12.3. Here likewise it is a sin that even things difficult to do be denied to you, whose affection it the less befits to be cheated, the more steadfastly it fears no rebuff. We shall therefore hold to a certain middle course; and as I shall now compose no new epigrams, so I shall send you letters, if any shall be lying stuffed with verse—namely, before the necessity of my present office—asking that you be not so far a prevaricator of justice as to suppose that I shall never refrain from writing of this kind. For I should be no less increased by your suffrage, if perchance you should deign to deem me now modest rather than witty. Farewell.

9.13.1. Your opinion of my verses is indeed, I confess, so applaudable of old, so favourable, that you think me to be compared with all the most choice of poets, certainly to be preferred to very many. I would believe you, did you not, as much as you are wise, so also much love me. Hence it is that your charity can lie about my praises, and cannot deceive.

9.13.2. Besides this, you ask that I send you some Asclepiads, formed on the Horatian anvil, on which you may exercise yourself by reciting them over your drink. I obey what is enjoined, although, if ever, now most of all I am pressed and occupied by the prosaic kind of speaking. In short, you will prove that, among us, the studies of metres for the most part grow cold; for it is not easy to do well one and the same thing both, and seldom.
Long ago we played at smooth hendecasyllables,
the thumb worn down upon the reeds,
which you might sing more nimbly for choriambics,
the foot shaken out;
but you wish that our track henceforth
run along the causeway of the Calabrian path,
where Flaccus turned his lyric horses
to the Pindaric melody with quill-mighty reins,
while the string is struck in Glyconic metre,
and also in Alcaic or Pherecratean
joined to Lesbian or anapaestic,
blooming through the eclogues of varied song
with the many-coloured violets of words.
That, grant pardon, is hard for the ancient bards
to fashion, hard for me too,
that a mouth sounding diverse epigrams
should in no way stumble, because of frequent letters,
which a masculine diction forbids
to grow wanton in song and luxuriant measures.
That scarcely Leo, king of the Castalian choir,
scarcely Lampridius, who follows him, could do,
declaiming under the weight of a twin style
before his Bordeaux disciples.
Does this befit me and you? Spare your jests, I pray;
I beg, let care preserve to the end the modesty
promised to the orator's work,
than which nothing is worse, if it should be at once
rigid in its first parts, soft in its last.

9.13.3. Nay rather, as often as you shall be cheered by the feast of a more sumptuous table, give yourself to religious narratives, which I more approve; let frequent conversation serve to bring these forth, anxious hearing to learn them again. Certainly, if to these most wholesome diversions, as one still young, you are too tepidly bent, borrow at least from the Platonist of Madaura the formulas of convivial questions, and, that you may be rendered more instructed, solve these set before you, propose these to be solved, and exercise yourself in these studies even while you are at leisure.

9.13.4. But since mention of banquets has once fallen in, and you so diligently demand of me a poem composed for another cause and person, that you can no longer have me as a hesitator over publishing it, receive willingly what, in the times of Augustus Majorian—when at the request of a certain comrade we had come together to dinner—I poured out, suddenly, upon a book of Peter, the master of letters, suddenly brought forth, my fellow-companions too, while the king of the feast wove delays about the ordering of the fish-sauce, composing equal verses—Domnulus, Severianus, and Lampridius (I have said this boastfully; nay, better ones); whom the emperor, summoned from all the cities into one city, the inviter into one dinner, had by chance drawn together.

9.13.5. The only delay was while we apportion the kinds of metres by lot. For it pleased us, for the charity of the company, that, although the same matter of writing existed for all, yet the epigrams of each should not be brought forth in one kind, lest any of us, who had spoken more meagrely than the rest, should be bitten first by modesty, afterward by envy; for it is more quickly recognized, in any reciter, whether he sings in the metre in which the rest sing, and writes too with the same talent. But you will then more opportunely praise the things appended, when you have wholly indulged in leisure. For it is not just that you begin, as a censor, to discuss with severity what a friend could not dictate at leisure.
Come, youth assembled,
the place, the hour, the table, the cause
bid that you exalt to the stars, with your studies,
this volume, which you learn
both by ear and by mouth.
Peter is to be read by you,
an author sufficiently instructed
in either discipline.
Let us therefore celebrate, brothers,
the holy festival of letters.
Let a genial furnishing
pass the falling day
with feast, cups, and dances.
Bring the ruddy embroidery on fine linen
and the ruddy purples,
which the Meliboean wave dyes,
the cauldron re-boiling them,
that with unmixed colour it may enrich
the thirsty fleece;
let the foreign furniture give
the woven mountain-ranges of Ctesiphon and Niphates
and the swift beasts
on the spreading cloth,
whose fury the well-feigned wound
sharpens with scarlet,
and, as from a piercing dart,
bloodless gore comes forth;
where, grim and bent back through art,
his face turned upward,
the Parthian goes by horse and returns by spear,
fleeing and routing
the images of beasts.
Let the table bear linens fairer than snow,
and be covered with laurels
and ivy and green vine-shoots;
let capacious baskets bring
cytisus, crocus, asters,
cassia, privet, marigolds,
and let them paint the side-board and the couches
with fragrant garlands.
Let a hand anointed with the juice of balsam
tame the bristling hair,
and let the smoke, rich with the Arabs' harvest,
seek the high roofs;
and likewise, as night comes on,
let a numerous lamp be raised
upon the high parts of the vault,
amid the gleaming panels;
and the lanterns, knowing not
oil and gluey fats,
with swelling belly pour forth
the balsam-juice.
Let the bearers, bending their heads
under the embossed metal,
bear on laden shoulders
the prouder feasts.
Let bowls, cups, basins
ally Falernian with nard,
and let the sewn rose crown
the tripods and the goblets.
It is pleasant to go among the garlands
fanning the alabaster vases;
it is pleasant too, with wandering whirl,
to give broken limbs to the dance,
or to feign the trembling Bacchantes
with foot, dress, and voice.
Let twin-harboured Corinth send back
its harp-girls, learned in stage and palaestra,
to the warm workshops,
whose singing fingers,
the tongue sounding alike,
weary, in the place of a plectrum,
the living strings by their stroke.
Give too the piped bronzes,
dear to the naked Satyrs;
give the hoarse flute-players,
through whose throats of the palate,
to be blown again with rattling cheeks,
the pipe's breath groans;
give things sung under the comic sock,
give things spoken under the tragic buskin,
give whatever the advocates,
give whatever the poets too
clamour in varied action:
Peter surpasses both these and those.
We hold the work brought forth,
which, weaving with art the double metre,
ran the rough way and the
labyrinthine paths;
but, labouring in all things
and approved by all,
he snatches the palm hence and thence,
and is borne through learned mouths.
Far from here let us drive both Hippocrene
and the Aganippic founts
and tuneful Apollo
with the attendant Muses,
and Minerva,
as though the patroness of singing;
remove things feigned in speech:
one God bestows these things.
The power of the diadem stood amazed
at the man speaking,
the toga, the soldier, the equestrian order,
and the people of Romulus;
and still the forums, temples,
fields, and camps revolve their "Bravo,"
above these the Po gives a roar
for its foster-child, and the love
of the Ligurian cities.
A like favour echoes
through the cities of the Rhône,
and the fierceness of the Iberians
will imitate the Gauls.
Nor, delaying on this axle,
will it swiftly make for the fields,
but be borne off by the east wind and the north and the south
and the west winds.

9.13.6. Behold, while I ask what you sing, I myself have sung. For such trifles, gnawed by mice in the lowest depth of my writing-case, I bring forth into the light after about twenty years—such as Ulysses, absent for an equal time, could have found when he returned home. Accordingly I ask that you willingly forgive the present sportive things; but this I enjoin neither bashfully nor impudently, that what I myself pronounced concerning the whole book of my friend, this you, as though solicited by the necessity of the example, may feel concerning mine. Farewell.

9.14.1. I am doubly tormented, that each of us is held by his bed; for nothing is harder than when friends, though present, are divided by the common share of a sickness; since, if it happen that they do not even lie in one chamber, there are no words, no solaces, no exchange in turn of mutual entreaty: so to each there is a huge grief, and that more on account of the other; for you can little, though yourself sick, fear for yourself when one you love is in peril.

9.14.2. But God, most loving son, has shaken out for me, fearing for you, a most violent scruple, because you begin to recover your former strength. For you are said now to wish to rise, and—what I more desire—now to be able; you at least consult me in such a way, and, with an almost premature solicitude, you now exercise me, as though wholly vigorous, with the little questions of letters, desiring more to hear, though still sick, Socrates disputing about morals than Hippocrates about bodies; wholly worthy that Rome should cherish you with applauding arms, and at whose reciting the wedge-shaped benches of the resounding Athenaeum should be shaken.

9.14.3. Which without doubt you would attain, if the condition of peace and place permitted that you be there educated, mingled in the company of the senatorial youth. Of which glory and fame alike I judge you capable from the quality of your oration, in which, as you most becomingly recited it lately—the things, indeed, which you had written extempore—the benevolent admired, the proud marvelled, the skilled lingered. But lest we impudently press your modesty of our own accord with excessive praises, we write the heraldings of you more justly concerning you than to you. Let us rather bring in this, whence is the cause of our discourse.

9.14.4. So you ask, through your post-boy, which verses I call recurrent, that I may quickly explain, but under an example. These, of course, are recurrent which, the metre standing and the letters not moved from their place, are read back from the end to the top just as from the beginning to the end. So is that ancient one: "Roma tibi subito motibus ibit amor." And that: "sole medere pede, ede perede melos."

9.14.5. Likewise those are held for recurrent which, the law of the feet kept, even if not through single letters, yet through single words, are folded back—as is one distich of mine (such as indeed I think I have read many of many men's), which I played about a little stream, which, fed by the sudden falling of storms, and having overpassed the public causeway with a rough flood, had inundated the fields beneath the road; though about soon to lay aside its insane abundance, since indeed, swollen with the appendages of the rains, no weights of an upper perennial vein were inflating it.

9.14.6. So there (for I had come as a traveller), while I seek the bank rather than the ford, having jested with such an epigram, I went over the back of the turbulent torrent with at least these feet: "Praecipiti modo quod decurrit tramite flumen / tempore consumptum iam cito deficiet." This, if you run it back, is read thus: "Deficiet cito iam consumptum tempore flumen / tramite decurrit quod modo praecipiti." There you have verses, whose plan you may marvel at syllable by syllable; for the rest, the pomp which they do not have they will not teach. I suspect I have sufficiently shown what you thought ought to be inquired.

9.14.7. You yourself do something like, if you restore things set before you and, on the other side, unfold by repeating what you expound; for there hangs over you the votive return of a most celebrated theme—namely, the praise to be delivered, which you meditate, of Julius Caesar—a matter so grand that, if any of the students should be the most copious, he ought in it to guard against nothing more than saying anything too little. For if the things which are written about the titles of the unconquered dictator in the Paduan volumes be omitted, who, by speaking, would equal the works of Suetonius, who the history of Juventius Martialis, or who, lastly, the journal of Balbus?

9.14.8. But these things we reserve for your tablets. It is rather our office to set the benches for the hearers, to prepare the ears for the roars about to thunder, and, while you tell the virtues of others, for us to tell yours. Nor would you fear that I shall summon any Catonian judges, who cover now their envy, now their ignorance, under the veil of an assumed severity. Although pardon is owed to the unskilled; for the rest, whoever is so bad that he understands things well written and yet does not praise them—him the good understand and yet do not praise.

9.14.9. Accordingly I absolve your cares from this fear: all will hear with favour, all with warmth, and we shall enjoy together the joys which your face will refresh. For very many will praise your eloquence, very many your talent, all your modesty; for it will be borne to no less praise that a young man—or, what is fairer, almost still a boy—brings back from the wrestling-school of a public examination the suffrages of his character as much as of his letters. Farewell.

9.15.1. You prove (nor do I deprecate it) that I have done wrong; I have done wrong, since I have not yet joined to my work any letter under your name. But yet you write that what I erred in will be pardonable, if I send something for you too to sing from the example—because, of course, I sent to my Tonantius letters in double metre, to be of use for a like cause; besides this you complain that my page, if it be loosed into sport, is frequented by hendecasyllables alone. On which matter, the trochaic garrulity suspended, you ask for some little senarii besides. I serve what is enjoined; only do you receive it placidly, whether you prefer to call this very thing an ode or an eclogue. For a metre long unfrequented is woven the more harshly.
You bid, friend, that through our volumes
the fierce iamb resound in more incited measures,
as the trochee hitherto;
and that the spondee add its slow pairs
and fourfold times,
that the wing-footed trimeter
may have a little delay grafted in,
and that swiftest foot resound, mingled in,
well named of old from the Pyrrhic art,
to be placed somewhere in the last position;
and the anapaest, about to give a base to the verse besides,
now in the first part, now in the last,
though it itself be pronounced more absolutely,
when the third following long
cleaves to a twin and short syllable.
Which a common poet scarce avails to temper,
such as you yourself see Sollius to be;
for me the quill goes astray, nor through the hollow mouth
does the wandering tongue fittingly unfold the bent epos;
but Leo would have prepared this more aptly,
Leo, or one who has followed his tracks
in Latin song, since first among the Attic
is he, the survivor of his father, of the Consentii,
who in faith, voice, metres, at the streams of Pegasus,
is said to have sung an all-formed song,
and as often as he set Greek words to verse,
to have held the lofty stars, joined to Pindar,
and, victor, gone over the two-peaked mountain,
second to none among the Delphic caves.
But if either of the bards should fit a Latin song
to the poetic lyre, without the Doric,
you, Flaccus, would draw forth the Venusine quills ineptly,
and, the home-bred swan of Iapygian Aufidus,
when Atax thunders with its own swans,
would, conquered, groan with your white and tuneful neck.
Nor are these the only skilled hearts,
though to the skilled these be more skilled:
Severianus the rhetor would have composed these more loftily,
the African and crafty Domnulus more elegantly,
and the scholar Peter, under rounder Muses,
more keenly—nor would the epistolary style,
everywhere, forbid the man to compose astounding things.
This could always have done it more effectively,
Proculus, sprung from the soil and race of Liguria,
to sound on melodic strokes,
polishing all his witty poems so
that he might challenge Venetian Mantua in favour,
and, himself too equal to Homeric glory,
follow the wheels of Maro with matching art.
But I, justly despicable in heart and mouth,
what should I chatter among these at your asking,
proving the impudence of loquacity
and the wishes of a mind destitute of letters?
But what shall I deny, not terrified by shame?
Love knows not to fear: thence I obeyed.

9.15.2. Forgive one returning to disused things, and one who, for having fulfilled what you had bidden, awaits nothing more than the indulgence of my rarity. For the rest, if you bid me like things hereafter, that I may be made more compliant, you will so take care, in turn for a poem, either to dictate what I may sing or to dance what I may laugh at. Farewell.

9.16.1. If you recall, my lord son, you had enjoined this upon me, that this ninth little book, dedicated particularly to you, should be joined to the other eight which I wrote to Constantius—a man of singular talent, of saving counsel, certainly in public discussions excelling the other eloquent men, whether he decree diverse or like things, by the gifts of a more excellent eloquence. The pledge is fulfilled, not indeed exactly, but at least promptly.

9.16.2. For when, the dioceses being traversed by chance, I came home, if any draft lying carelessly about was contained in rotten and mouldering little papers, a hasty translator, I copied it out swiftly and forcibly, retarded by nothing in the winter season, but that I should at once complete what was bidden, although the unfreezable page hindered the copyist by its frost, and the drop, harder than the pen, which you would have judged, to the impelling fingers, not to flow but to break; even so, however, I took care to discharge my duty before the Favonius should wed, with its warm blast and its natal rains, our twelfth month, which you call the month of Numa.

9.16.3. It remains that, with you as arbiter, we be not required to render back things altogether most discrepant—maturity and speed. For as often as any book is bidden to be written quickly, the author looks for honour not so much from his merit as from his compliance. For the rest, since you pronounce that the iambics I lately sent to Gelasius, a man kind enough, pleased you, through these I will gift you too with the home-bred children of the town of Mytilene.
Now through the alternating sea of speaking
my skiff has driven its bold course,
nor has it feared, in the twofold flood,
to turn the helm.
It has loosed the yard-arms, gathered the high sails,
the hand sets down the little oar, and, the benches
joined to the shore, with a leap it seeks
the sand to be kissed.
Though the muttering chorus of the envious
betray with canine snarl their rage,
it says nothing openly, indeed, and fears
the public votes.
They beat the stern, shake the keel,
fan the rounded gunwales of the sides;
about the mast fly the hisses
of a sinister tongue.
But we, the prow set straight by attendant art,
fearing in nothing the swelling storms,
stand in harbour, having gained
the leaf of a twofold crown,
Which the people of Quirinus granted me,
or which the purple-bearing senate bestowed,
which the consort order of the skilled
in judgements gave,
When Nerva Trajan saw a perpetual statue
set up with my titles,
fixed among the authors
of either library;
And which afterward—seen, as it were, near—after twice five years'
time I received, taking up the honour
which alone once governs at once
the rights of fathers and of people.
Besides the heroic, I have woven many jests
on many patches; the elegiac I have frequently
rolled out, set under six feet,
with double colon.
Now wont to ride through eleven
syllables, I have played the swift, and in the
Sapphic metre often sung, in the quick
iamb rarely.
Nor can I recall how much once
I wrote in the first heat of youth;
whence would that the greater part
could be silenced and hidden!
For, the goal of old age nearer,
the more we are joined to our last years,
the more it shames us now to recall
if our age has played anything light.
Shuddering at which, I have transferred
every kind of care to the cultivation of letters,
lest, being guilty by a too wanton song,
I be guilty by my act;
And lest I rot, dissolved by pleasant sayings,
if I join figure and trappings to my pages,
lest the reputation of a poet
stain the rigour of a cleric.
In short, to any epigram hereafter
I shall not be borne prone, and by tender metre
or grave I shall be compelled hence to bring forth
no song quickly:
Unless perchance I tell the inquisitions
of the persecutors, and the martyrs who, deserving
heaven, have purchased, by the price of death,
the rewards of life.
Of whom let a hymn first chant for me
that one who held the chair of Toulouse,
hurled down from the highest step
of the Capitol;
Whom, denying Jupiter and Minerva
and confessing the good things of Christ's cross,
the raging mob bound to the flank
of an unyoked bull,
That, the ox driven down a steep,
it might scatter his torn corpse in its course,
the crags stained with the warm pulp
of his loosened brain.
After Saturninus I would have the quills sing
those whom I have proved my remaining patrons,
who through anxious labours
helped me in my hardships,
Each of whom now pious words
cannot, by name, contain in verse;
yet whom the strings cannot sound,
our hearts shall sound.

9.16.4. Let us return at the end to the oratorical style, about to finish the present matter in the order once proposed, lest, if we close a prose work with musical epilogues, according to the rules of Flaccus—where the wine-jar began to be fashioned—a pitcher should rather seem to have come out. Farewell.
